#8258. Traversing the Saiga Silk Road

As we skidded off the main road and onto a mud path maintained only by tire treads, lines began to blur.

Flanking our two-track trail were a series of parallel lanes no more than a foot wide, which forked, merged, and crisscrossed our own. In the distance, I saw what looked like a ghost train, faintly visible and thrust forward by howling Siberian winds.

Through borrowed binoculars, I soon got my first glimpse of an ancient tableau, seemingly untouched since Neanderthals roamed the earth. On the far horizon, hundreds of nomadic travelers pierced the frigid air with their ringed horns, inhaling the brittle shards through Snuffleupagus snouts as they sprinted across the desolate steppe.

Watching them charge through the treeless plain at full bore, I was reminded of a saying I’d heard shortly before arriving in this remote corner of Kazakhstan: “The saiga is a freedom-loving animal.”

Since time immemorial, saiga antelope have blazed trails across Central Asia while other civilizations rose and fell around them. They once inhabited a world dominated by woolly mammoths, saber-toothed cats, and giant deer with antlers 12 feet across—and outlived them all. When pioneering human caravans first attempted to navigate this unforgiving land, they considered the saigas to be their guides.

Ahead of my arrival, seasonal rains transformed once-green grasslands into sludge punctuated by tufts of withering brush. Driving through such muck is, I would soon discover, akin to controlled hydroplaning. The steering wheel bucked wildly as our tires swerved, shredding deep into the gunk and desperately gripping anything remotely solid enough to push off from.

In the front seats were Alexandr and Albert, two team members from the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan, or ACBK. Between them, they have more than twenty-five years of experience following saigas across the steppe, and I’d arranged to join them for the western leg of one of their field audits.

Our visit was timed to coincide with the rutting season, a critical part of the year for saigas. This is a gathering time, when antelope from across the region sprint together in massive single-file lines, before congregating for a series of competitive battles and subsequent mating rituals.

For males, it’s a time for strutting and headbutting to demonstrate one’s physical prowess to female onlookers—an activity so energy-intensive that many will forget to eat and keel over from extreme physical exhaustion. For females, this is a time of choosing. In addition to assessing fitness, they pay particular attention to one distinctive feature: a potential mate’s floppy, elongated nose. The saigas’ sniffers are essential for filtering out dust in the semidesert plains and for warming frigid winter air before it reaches their lungs. A large nose is the ultimate sign of virility, so as the males marched into these annual gatherings, they were doing everything they could to accentuate their schnozzes.

Because of the saigas’ preference for large-scale migrations across a landscape almost entirely devoid of trees, they have long been a favorite of global wildlife trackers. The isolation and starkness of the saiga world is a strength when it comes to GPS collars, which deliver a reliable stream of daily pings without risk of visual obstruction. Prior to such breakthroughs, conservationists would sometimes spend weeks roaming the boundless steppe unsuccessfully trying to locate the nomadic herds.

The wildlife sanctuary we were traveling through was created only a year prior, with its boundaries informed by tracking data that Albert and his team personally collected. He seemed pleased that the animals were continuing to use the newly designated space as intended. Standing along the roadside, Alexandr spotted a stream of the famously skittish ungulates wrapping around the contours of the earth. As he did, ripping wind and snow started blowing in sideways—the outer ring of an encroaching storm.

These were no fluffy flakes. This was the harsh, crunchy ice of a walk-in freezer, which instantly hardened our truck’s caked-on mud like liquid nitrogen.

Seemingly unperturbed by the dropping barometer, Albert chirped, “Who’s hungry?” Setting up an impromptu picnic, he and Alexandr dug into a prepared meal of fresh bread, tea, and dried meats of unknown provenance. In a muted attempt to thaw my face, I opted to guzzle spicy instant noodles.

A tradition of nomadism has loomed large in this corner of the world since at least the Early Iron Age. The very word kazakh is thought to be derived from the Turkic word qaz, which means “wanderer” or “vagabond.” For millennia, small human groups routinely migrated to higher altitudes in the hot summer months, where melting snow made for abundant water and greenery, before returning to sheltered valleys ahead of winter’s whipping winds. At various times of the year, disparate nomads would also congregate for formal meetings and large cultural festivals, complete with physical challenges like wrestling and tug-of-war. When the gatherings were finished, the nomads dispersed once again.

Historical analysis has shown that nomads’ seasonal migrations and time-honed transit corridors may have helped pave the way for portions of the Great Silk Road, which was less a singular route than an ever-evolving web of pathways and bypasses that linked together reliable stopovers. At the Silk Road’s peak, this corner of western Kazakhstan along the fertile banks of the Ural River became a vital transcontinental crossroads. To this day, the river still serves as a natural boundary between Asia and Europe, meaning this part of Kazakhstan is, quite literally, where East meets West.

The land above the Caspian Sea also served as a main artery that linked together key transit points. Strategic settlements along the riverbank allowed weary caravans to rest their heads, unwind in large public baths, exchange knowledge, stock up on essential supplies, and regroup before moving onward.

Among overland voyagers traversing the continental divide, saigas have long been spoken of with an almost mythical reverence. Cave paintings of the antelope created as far back as the seventh century BCE depict them as resilient, elusive, and charismatic. Expert navigators who embody the true spirit of a most inhospitable terrain.

In human society, traditional nomadic practices persisted even as the land itself was variously claimed and reclaimed by Turkic tribes, Genghis Khan, and the Russian Empire. Only with the rise of the Soviet Union in the twentieth century did mandatory sedentarization efforts successfully manage to lock nomadic people in place, force them to farm, and extinguish a cultural flame that had burned brightly for millennia. Denied the ability to live in perpetual motion, people’s navigational muscles began to atrophy.

This transition was viewed by many as an inevitable shift toward “modernization,” but it also represented a significant diversion from our own history as a species. Of the roughly 300,000 years that Homo sapiens have existed, we spent the first 288,000 of them living in small, mobile groups that followed the migratory patterns of other animals. Forcing nomads into agricultural plots was also a colossal failure because much of the steppe soil was unsuitable for growing crops, which is why so many people were nomadic in the first place. Iconic filmmaker Werner Herzog once remarked that “whatever went wrong and makes our civilization something doomed is the departure from the nomadic life.”

Whether by choice or necessity, most Kazakh people now lead stationary lives in urban centers. The world that nomads once freely roamed has also been feverishly transformed, not only by agriculture but through the construction of new roads and railways.

For the saigas, whose nomadic days never ceased, these new layers now represent an existential threat.

With the weather taking a turn for the worse, Albert and Alexandr ultimately decided to call it a day and start fresh in the morning. After a blistering drive through whiteout conditions, we hunkered down in a tiny village less than 10 miles from the Russian border, where Albert pulled out his laptop and showed me how saiga movements have changed over the years.

“They would routinely trek hundreds of miles as part of an expansive migratory route across the Eurasian steppe,” he said. “Saigas could be found from the Caucasus Mountains to Mongolia, and everywhere in between.”

For millennia, they lived with few barriers and obstructions on the landscape. Then, seemingly overnight, rattling railways and roaring roads began to crisscross the region, fragmenting the saigas into smaller, more isolated groups. As the interior steppe got more accessible to vehicles and passengers, development begat more development.

On his screen, Albert clicked open a recent map that showed how a population of GPS-collared saigas once routinely traveled deep into Uzbekistan before being unceremoniously clipped off by a new rail line in 2014. The data from the years prior to the railway’s construction showed a flurry of squiggly lines representing individual animals zipping back and forth with the seasons. The post-construction slide showed those same animals spinning around despondently on the northern side of the tracks, while the fresh grasses and water they had come to rely on withered away to the south.

Such interruptions can lead to a complete collapse in spatial knowledge—a loss that science writer Ben Goldfarb once wrote is “as thorough as the erasure of a language.” Just as human nomads forced to stay in one place eventually lost connection to the physical landmarks of their ancestors’ journeys, young saigas learn where they can reliably find food and shelter, as well as places to stay away from, through active participation and observation. This cultural exchange keeps their world in orbit and is one of the reasons they have been successful at navigating a terrain fatal to so many before them. As the land they know is cleaved and partitioned, whole stretches of the Saiga Silk Road begin to fade from memory.

To unwind this damage, Albert’s team has partnered with the Kazakh government to construct dozens of saiga-friendly crossing points, where slightly sloping dirt ramps rise up to match the height of the train tracks, making it appear from a distance as though there’s a natural gap in the rail line. Cattle-guard fences positioned far away from the crossings ensure that trains and saigas never actually run into each other at these intersections, which would shatter the illusion of safety.

ACBK has also worked with the Uzbek government to reshape its border fences from a barbed-wire wall to an X-shaped barricade that blocks vehicles from driving through but leaves just enough space for saigas to pass. Over time, Albert hopes such efforts can rebuild the trust necessary for them to confidently return to a plateau they once relied on.

The next morning, I was astonished by how austere the steppe looked compared with the day before. Gone was the slippery muck and browning grasses of shifting seasons, replaced by a blanket of crunchy snow. Against this stark black-and-white backdrop, the fresh crystals functioned like fingerprint dust, illuminating the only remaining pops of color: the rust-red streaks of human and nonhuman pathways in the dirt.

Parked in an otherwise empty tract of prairie land, we watched in stunned silence as thousands of saigas seized the day, flying like banshees across the periphery, their hooves gouging the frozen crust and stamping pigment into an earthen canvas.

As I gazed east toward the colorless horizon, I tried to envision how it might have looked in the thirteenth century, when this corner of the world boasted a vast network of caravanserai, or road inns, where exhausted travelers could rest and recover before continuing onward into the great unknown.

I pondered what it must have felt like for an intrepid merchant to know that they would not see another human being for many days, maybe weeks. To be fearful of what you may soon encounter, but take solace that the space between is not wholly empty. For there is life beyond humanity’s margins, and among nonhuman communities, that in-between space is the center of everything. That, I imagined, must have offered some measure of assurance that the road ahead, perilous though it may be, is well traveled.

This essay was adapted from the new nonfiction travelogue The Hidden Nations of Animals and is published here exclusively for Adventure Journal, with permission from Penguin Random House.

#8257. Secrets for Deer Hunting the Big Woods, According to a North Country Expert

Published Nov 3, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Hunting whitetails in the North Country forests of New England and the Upper Midwest is an undeniably challenging pursuit. Up there the landscapes are massive, think tens of thousands of acres of forest. Food sources and deer sign are more subtle. There are no edges of agricultural fields to target, and there might not even be stands of oaks dropping acorns. Lastly, deer densities are low, with some areas having maybe five deer per square mile.

It’s within this environment that Brett Joy, a member of the Just Hunt Club, has made a name for himself. Using a mix of old-school and modern hunting strategies, Joy has found success killing mature big woods bucks season after season.

I sat down with him for the most recent episode of the Outdoor Life podcast to learn his strategies for targeting mature bucks in the northwoods. Even if you don’t hunt big woods deer yourself, you can learn from Joy’s tactics and experience.

Joy uses digital maps to identify areas where two or three types of habitat converge.

“Whitetails, whether they’re in a cornfield in Iowa or on a mountain in New Hampshire, are edge habitat creatures,” Joy says. “They live on the edges, but those edges can look a lot different depending on where you are in the whitetails’ range.”

In the big woods, look for edges between hardwoods and softwoods, swamps and mature timber, mature timber and early successional growth (recently logged areas). Once you’ve identified these spots, scout them in person. Ideally, you’ll be a mile or more away from any road.

Joy believes that because the habitat is so vast in the big woods, bucks tend to have larger home ranges and core areas. They also have a variety of bedding areas — even in the early season. Whereas in the agricultural country, mature bucks tend to have only a couple woodlots and thickets where they like to bed.

“Our deer could bed on any different point of a mountain in any cut, in a swamp on any given day,” Joy says. “[Those bedding areas] could be miles apart day to day. They’re almost more of a nomadic deer … but they do have areas that they come back to year after year.”

The key is that even if you’re in a buck’s core zone, you might not see him for a week or more.

Like everywhere else in whitetail country, during the rut big woods bucks will travel between doe groups searching for does in estrus.

“But here, you may have only three does that live within 500 acres,” Joy says. So bucks have to cover more ground and do more checking. And this need to travel long distances makes rutting bucks more vulnerable.

“I like to hunt them during the rut and really focus on those areas they frequent when they’re traveling from A to B, or I hunt near one of those doe groups … and if you can find a big primary scrape or pinch point within the core area of those does, you can catch bucks going through there semi-consistently.”

Trail cameras are a critical component of Joy’s strategy because there’s essentially no visibility in the areas that he hunts. In other words, there are not places to glass from in the big woods.

“If I cared less about what buck I was targeting, I could hunt sign and not use cameras and be successful, but I really do rely on them heavily for my strategy,” he says.

Joy positions most of his cameras on large community scrapes because they serve as social gathering spots that will attract deer in vast landscapes. On top of that, Joy focuses on secluded, high-elevation areas that bucks tend to prefer.

Joy aims to run cameras from about October 15 through December 15, which gives him the full range of rut activity.

When you’re hunting the rut in the big woods, you need to have a good understanding of peak rut activity dates.

“What dictates everything is does coming into estrus,” Joy says. “And those bucks absolutely know those dates in this landscape and they will show up checking those doe groups on the same few days year after year.”

Joy conducted an in-depth trail camera survey using several years worth of his trail camera photos, plus his buddy’s photos to identify peak deer activity during the rut. He found that peak activity in his area was November 19th.

He then paired his trail cam data data with a biologist’s data on fawn conception dates in New Hampshire and he found that the peak conception date was November 19 as well.

“If I had to pick five or seven days, I’d put November 19th right in the middle of it,” Joy says.

Joy adds that he hasn’t witnessed a shutdown in activity due to lockdown. Bucks are covering the most ground during daylight during peak breeding dates.

But peak activity is different throughout whitetail country. You must examine your own trail camera photos and examine historical data to nail down the key dates where you hunt.

Read Next: North Woods Legend Hal Blood on Snow Tracking Bucks

“Now to kill deer in these landscapes you can’t just expect to hunt one weekend,” Joy says. You need probably a week of hunting and you need to hunt for the entire week, dark to dark, he says.

Joy will set up different stands within an area for different wind directions, but once he picks an area he sticks with it and does not jump around from spot to spot — even if he’s not seeing deer right away.

“Sometimes I don’t make a decision about where I’m going to sit until the day before … I’ll wait until I have all the information on a particular spot, but once I decide to [hunt there], that’s it. There’s no deviating. Once you start to doubt and jump around, you’re done,” Joy says. “The day you’re not there is the day he’ll come by.”

If you have good trail camera data and historical data on a spot, it makes it easier to commit to it for a week of hunting. Other keys to staying in the hunt long-term are: efficient access to your stand, good clothing to keep you warm, quality food to eat throughout the week, plenty of rest at night, and staying hydrated. Most importantly, you’ve got to keep the faith.

“Sitting in the cold for 11 or 12 hours a day, day after day, it really does wear on you and you start to doubt yourself and doubt your spot. You start to become negative, and once that stuff compounds … you’re not going to be there when that buck comes by.”

If you are able to stay patient and stick it out, there’s a good chance that an old northwoods buck will eventually walk by. And no matter how big his rack is, he’ll be a true trophy whitetail.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

#8256. There Are Over 40 Resorts Planning To Open In November—Here’s Where Experts Say Conditions Will Be Best

Mammoth Mountain opening day 2025 (Photo: Courtesy of Mammoth Mountain)

Some folks may think skiing in November is crazy: the snow is rarely good, and the mere thrill of lifts spinning often attracts crowds larger than downhill capacity should allow.

It can be difficult to know where, if anywhere, it is worth skiing in November. While resorts are making snow around the clock, the decision to open boils down to weather.

For Colorado skiers, the weather may finally be on your side. According to Open Snow meteorologist Joel Gratz, November is set to start with a “bang.” He predicts a storm arriving Sunday will drop 6 to 12 inches on nearly all mountains, with some spots seeing up to 20. Did someone say powder day?!

Several Colorado resorts are opening their lifts before Halloween is over. Arapahoe Basin opened Oct. 28, Keystone follows on Oct. 30, and Wolf Creek on Oct. 31. Snow is thin at all three for now, but their high elevations should set them up for a stronger start to November.

Breckenridge and Copper Mountain are planning to open on Nov. 6, and if the snow comes in like Gratz is predicting, their opening days could feature more than just a white ribbon of death.

A little later into the month, Vail and Eldora are both planning Nov. 13 opening dates. It’s too early to tell if temperatures will preserve the snow from earlier storms, but as long as cold air remains, these are resorts to keep on your radar for potentially decent skiing.

Neighboring Utah resorts aren’t expected to receive as fruitful a snow bounty. They’ll see the same storm as Colorado, with the highest accumulations on Sunday, says Open Snow forecaster Evan Thayer. “Cooler air will eventually lower snow levels, with some decent accumulations possible up high.”

As of the time of publishing, Brian Head is planning on opening on Nov. 6. If Thayer’s prediction is accurate, the Southern Utah resort could see “decent accumulations” on its highest peaks. Alta, Park City, and Solitude are all planning on opening on Nov. 20. It’s too early to say how these resorts will fare, but cold temperatures will be the biggest asset.

California skiers will have to wait a bit longer. Open Snow forecaster Bryan Alleretto predicts the Tahoe region’s snowy start will likely come after Nov. 10, which could be good timing for Mammoth Mountain, set to open Nov. 20. Mammoth isn’t a Tahoe resort, but it tends to share weather patterns with those to the north.

The East Coast has had a warm fall, but that could change. There’s no official snow report yet, but Maine’s Sugarloaf plans to reopen Nov. 20, likely making it the region’s first resort to welcome skiers back. Vermont’s Sugarbush follows on Nov. 21, while nearby Killington, which often opens early, hasn’t announced a date as of press time.

#8255. Whatever You Think of Him, Mark Dowdle Is Built for the Backyard Ultra

At lap 87 of the Last Soul Backyard Ultra in Bornheim, Germany, this August, Mark Dowdle transformed (or regressed, he’s not entirely sure) into the football and lacrosse player he was in college.

To be fair, Ayyoub “Ello” El Osrouti pretty much started it. A backyard ultra, as you probably know by now, is a last-person-standing race not much different from “The Long Walk”—the movie about 100 boys who walk until there’s one left—except the runners in backyard races aren’t shot after they drop.

Now at 4 a.m. on August 18—three days and 15 hours into the race—it was just down to El Osrouti and Dowdle, who were engaged in a Hamilton-like duel to determine the winner. Ello busted out of the gate. The German had been trying to run faster laps to break Dowdle, but this was, by comparison, a sprint. Dowdle, deviating from his tactic of running his own race, decided to stay right with him.

Dowdle completed the lap in 38 minutes—his fastest of the race by over 5 minutes. El Osrouti got up and finished four minutes later, also his fastest lap.

But about half way through the lap, El Osrouti stopped and sat down. Dowdle stopped, too, and just stared at him in silence. It was both competitive and a little chilling, like Dowdle thought the Last Soul race was a literal invitation to collect his competitors’ souls along the way.

Dowdle’s behavior left many of his hundreds of thousands of followers on Instagram, Youtube, and TikTok a little stunned. The 29-year-old Minnesotan has become a wildly popular Internet figure through dishing out zen advice and positivity. Rich Roll, the addict turned endurance athlete who serves up mindfulness every week on his podcast, called Dowdle a “changemaker” when he had Dowdle on the show. There was a good reason for it: Basically every time Dowdle took a breath, he said something enlightening or inspiring about hard work, endurance, or self-improvement.

With two backyard ultra wins in 2026 alone, there’s little doubt that Dowdle is one of this year’s ultrarunning breakout stars, partly because of his success in the backyard format and partly because of his social media savvy. But he didn’t get that way by reading scripted platitudes on TikTok; Dowdle isn’t faking that zen.

When I told him about the Taco Bell 50K and how it attracted those who wouldn’t normally even consider running an ultra, he said, “people want to be challenged. Sometimes they just don’t know it yet.” Even when he was a football and lacrosse player at the University of St. Thomas in Saint Paul, Minnesota, drinking way too much and trying to please others at the expense of himself, he would think about the meaning of life and why people do the things they do. He attributes his personal growth to running, but also to journaling.

“These are the kinds of things I think about all the time,” Dowdle said. “I was constantly thinking about this connection between words and action and who I wanted to be.”

Dowdle works as a motivational speaker now. But deep down, he’s got an edge.

It’s that edge that makes him stand out (and ruffle feathers) in a sport known for its kumbaya positivity, especially the camaraderie-focused backyard ultra community. Dowdle likes being a little weird and competitive and even scary: He once made a YouTube video called “Ultrarunning Has A Mark Dowdle Problem.” He compares himself to Dennis Rodman, the wildly divisive and brilliant NBA player.

“I’m sure that some of these other guys who are competitive will want to put that competition right back on me,” Dowdle said. “I welcome that.”

His friend and rival Harvey Lewis seems like a golden retriever to Dowdle’s heeler. Dowdle sort of agrees with that comparison and sort of doesn’t. He points out that he and Lewis aren’t that different. (Lewis agrees with him, for what it’s worth.)

“I think Harvey Lewis is competitive in a way that’s much tricker to identify,” Dowdle said. “But I don’t hide it. There are times I don’t care. I’ll show everything on my sleeve.”

Lewis believes that Dowdle’s zen, more than his competitiveness, is what’s carried him to so much recent success. On October 17, 2026, they came together as teammates: Lewis, 50, and Dowdle lined up as part of a U.S. team of 15 against the world’s best at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship. Team USA competed on the Big’s Backyard Ultra course in Beltbuckle, Tennessee, the original backyard ultra devised by Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell. Dowdle went on to run 107 laps, or 446 miles—a personal best—to lead Team USA to victory over Australia. Lewis ran 83 laps.

The Backyard Ultra World Team Championship is held every two years, alternating with the individual world championship. The 2026 race began at 6 a.m. Mountain Time on Saturday, October 17, with 69 national teams competing simultaneously around the world.

The format is simple: Each team of 15 runners runs a 4.167-mile loop every hour, on the hour. The country with cumulatively the most loops completed across all 15 runners wins the team title. Team USA races on the original backyard ultra course in Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee.

Mark Dowdle led Team USA to the win with a cumulative 1,120 laps (yards) to defeat Australia by 51 yards. He was the last American standing with 107 laps, or 446 miles—a personal best. Belgium’s Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts broke the individual backyard ultra world record by each running 124 yards (512 miles) before deciding to call it quits due to boredom, on-the-ground photographer Jacob Zocherman reports.

Since its inauguration in 2020, Belgium and the U.S. have each won two team titles.

Lewis said Dowdle’s “why” is perhaps the strongest he’s ever seen. It “cements his discipline and his unwavering desire to not give up.”

“Mark has a great energy force,” Lewis said. “He has a level of enthusiasm that’s immeasurable.”

But what, exactly, is an energy force? Is it zen or competitiveness? Dowdle likes to ask it another way: Why can’t it be both?

Take a wild guess who inspired Dowdle as a collegiate football and lacrosse player to turn his life around and start running. It wasn’t Joe Rogan, but if that was your first guess, you’re on the right track.

Feeling sorry for himself on the bus ride home after losing two of three lacrosse games his senior year, he listened to David Goggins on Joe Rogan’s podcast. Goggins talked about how running carved him into the person he was today. The way he bragged about pissing blood, shitting himself, and eating only saltine crackers during his long runs spoke to Dowdle. Dowdle already knew he needed to change.

He went for a run when they got back to campus—even though it was 2 a.m.

If Goggins lit the fire, James Lawrence, the Iron Cowboy, stoked it. Lawrence had completed the 50/50/50 challenge, or 50 Ironman-length triathlons in 50 days across 50 states. The way he leaned on his family during that journey spoke to Dowdle. Dowdle, to this day, gives all the credit to his wife, Lucy, for centering him and scolding him whenever he acts, for lack of a better description, too much like a bro.

Dowdle tried for many years to make it as a running guru—some might say influencer—and ultrarunner. He found some limited success. Runner’s World interviewed him in 2023 for his calendar challenge, when he ran the number of miles corresponding to the day of the month, for a full month. (For example, 26 miles on the 26th.) By the beginning of 2026, he had 40,000 Instagram followers and a modest apparel sponsorship that netted him $200 a month. And then he entered the BPN Go One More backyard ultra this April.

Dowdle had already won the Arrowhead 135-miler in January, finishing in 35:48:00—a four-hour improvement over his 2025 fourth-place finish. But he chalked that up to his ability to withstand the Minnesota winter conditions that dropped to minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit.

The BPN Go One More was another story; he hadn’t even made it to 100 miles in a backyard ultra before. He could sense other peoples’ doubts—they didn’t drive him, but they did irritate him a little. He mumbled at one point that they “had no fucking idea.”

Dowdle ended up running 306 miles in 73 hours of rainy and muddy conditions, and the way he did it captivated people: He looked fresh and happy most of the time, like he was playing tag on the playground. In a few days, his Instagram following jumped to 108,000, and brand deals were knocking at his door. He also began booking keynote speaking events, sometimes for conferences that he helped set up the year before for one of his odd jobs to get by while he pursued running.

He proved that BPN was no fluke two months later, finishing second to Lewis at the Mid-State Mile, a last-person standing event in Franklin, Tennessee.

But Last Soul sent him into a new stratosphere. After their fateful showdown on lap 87, Dowdle and El Osrouti dueled for another six hours. And despite the German banking a cumulative five hours of extra rest over the course of the race, after that 93rd lap he gave out. Dowdle ran the final lap solo to win the race with 94 loops, or 391.7 miles. The race attracted 10 million viewers to the livestream and more than 100,000 at any one time, attention that Lewis called “freakishly different” than any other ultra in history, even Western States or Rachel Entrekin’s historic overall win at the Cocodona 250.

After Last Soul, Dowdle’s Instagram following jumped from 108,000 to over 400,000.

“It’s been everything I’ve been trying to build for several years now,” Dowdle said. “But nothing really has changed. It’s sort of weird because I’ve been saying the same thing now that I have over the past seven years. But people are willing to listen more when I go 94 hours in a backyard.”

Dowdle, a Christian who has described his goal in races to experience suffering in a way that brings him closer to Jesus Christ and to others, says he’s handled his newfound success because of his wife. Everyone, he said, should get a Lucy. On the way home from the BPN race, Lucy saw his phone blowing up and reminded him that many of those people were loving him because of what he just did, but that she and his friends loved him for who he was.

Dowdle’s breakthrough would not be possible without the backyard ultra format, and not just because he’s one of the best in the world at it. The race, as Lewis alluded to, is insanely popular: What started as another one of Laz’s harebrained ideas with the Big’s Backyard Ultra in 2011 has ballooned to over 1,000 independent backyard ultras across the globe.

Lewis was perhaps the event’s first breakout star. He was known, he said, after winning Badwater in 2014, but the attention was far different after he won Big’s Backyard in 2023, his second victory, and set a backyard world record by running more than 450 miles. The format changed the high school teacher’s life.

“I was doing other cool stuff but never got noticed,” Lewis said. “But after the backyard, I was invited to all these running events, at no cost, places I’d never get to go to as a teacher. Australia, Botswana, all over the place. In Botswana, people knew who I was, and I was like, ‘really’? It just created so many more doors opening.”

Backyard ultras favor a unique skillset. Neither Lewis or Dowdle have the legspeed to compete for a top spot at a “fast” ultra like Western States. But, Lewis counters, a top contender at Western States may struggle at a backyard ultra.

“I’ve seen collegiate-type runners, and they get totally destroyed,” Lewis said. “It’s a different type of grit that’s required for running five straight days.”

Lewis and Dowdle possess that special mindset that doesn’t have much to do with a training plan. Lewis is writing a book on mindset, in fact, that will be released next fall. For Dowdle, the ultimate challenge (and intrigue) comes in the unknown.

“You have no opportunity to say ‘in 10 miles this race will be over,’” Dowdle said. “You just have to wrestle with the discomfort.”

Dowdle does that, he said, by using skills he learned from his parents. His relentless, even disturbing, will comes from his mother, and he got an addict’s penchant from his father. His dad, he said, has been sober for nearly 30 years by using his addictive personality for good, investing his energy in Alcoholics Anonymous and helping others overcome their itches.

But Dowdle also excels by finding out who he was as a person: “Running helped me figure out the person I was running away from and also running toward the person I wanted to be.”

There is a dual narrative in his head, one that every ultrarunner facing the highs and lows of a long race knows. The first tells him he’s not worthy. The other feels only elation. Neither, he said, is true.

“I know that the narrative playing in my head at that moment is not the full truth,” Dowdle said. “And the narrative that tells me I’m not good enough. As long as my feet are still moving forward, I can combat that thinking and know that’s not the full truth.”

Proving that imposter syndrome wrong is his part of his “why,” the magic power that he and Lewis seem to possess that helps them run much farther than just about anyone else. But that’s not his only motivation.

Dowdle was, at one point, a football coach. But when he examined his life, he didn’t think football was the right avenue for what he truly wanted to do. He wanted to connect with young men and try to help them crawl out of the same situation he was in years ago, before he began running and journaling. So he traveled across the country and hosted beer miles. He still does this, though he drinks non-alcoholic varieties now, or he simply challenges athletes to beat his beer mile time. (It’s 5:51.57.)

When the race is over, he sits down with athletes and talks with them about their lives. He tells them he was like them once, a little lost and full of doubt and pain, with only alcohol seeming to help. There are other ways, he tells them. Running could be one. A personal journey, like that of the Iron Cowboy, could be another.

“I watched the Iron Cowboy documentary, and it made me realize that I do have control, and that I can do hard things and I’m capable of more,” Dowdle said. “That’s the gift he gave me in that moment. Now I’ve been on a mission to try to give that gift to other people.”

#8254. The FN Mauser Is the Best Deer Rifle that History Forgot

Published Nov 3, 2026 12:01 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

Hunting rifles come and go and sometimes even good ones don’t stay around. The decades following World War II saw a boom in hunters and a voracious appetite for new rifles and cartridges. This was the heyday of the Pre-64 Model 70 and the Winchester Magnums, but we no longer hear much about the many Mauser sporting rifles made by FN and imported from Belgium.

I recently got my mitts on one of these rifles, which belonged to my great grandfather, chambered in .270 Win. While this gun undoubtedly rode around in the rifle rack of Grandpa Curtis’s truck when I was a youngster, I’m looking at it anew. According to my dad and uncle, Grandpa’s brother was a gunsmith and built the rifle for him. This was after he’d raised a family in a log cabin in Colorado during the Depression and developed a taste for July mule deer. He used this rifle to shoot a lot of deer and elk.

A family heirloom like this gives me a perspective on what a quality hunting rifle looked like in the 1950s, and an idea of how well it’s held up over time. It’s also fun to compare it to the rifles we have today.

It’s common to hear or read about the many sporterized military rifles that post-war hunters adopted. These would typically be either 1903 Springfields or remnant military Mauser rifles. But these FN Mausers weren’t sporterized — they were manufactured for a couple decades as sporting-specific guns. Many, including this rifle, were imported by Firearms International Corp. and marked as such on the receivers.

They were brought in and sold by various companies and in numerous formats. An ad in the November, 1951 Issue of Outdoor Life displays the JC Higgins Model 50 — which was simply an FN Mauser and sold at Sears, Roebuck. They had the chrome vanadium steel barrel and even came with a 2.5-power scope, for $135. Another ad, from the September, 1952 issue, for the Parker-Whelen Gun Catalog, lists .30/06 and .270 FN Mausers for $137.50 without a receiver-mounted rear sight. That would cost you another ten bucks. This could be a clue to the specific origin of this .270, as the front of the barrel has markings that appear to be where a front sight was once mounted, but there is no evidence of a barrel-mounted rear sight like you’ll see on Pre-64 Model 70 rifles and others like the Remington Model 721.

Ultimately, lots of these guns were imported in various forms and were sold by companies like Weatherby, Harrington & Richardson, and Colt. Complete FN rifles, according to what little I could find, had a specific pearl edge to the checkering on the grips, but it’s likely that not all of them did. Barrelled actions were also imported and built into custom hunting rifles.

This particular rifle appears to be either one that showed up as a barrelled action — possibly with a front sight. The barrel and receiver both bear the appropriate stampings for a matched pair that left the factory in Belgium. But the 22-inch barrel appears to have been cut down and re-crowned — as these were generally 24-inch barrels. It’s stamped with the year “1951” and bears matching 2837 serial numbers.

The stock has a handsome grain and good ergonomics. It lacks any checkering, but the fore-end has a nice belly and is capped with an ivory-colored plastic cap. The grip is capped with a similar plastic cap and its vertical orientation provides a wonderful balance of trigger reach and allows a crisp perpendicular squeeze. The raised comb is, in part, made from a separate block of wood. It’s pinned atop the buttstock and shaped to match, but the seams are still visible.

The floorplate isn’t hinged on this rifle. Rather, it’s detachable and retained by a spring-loaded button at the rear and retaining lip at the front. The fitting of the stock is very precise and, despite being bedded from the tang to the cap on the fore-end, very little bedding material is visible alongside the metal. Pillars around the action screws also help create an incompressible bridge between the bottom metal and action. The precise fit of metal and wood are things we’ll only see today on custom rifles and the highest-end production guns. Factory stocks — both wood and synthetic — are either CNC-milled or molded with baked-in tolerances rather than hand fit. The workmanship on my 1954 Model 70 is good, but not to the same level.

The barrel is a pretty standard sporter taper, finishing at .635 inches. I assume it has been cut down from 24 inches to 22. It’s a heavier barrel than you’ll see on classics like the M70 featherweight and contributes to the rifle’s roughly 9.5-pound overall weight.

The action and barrel share all matching and appropriate proof marks, and remain in good shape, with the bolt sliding like glass down the slick raceways. The bottom of the bolt handle is flattened and knurled for a better grip, and is generally smoother to operate than my previously mentioned M70. The safety switch is textured on both sides. It appears to be pitting because of its irregularity, but no other parts show similar signs of corrosion.

The receiver is topped with a one-piece Redfield mount and Bear Cub 2 ¾-power scope that uses a post-style reticle. In the early days of magnified optics, this gave a sight picture similar to that of a front post iron sight — to which most shooters would be accustomed. It was fitted with a Canjar trigger — a premium aftermarket upgrade, that breaks at 3 pounds, 7 ounces as set.

To test the rifle for accuracy, I fired four five-shot groups with several different types of contemporary .270 ammo. Where we would normally aggregate these five-shot groups into a single 20-shot group for each type of ammo, It was apparent that the system was limited, in part, by the optic, so I’m just sticking with the group size averages.

I believe the rifle is certainly capable of better accuracy than this but, considering the vintage scope, it proved itself perfectly capable of hitting a deer or elk cleanly out to 200 to 300 yards. Frankly, it’s not uncommon for us to test modern rifles with high-magnification scopes that average worse. A low-power optic itself doesn’t prevent a rifle from shooting accurately either, but this style of reticle requires the correct-sized target and a lot of concentration to maintain a consistent hold. The post covers about four inches of a 100-yard target. When the barrel warmed, mirage definitely affected sight picture too. I tried both a six-o’clock hold and a navy hold (dead center), and saw some vertical stringing with both methods.

Read Next: 10 Classic Hunting Rifles Every Hunter Should Own

For as much as we hear about classic rifles like the Savage 99 and Winchester Model 70, I’m surprised that Mausers like this haven’t carried a similar reputation. So many rifles, including the Winchester, were derived from the Mauser action itself. The rifles even commanded a higher price than Model 70s at the time. While precision manufacturing, materials, and coatings have gotten better, a rifle like this one could still hold its own today.

#8253. We Tested Survival Knives to Find the Best for Any Situation

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

When you’re heading outdoors, you can never be too prepared—and that includes having the right survival knife on hand at all times. No one wants to find themselves in a life-or-death scenario in the wilderness. However, it can happen to anyone, even the most experienced hunters, anglers, hikers, and backpackers. This is where a good knife can help tip the scales in favor of one’s survival. Few success stories don’t include one at some point.

Whether used for shelter construction, fire starting, food preparation, or defense, knives are a catch-all tool. And while any knife could technically be a survival knife, some are better suited for emergency situations and extreme conditions than others. With that in mind, we put a handful of blades through extensive tests to find the best survival knives for every budget and every scenario.

When I previously tested bushcraft knives, I found the Tops Fieldcrafter to be the best. With bushcraft and survival so intertwined, it only made sense that this knife is also my top pick for this category. In short, this blade is a beast. Tops built it quite ruggedly with 150CM stainless steel. It has an extremely beefy feel in the hands. The blade shrugged off wood batoning tests as if it were nothing.

I used this knife to field dress a Wisconsin whitetail last November, and it handled the task easily. The sharp spine is also a great scraping and fire-starting tool. The only potential con is that the knife’s scaling feels a little slick to me. I haven’t had an issue with it slipping, but I would appreciate more of a texture to the handle. Fortunately, the finger groove and jimping make up for that shortcoming. It’s not a cheap knife, but this is one of those cases where the price of admission is worth it.

I’ve owned the Kansbol for a few years, and it never fails to impress despite its bargain basement price point. Because it weighs less than 4 ounces, this is an excellent option for backpackers. I sometimes forget I have this one in my pack because it’s so light. The versatility of the blade can’t be understated either. Morakniv gave it a unique modified combination of Scandi and flat grind. It will handle everything from light woodwork to food processing.

I love the spine on this knife. It is sharp and throws a huge spark for fire starting. This spine does it better than some of the $300+ knives that I own. The handle is simple and surprisingly ergonomic despite a plain appearance.

The only real downside of the Kansbol is that it is not a full tang. It’s not something to split wood or use on other heavy projects. However, the trade-off is worth it because this knife is practical for many other tasks. For under $40, it’s a true bargain. It’s worth consideration as a secondary knife, even if you already have a primary one. That’s how much I like this knife. Even seasoned survivalists will find a lot to like with the Kansbol.

Benchmade didn’t play around when they designed the Mini Bushcrafter. This rugged knife is beefy and ready for abuse in a survival situation. The CPM-S30V steel gives this knife some incredible edge retention qualities. I’ve been testing it for several months and haven’t worn down the factory edge yet. This knife is much lighter and more natural in the hands than the original Bushcrafter.

I love the balance of this blade. Despite a shortened blade length, it carves, notches, and slices on par with my best knives. It’s also just a great-looking knife. Benchmade paired it with an excellent Ferro-rod ready sheath. The knife might be slightly undersized for some tasks, like wood batoning. However, during my testing, I managed to split the wood with it. It just takes a little more awareness of the shorter blade length. There is no denying it’s thick enough for high-leverage jobs. The CPM-S30V steel also drives the price point up quite a bit. However, for situations where one’s life might be on the line, this is one knife where it’s worth not skimping.

Wargoat is an awesome name for a knife, and it has the performance to match. During my testing, this Montana Knife Company knife sliced through most materials like butter. This is technically a defense knife. However, it effortlessly carves and feathersticks wood without affecting the edge. The choice to use MagnaCut steel with a Cerakote finish is inspired. It’s meant to cut down on flash that could give away the user’s position. Consequently, it also gives the knife the perfect edge retention and corrosion resistance combination. This gives this knife some excellent peace of mind for survival scenarios. Maintenance is going to be minimal.

I love the handle on this knife. MKC added texturing to the G-10 handles, making it rock solid in the hands.  This knife is extremely expensive, at over $300. Part of that price comes from its being made in the USA. Its smaller size also limits it for some survival scenarios. This tactical knife is better as a secondary knife for defense in the wild. It will probably be a popular item for soldiers and game wardens who work outdoors frequently. Overall, I love the quality of the craftsmanship here. This knife was designed and manufactured with care, and it shows.

The Izula is an impressive little knife with a versatility factor that’s off the charts. When I think of tactical, I think concealable. That’s what the Izula does best. It’s an excellent neck knife but it also works well for horizontal carry. Because it weighs under 2 ounces, it’s a knife that’s easy to carry and forget until needed. This knife has the thinnest profile of any that I own. It’s great to slip in those narrow front pockets of a survival pack as a backup.

It amazes me that this knife sells for under $70. I like it for light carving, trap construction, and wild game preparation tasks.  This knife is a little undersized for some survival tasks. No one is going to baton wood with it. It also doesn’t come with scales, which can provide a better grip. However, I don’t think that’s a dealbreaker. Aftermarket scales are plentiful and cheap. This is also a great option for anyone who likes making paracord wraps. Ultimately, this knife has many uses in a survival scenario, making it worthy of consideration.

The Buck 119 is a classic knife design that never goes out of style. It features a versatile clip-point Bowie-style blade that excels in nearly every facet of bushcraft. Buck touts this one as a hunting knife. Subsequently, we like it best for survivalists who expect to clean game and fish frequently. However, the full-tang design is also beefy enough for wood splitting and shelter construction projects. The 6-inch length makes for an ideal, do-all type of knife. We also like the ergonomics of the handle. It has subtle finger grooves that conform to most hands perfectly.

The finish of this knife is easily scratched, but for survival purposes, it doesn’t matter much. Some users will like the sheath, and others will hate it. That feature is more a matter of preference than any other part of this knife. However, this knife does deliver something for everyone. Buck also builds variants in three different steel qualities. That gives it more versatility budget-wise than other fixed-blade survival knives.

This Uncharted Supply Co. knife isn’t well-known, which is a shame because it is a solid survival knife. I’m a sucker for ergonomics, and I love what it brings to the table. The rubberized grip has never slipped in my hands. Add a perfect finger groove and ramped-up jimping, and it fits my hand like a glove. It’s beefy enough for heavy tasks, too. I easily split wood with this knife. Uncharted includes a small whetstone and a decent fire starter. This knife is also my pick for the best with a fire starter. It throws a big spark with the included rod.

At $40, it’s incredibly affordable. It’s worth throwing one in the glovebox or boat as a backup. This knife has some serrations, which I know some survival enthusiasts shy away from. However, I think they have a case use here. It’s good for ice anglers and bush pilots who might need to cut their seatbelt quickly in an emergency. There is also a glass breaker on the end for exiting a sinking vehicle quickly.

The Hunter Pro Alox is a gorgeous and robust folding knife. During my testing, I found that the blade locks into place with a meaty snap. As a folder, it doesn’t have the ability to split wood, but it is still very capable. I noticed zero wiggle or play in the blade when locked into place. It handles light carving and bushcraft tasks quite admirably. I haven’t field-dressed a deer with this blade yet, but I can already tell it would be up for the task. A slight finger groove and subtle jimping give great control to the blade tip. I like the feel of the aluminum scaling. It’s not as tacky as I normally like my knife handles, but I’ve never had this knife slip.

I tested this knife on everything from wood to paracord and cardboard. It still has a great edge. The main downside of this knife is that the aluminum scaling won’t be ideal in a cold environment. It makes the knife a little difficult to grip in cold conditions. For every other scenario, it is more than capable. It’s a solid EDC knife that can easily transition to a survival situation in a pinch.

Fortunately, I haven’t found myself in a survival scenario. However, I have spent time testing various knives in survival tasks. These include starting fires, splitting wood, sticking feathers, carving, and more. Some of these knives were given heavy-duty cardboard ripping tests. Those tests were great for judging edge retention because of how quickly the material dulls an edge.   Additionally, I evaluated knives based on ergonomics, sheaths, and carrying ability. Some knives were chosen based on input from other outdoor enthusiasts I know and trust. Other factors that were considered during testing include:

Any knife is better than no knife in a survival situation. However, some types are better suited for different purposes. It depends on what one’s goals are for a survival situation. Knives best suited for light food prep are vastly different from shelter-building tools. These are some of the more popular options.

Fixed blades are the more popular choice for survival because of their versatility. With a full tang, a fixed-blade knife can seamlessly transition from wood splitting to food prep to shelter construction. With a proper sharp spine, it is the safest way to start a fire using a Ferro rod. This style is also excellent for field dressing and skinning wild game. The main downsides to a fixed blade are weight and ease of carry.

Folders offer a huge weight savings advantage over fixed blades. However, these knives aren’t robust enough for tasks like wood splitting. They are good for lighter tasks like food preparation or light trap construction. Some folding knives are also a good choice for cleaning game animals or fish.

The proper grind is essential for survival. Most survival experts prefer a Scandi, which is more of a wedge shape, for chopping and splitting. Flat grinds work better as an “all-purpose” type of grind. Consider the flat grind if planning to do food prep with the knife. When it comes to edges, a simple straight edge is best. Mainly because it’s the easiest to sharpen. I did include one partially serrated option on this list. That edge is handy for cutting heavy fabrics and fibers, like a seat belt.

In most instances, a slightly larger knife is better. Knives in the 8 to 10-inch overall length range are best. Blades in the 4.5 to 7-inch range are better for heavy tasks like wood batoning. Bigger isn’t always better, though. Knives that are too large can be a burden to carry.

Most experts agree that a drop point is usually best. These blades usually have a Scandi grind that’s easy to sharpen in the field. That grind is ideal for wood carving tasks. This knife shape usually has a deep belly, which is especially handy when skinning game animals.

#8252. A Veteran Bowhunter Finds Two Bucks Locked Together Deep Into Public Land. Should He Shoot Them?

Published Nov 3, 2026 2:09 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Robert Denninger was in a tree saddle the afternoon of October 23 when he spotted a deer in a creek bed about 75 yards away. He’d accessed the Oklahoma public hunting area by kayak, paddling up a creek to a remote spot that he’d pinpointed the previous day.

“I decided to slide down quietly with my bow and get a better look at the deer in the creek,” Denninger tells Outdoor Life. “When I got close to the creek I spotted two big mature bucks fighting and they were locked up tight by their antlers.”

He knew he was witnessing an epic outdoor event and he shot video of the fight on his phone.

“The bucks were plowing into each other and into the creek bank,” says Denninger, a 42-year-old retiree from Dallas. “Mud was flying everywhere. My mind was racing – would attempting to harvest these bucks be a hunter’s gift or a violation of fair chase?”

It was clear the bucks were not able to separate their antlers. Denninger struggled with what to do and pondered if it would be ethical and legal to shoot the larger of the two bucks, which was a 12-pointer with a typical rack. He recalled a friend telling him a story of once finding a pair of locked-antler bucks dead in a pond. They had been killed and half eaten by coyotes.

Before deciding what to do, Denninger called a game warden.

“I spoke with a local [Oklahoma] Game Warden who assured me he didn’t have any on-call vet who could have come out to sedate the animals and attempt a safe unlocking,” Denninger says.

“The thought of letting ‘nature run its course’ and coming back in the following days to spook a pack of coyotes off two rotten carcasses or trying my best to put an ethical kill on these animals were what I believed my choices were,” he explains. “I decided to shoot the 12-pointer.”

His first arrow was deflected by brush. But his second arrow found the deer’s heart, and it quickly died.

“I watched to see if the eight point could free himself, but he only struggled more, barely able to move the weight of the harvested 12-pointer,” the bowhunter says.

Denninger had no way of freeing the deer, so he decided to shoot the second buck with his bow. Even when both deer were dead, it was impossible to unlock their antlers.

That’s when he called a couple younger buddies, who eventually arrived with a wheeled wagon.

“We tried to unlock their racks many times, and were unable to,” Denninger says. “We field dressed them. But it was a rugged haul to get the two bucks out, taking well over three hours to get them to a truck and out of the woods. It was almost midnight [by the time we were done].”

He called his Texas friend and taxidermist Dustin Moon and told him about the locked-antler bucks and his hunting tale.

“Dustin and his wife Stephanie of New Story Taxidermy drove five hours (on their sixth wedding anniversary) to where I was so they could see the bucks and help my deer processor get their antlers unlocked.”

Eventually they succeeded and the deer were separated. They will be mounted, though Denninger doesn’t know if he’ll have them in a locked-horn mount or separate mounts.

The 12-pointer is believed to be 7.5 years old and has a rough green score of 152 inches. It’s the biggest buck Denninger has taken during his dedicated bowhunting career. The 8-pointer is thought to be 5.5 years old and scores 132 inches. Both bucks have typical racks.

“I think what I did was the most ethical thing I could have done with my two Oklahoma buck tags, especially considering the alternative of having them suffer and die in their struggle, or have coyotes kill them.”

Bob McNally has been an outdoor writer since shortly after the earth’s crust cooled. He has written 12 outdoor books, more than 5,000 outdoor magazine stories (including many for Outdoor Life) and more newspaper outdoor columns and features than there are hairs on a grizzly bear.

#8251. How to Mount a Riflescope Like a Pro. Follow This Step-By-Step Guide

Published Nov 3, 2026 4:24 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

When mounting a riflescope, you’re dealing with the most fragile and failure-prone point on your gun—so it pays to do it right. The process isn’t complicated, but it does require an attention to detail and some basic equipment. So in part one of our seven-part series on mastering the use of precision riflescopes and shooting to your rifle’s full potential, I’m going to dive in to how to actually get one of these bad boys mounted properly.

To correctly mount a riflescope, these conditions must be satisfied: The reticle needs to be level with the rifle. The scope must be positioned at the correct height above the bore. The proper eye relief needs to be established. And the fasteners in the rings and bases need to be tightened the right way. Before we get into detail on each of these points, here’s a basic outline of the process.

• Clamp the barrel in the padded jaws of a bench vise. If you don’t have a bench vise, you’ll need a solid gun cradle that will hold the rifle steady.

• Use a bubble level to level the rifle action. The flat on top of the Picatinny rail works. With some actions you can remove the bolt and have enough clearance on the tang (assuming it is flat) to set a bubble level as well. As a last resort you can attach the bottom half of a scope ring to the scope base and rest the level on it.

• Set the scope in the rings and lightly tighten the fasteners so that the scope will stay put but can be rotated and moved by hand. If your scope has a flat spot on the elevation turret, place the bubble level on it to level the reticle.

• An alternate method to level the reticle is to look through the scope on your leveled rifle at a plumb bob and orient the vertical crosshair with the string.

• Once the reticle is level, remove the rifle from vise and check your eye relief. Make adjustments as needed. Do this by placing the rifle back in the vise, making sure it is level, and then moving the scope.

• Tighten the fasteners to the correct torque levels with a torque wrench.

The depth of the scope rings controls how far above the bore the scope sits. The primary concern is that both ends of the scope have adequate clearance above the rifle. Having the objective end of the scope in contact with the barrel is an obvious no-no, but you want to make sure the eyepiece isn’t cramped either. Rings that are too low can limit the horizontal travel of the scope in the rings making it more difficult to get the right eye relief.

If your scope is too high, you’ll have a hard time lining up behind the rifle when shooting prone, though a stock with an adjustable cheek piece can mitigate this.

Ultimately, this is a Goldilocks situation where the scope should neither be too high, nor too low. As a rule of thumb, a gap between the objective bell and the barrel of .25 to .5 inches should be just right—but the profile of your barreled action and stock might dictate otherwise.

With proper eye relief the shooter is able to look through the scope without any part of the image being blacked out. The way to test whether eye relief (and scope height) are correct is to get set up behind the rifle in the prone position, close your eyes, rest your check firmly on the stock by taking the tension out of your neck, then opening your eyes.

You should be looking right down the center of the riflescope and have a clear view of the reticle and image without needing to move your head.

Fortunately, many long-range rifles make fine tuning this easier by have adjustable lengths of pull and cheek piece height. Rifles equipped with Picatinny rails—which most precision rifles are—provide greater flexibility with the forward and aft placement of the scope to establish good eye relief.

Read Next: The Best Scope Rings of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Some manufacturers provide values for the fasteners in their scope rings. Many don’t. As a rule of thumb, you can tighten the screws on scope rings to about 20 inch-pounds and be good to go.

It always makes sense to check the screws on your Pic rail or scope base as well. They tend to be beefier, so you can torque them to about 30 inch-pounds without worry.

You can use a torque wrench with preset fittings, like Fix-It Sticks or the Wheeler Fat Wrench, or one with an indicator dial like this one from Seekonk Precision Tools.

Before tightening the screws, you should consider doing one of two things. Either use a sparing amount of blue Loctite on the treads—a single small drop will do—or spray the screws with some degreaser. These will help the screws acquire a more secure hold.

Tighten the screws as you would lug nuts on a truck tire. Tighten one a bit, go to a screw on the other side of the ring and tighten that a bit, and repeat as you work your way through all the fasteners.

Tighten them gradually so that the rings are applying an even clamping force to the scope tube. When done correctly, the gap on either side of the rings should be even. That’s a good sign that whoever put the scope on the rifle knew their stuff.

#8250. Swarovski NL Pure Binocular Review: The Best Glass Money Can Buy

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

Let me tell you a story about how good the Swarovski NL Pure binocular is. On a combined elk and deer hunt in Montana, a fellow writer, two guides, and I were glassing a bedded whitetail buck from long way off, trying to figure out if he was worth a stalk. I was looking through the NL Pure, and the other guys were peering into various other high-end binos, none costing less than a grand and some costing much more than that.

Studying the deer, I said, “He’s got decent mass but isn’t super tall or wide. He might go 130 inches.” The other guys asked how I’d surmised all this from so far away. I handed him the NL Pure, and one after another, they said, “Oh!” and “Ah!” and “Holy sh*t!” Finally, they all agreed that the buck was somewhere between 125 and 130, and we tromped off to go look for another.

That’s what next-level resolution does for you. It doesn’t come cheaply, of course, but it makes a real difference in the field. And so, with that in mind, let’s take a close look at the Swarovski NL Pure, how it performed in my testing, and why I think it is the best hunting binocular you can buy today.

Related: The Best Binoculars of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

The NL Pure is not new. Not by a long shot. The first models in the series hit shelves way back in 2020, one of the few good things to happen in a no-good, rotten year. All the more impressive then that now, six years later, the NL Pure is still as good a binocular as you can find.

Not long after those first NL Pure offerings debuted, I awarded the 10×42 model our “Best Binocular at Any Price” award in F&S’s annual binocular test—and it has not relinquished that distinction since. Every year, I test the latest and the greatest glass, and I keep a 10×42 NL Pure handy to compare to the newest contenders. And for now, at least, it is still at the top of the heap.

I have written before that the gap between good and great binoculars is closing. That’s great news for hunters. But a handful of models still stand totally apart, and the NL Pure is the finest example of that. My 10×42 test model notched perfect scores in the resolution and image quality tests. With lots of binoculars, you have to look and look and strain your eyes to detect small differences in resolution. Not with these. The NL Pure’s advantage in resolving detail is immediately obvious, and the picture is as clean and bright as you could want, with virtually zero color shift, field curvature, or stray light. But it’s not enough to say that the binocular’s optical performance is the best or even perfect. It’s more like a revelation. You peer into it, and the world looks like a better place.

Meanwhile, the NL Pure’s innovative hour-glass, open-bridge design saves weight and balances perfectly in the hand, making it easy to stabilize the binocular on long glassing sessions, and an available forehead rest adds to the comfort. The focus wheel is large, precise, and silky. The diopter and eyecup adjustments are positive and exact.

Related: How to Use Your Binoculars and Spotting Scope to Hunt Elk, Mule Deer, and Antelope in the West

If you want to see exactly how I tested the NL Pure, you can go to our annual binocular test and look at the section called “How I Tested and Score Binoculars.” In a nutshell, I used a 1951 USAF Resolution Test Chart to test resolution in daylight and low-light conditions. I used a color-artifact chart to test for chromatic aberration. I also tested for edge-to-edge clarity, feeling of immersion (which we’ll get to), overall image quality, handling, ergonomics, build quality, and weather resistance.

In all of the optical categories, the NL Pure set the standard. Resolution was nothing short of astounding. But world-class glass like this offers more than just stunning detail; it immerses you in the image. An optics professor I used to test binoculars with calls this “feeling of immersion.” With the NL Pure’s huge field of view and field-flattening lenses, you get the sense that you’ve stepped into the picture and that everything there is brilliant and vivid and free of the little imperfections that otherwise distract you from the experience.

The quality of the construction is obvious the second you put this binocular in your hand, and everything from the focus wheel to the diopter functioned just as it should. All of that said, the NL Pure is not flawless. To my surprise, it pretty much bombed my weather-resistance test, which involved a half-hour submersion in a creek and then a half-hour visit to the deep freeze. After the submersion portion, the image was usable but not especially clear, and it was close to unusable coming out of the freezer. I should be clear that my test is obviously tougher than what most hunters will face in the outdoors. Still, it provides an apples-to-apples comparison, and only one binocular out of about 10 tested did worse.

That, however, is the NL Pure’s only flaw. In every other way, this binocular is spectacular. The other thing that is spectacular—as in breathtaking—is the price. The NL Pure now comes in seven configurations, from 8×32 to 14×52, and ranges in price from $2,799 to $3,849. For most of us, that’s a whole lot to spend on a binocular. But some hunters are willing to pay top dollar to own the best of the best. And the NL Pure is exactly that. Give it a little extra protection in rough weather, and it will show you things other hunters will never see.

Experience After graduating college, Hurteau launched a regional hunting and fishing magazine from an apartment in Ithaca, New York, and soon parlayed that into the job at Field & Stream. He’s had no less than eight titles with F&S, from gear editor to contributing writer and, now, executive editor. He’s been nominated for a National Magazine Award as a writer and was part of an F&S editorial team to win two National Magazine Awards for General Excellence—the highest honor in magazine journalism. Hurteau oversees much of the brand’s hunting, gear, and general outdoors coverage. An serious hunter and angler himself, he is co-author of The Total Deer Hunter Manual and the The Total Bowhunting Manual. #8249. Why Québec is the Ultimate East Coast Ski Destination

Owl's Head Ski Resort at sunset. (Photo: Cantons-de-l'Est © Cantons-de-l'Est/BBT Productions)

Nope, it’s not too much to ask: You can get great snow, both natural and man-made, wild terrain, incredible food, historic architecture, and rich cultural immersion all with just a short drive and no time zone change. That’s right. In Québec, winter is so good it feels like it should be hard to get to, but it’s just across the border.

Let’s start with the snow. Canada’s French-speaking province boasts some of the nation’s highest annual snowfall, with up to 250 inches per year. And you’ll find it in every form: deep powder, groomed tracks, and perfect corduroy, spread across terrain that varies from steep and wild to mellow and peaceful. And all that snow comes with dozens of vibrant mountain towns and more than 70 ski resorts—all within a stone’s throw of the Lower 48. (Montréal is just a 90-minute flight or six-hour drive from Boston, and New Yorkers can reach Québec City in less than two hours by air.)

Next, enjoy the rewards of going wherever the path of adventure takes you. The size of the province means you have lots of choices, but rest assured you can’t go wrong: in Québec, skiable terrain unfolds in nearly every direction. The only question is what kind of ski experience you’re looking for. Here’s what you’ll find in the four ski regions featured here—plus which resorts to hit to make the most of it

Looking for spectacular scenery? Unbelievably long runs? Buttery maritime snowpack coming in off the St. Lawrence River? Northeast of Québec City, you’ll find all three in Charlevoix, where the steep slopes of Le Massif de Charlevoix hover over the water, serving up mountain-meets-river views that are totally unique, and plunging valleys and sweeping bowls attract skiers looking to test their skills amid the serene quiet of a Québécois winter. Le Massif serves up the biggest vertical drop east of the Canadian Rockies, while Mont Grand-Fonds offers a compact layout, laid-back atmosphere, and terrain for all ability levels.

Use Québec City as your base camp and you won’t have to choose between good skiing and vibrant arts and culture. The province’s capital is an enchanting maze of European architecture and historic neighborhoods. An evening walk downtown feels like a wander through a snow-draped fairytale. The food and bar scene reflects a similar blend between time-honored traditions and modern flair. And at just 30 minutes from Mont-Sainte-Anne, it’s close enough to the slopes that you can fully immerse yourself in the true Québecois lifestyle without cutting into your ski time.

Close to Montréal, the Laurentian Mountains are speckled with charming, Alps-style villages—complete with classy accommodations, spas, bistros, and microbreweries—that support a robust après-ski tradition. Mont Tremblant offers a stunning variety of terrain, including both gentle runs and enough steep-and-deep to challenge the experts. Meanwhile, Mont-Blanc and Sommet Saint-Sauveur boast quieter settings, family-friendly atmospheres, and five-star night skiing.

The lush, forested mountains southeast of Montréal are densely packed with ski areas, making this the perfect region for some serious resort-hopping. Even better: with the L’EST GO Pass, you can nab discounted lift tickets on four of the zone’s best hills. If you like night skiing, head to Bromont, a local favorite that opens more than 90 runs after sunset. Prefer the solitude of the deep woods? Head to nearby Mont Sutton for world-class tree skiing and a far wilder feel. Laid-back resorts like Owl’s Head cater to families, while Mont-Orford’s high elevation makes it a motherlode of high-quality snow.

Each of the four ski regions featured here has its own distinct personality. What connects them is Québec’s unmistakable joie de vivre: a love of local flavours, lively après-ski, and taking fun seriously. It’s what makes a ski getaway here so full of character.

Québec isn’t far from America’s East Coast, but it feels like another universe. The province boasts a unique culture defined by its French language, historic neighborhoods, local cuisine, and a dynamic craft beer scene. In its urban areas, you’ll find 17th-century colonial architecture, complete with narrow streets, turrets, and flagstone courtyards.

Leave the urban centers, and historic brick quickly gives way to winter’s snow-flocked evergreens and white-blanket pastures. Barns and silos dot the countryside, and just beyond, mountains rear into the skyline like 5,000-foot beacons calling skiers home.

Québec’s unique combination of proximity and novelty make it one of the most unique ski destinations in North America. And yet it’s not nearly as pricey as some of the other life-list destinations you might have on your list. With the American to Canadian Dollar exchange rate, accommodations and food in Québec tend to offer a strong value on a complete ski trip, especially for U.S. travelers. To make the most of that value, explore ski packages and resort offers across Québec on maneige.ski to find the right getaway for your next winter adventure.

Between its vast and varied terrain, deep snow, rich culture, easy access, and affordable prices, Québec has everything skiers need to squeeze more adventure out of winter. Whether you’re looking for more terrain, more culture, or more discovery, you’ll find it here.

Ready to take your ski adventure further? From breathtaking mountain views and exhilarating runs to vibrant après-ski and charming resort villages, Québec offers much more than great skiing. Explore the regions and plan your winter getaway with Bonjour Québec.
