#8248. First Lite Uncompahgre Foundry Jacket, Tested and Reviewed

Published Nov 3, 2026 4:36 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

It’s not often that you get to hunt in an area that is the namesake for the jacket you’re wearing, but this fall, I did just that. The Uncompahgre National Forest covers almost a million acres of high-elevation backcountry in Colorado. At, and over, 10,000 feet, the wind and weather can be unpredictable. So your clothing needs to be versatile and ready for whatever Mother Nature might throw your way.

After wearing the Uncompahgre Foundry Jacket during my first-rifle elk hunt with fluctuating temperatures, driving rain, and even a healthy dose of snowfall, I will be the first to tell you that this jacket earned its name. It’s surprisingly packable, offers zippered ventilation around the triceps, and is incredibly warm. Since my elk hunt, it’s earned a spot in my treestand layering system as well. Here’s everything you need to know about this must-have outer layer.

As I mentioned above, the weather on my elk hunt was unpredictable at best. From driving rain for multiple days on end, to rapidly dropping temperatures bringing snow into the high country, I got to experience the full spectrum of temperatures and conditions. The Uncompahgre Foundry jacket was one piece of my kit that I wouldn’t have wanted to live without.

It remained durable after hiking through oak brush, deadfall, and large conifer stands, but more importantly, it kept me dry. Since I was living in a tent, my biggest fear was getting wet, and thus, staying wet with no way to really dry off given the conditions. Thankfully, this jacket both figuratively and literally had my back.

Upon returning home, I tested the Uncompahgre Foundry jacket throughout an October cold front here in Pennsylvania as well. While the conditions were drastically improved compared to the backcountry in Colorado, this jacket still fit into my kit wonderfully. Rather than wear it the entire walk to the stand, I simply packed it up into a ball and tossed it in my pack. After climbing in, I’d throw it on and enjoy my sit. It keeps me warm and surprisingly doesn’t make a ton of noise when you’re moving to grab your bow and draw back.

While I do really like this jacket, there’s always room for improvement. The first thing I noticed was the pocket design and layout. On the front of the jacket are four pockets. Two magnetic dump pockets, and just above those, two zippered hand warmer pockets featuring a warm tricot lining. Both are quite handy for different things, but I often found myself digging around in the wrong pocket due to their layout and close proximity to each other. If it were up to me, I’d leave the dump pockets where they are, and move the hand warmer pockets to a more traditional, hip-centric location.

I also had an issue, that was certainly in part user error, where the hand warmer pockets got wet during a popup rain shower. I had accidentally left the zipper open, but due to the design, the rain ran down the front of the jacket and right into those pockets. When the zippers were closed, no water intrusion occurred. User error aside, I’d argue it’s another reason to relocate the hand warmer pockets.

Where the Uncompahgre Foundry jacket shines truly is in its versatility. I was able to wear it in temperatures ranging from 20 degrees, all the way up to 50 degrees. Admittedly, 50 degrees might have been right on the edge of too hot for this jacket, it really did a nice job of ventilating when I opened up the tricep vents.

It’s incredibly windproof, waterproof, durable, and warm. Honestly, it’s an outer layer I didn’t even know I needed until I had it. And now that I have it, it’ll be accompanying me on every hunt for the remainder of the fall and winter.

As an avid hunter, I came to the realization years ago that you get what you pay for when purchasing hunting clothing. I hate being cold, and I hate being wet. Thankfully, the Uncompahgre Foundry jacket does a wonderful job of eliminating both of those concerns. If you’re hunting for a new outer layer to get you through the rut, rifle, and late season, look no further.

He graduated from Pennsylvania State University in 2018 and still lives in central Pennsylvania.

#8247. His Bow Exploded When He Tried to Arrow His Target Buck — But He Still Got the Deer

Published Nov 4, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Oklahoma bowhunter Max Wynn was sitting in a ground blind with his wife Hartley, not far from a big river bottom in central Oklahoma the evening of October 17. Eventually, he spotted a nice 8-point buck (which was his target deer) and it walked to within just 10 yards of his blind.

“I wanted to take a close [shot at the] buck with my recurve bow, but as I started to draw it, the buck spooked a bit and moved out to 25 yards,” the 24-year-old archer tells Outdoor Life. “I set the recurve bow down, picked up my 75-pound draw weight compound bow, drew it, and released an arrow.

“When I did, it sounded like a cannon went off inside my blind. I set the bow down and saw the string serving was split, the bow string was slack, and both bow cams were bent.”

The arrow that Wynn loosed only flew about 8 yards and hit the dirt. The lighted nock  flew farther than the arrow that it was on.

The bow essentially exploded in his hands, bruising his wrist. Otherwise he was unscathed, though he said he was lucky the broken bow limbs didn’t hit his face.

“The bow limb could have hit the top of my ground blind when I shot my arrow, and that may have caused the bow to explode like it did,” says Wynn, a compression therapist and waterfowl guide for Tine Flies Outfitters. “I was done for the evening and immediately went to Cabela’s and bought a Bear Archery compound bow setup.”

Wynn rigged his Bear bow and sighted it in on targets at home in the truck headlights. The next morning he was back in his ground blind, and shortly a doe came into range at 28 yards. He took the deer with a well-placed arrow.

“That gave me confidence in using that Bear bow, and I went back to the same ground blind that evening with my brother-in-law Maddox Allbright,” Wynn says. “He’s 17 and wanted a doe for the youth deer season. But he decided to wait before taking a doe to see if the 8-point buck I was after came back into the area.”

Indeed, the big buck did come back – following another smaller buck.

“He walked in on the same trail where the doe came that morning, but when he got to where I shot her, he skirted the spot and went a little wider from my blind,” Wynn says. “But he offered a 30-yard quartering away shot. It was a good hit, and he only traveled 35 yards before falling.”

They got the 186-pound 8-pointer out of the woods, and Wynn started processing the buck.

Read Next: Do Deer Really ‘Jump the String?’ Here’s What All Bowhunters Should Know

“I was working my knife on the deer near the ribs by its shoulder and felt something sharp,” Wynn says. “I dug around and pulled out a Slick Trick broadhead that was buried in its chest cavity.

“There were no marks on the outside of the buck’s hide from an arrow wound. The tissue all around the broadhead was healed. The deer looked perfectly healthy before I shot it. Just shows how tough whitetails are.”

Wynn says he was lucky in dressing his 8-pointer that he didn’t cut his hands on the broadhead buried in the deer.

“I think I used up a lot of my deer hunting luck during those two days in the ground blind, and then dressing the buck with another broadhead inside,” he says lightheartedly.

#8246. Matt Robertson Wins $1.25 Million in the Inaugural WBE The Champions Bass Tournament

Matt Robertson overcame a gauntlet of obstacles this past week to win the inaugural WBE The Champions tournament and take home $1.25 million—the biggest prize in professional bass fishing history. He bested 61 other anglers, outmaneuvering and out-fishing them in what turned into a chess-vs.-checkers matchup. Early on, Robertson chose to fish below Old Hickory Dam, and he stuck with that game plan for the duration of the tournament. He caught only two non-keepers below the dam during practice, but knew enough to gamble his entire tournament on that small stretch of water. On the final day, the gutsy call paid off again with a 20-pound, 2-ounce bag, enough to take home the top slot and $1.25 million.

One of Robertson’s biggest challenges throughout the tournament was navigating the lock connecting Old Hickory Lake and the Cumberland River. Even Robertson said he was shocked he could lock down and back all three days without issue. Normally, filling the lock with water to raise a boat to the same level as Old Hickory takes about 30 minutes. Locking down goes a little quicker. All in all, it could take about an hour for the lock to complete one full rotation. And that’s just with a small boat or two. With a barge, it could take much longer. Surprisingly, Robertson locked up and down all six times throughout the event, maximizing his fishing time at his premier spot.

Below the dam, Robertson targeted smallmouth, which must be 18 inches to keep, compared to the 12-inch spotted bass and 14-inch largemouth regulations. In three days of fishing, not a single spot or largemouth was caught below the dam. If you were going to get a bite there, it would be a smallmouth. That meant it had to be a dang good one to keep—and Robertson took advantage of his opportunities. His Day 1 bag (20 pounds even) and Day 3 Bag (20 pounds, 2 ounces) were the two biggest bags of the tournament by far.

The current below Old Hickory Dam was the magic sauce. It positioned the fish on cover and got them to bite. Robertson was fortunate to have moving water below the dam each day, which isn’t always a given. The current shifted dramatically day to day as different turbines fired at different times, but Robertson adjusted and still caught big bronzebacks.

For the armchair quarterback, it probably looked like a no-brainer to fish below the dam this week. But there was a lot to consider, and a half dozen things could have easily gone wrong and ruined Robertson’s run. But the Kentucky native defied the odds, avoided the catastrophes, and came out on top. He adjusted when the current shifted; he waited patiently to lock; he was efficient when he got bit. All of that added up to a handful of quality fish whose tails fell on the right side of the line. The end result was Robertson collecting the biggest purse in bass fishing history. And he did it in dramatic fashion.

#8245. Class 4 Terrain, Cozy Huts, Cold Beer: The Northern Alps Are Japan’s Best-Kept Secret

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Author and photographer Andy Cochrane spent months crafting this route from home in Bend, Oregon, consulting with multiple Japanese mountain guides, before flying to Tokyo to bring it to life. Along with four others, he ran this 100-mile technical traverse across the Northern Alps in a week, staying at mountain huts and soaking in Japanese hospitality along the way.

It’s not often that a local guide recommends helmets for a hut-to-hut trail running trip, but it’s always a sign of a good adventure if you ask me.

A couple of months before flying across the Pacific to Japan, I was on a mid-afternoon Zoom call—my third such conversation of the week—when my jaw hit the floor. I was meeting virtually with guides in the Northern Alps to learn more about the trails and huts of the range, hoping to suss out if a line I had plotted on a map was actually a feasible endeavor to run.

At the time, I wasn’t sure if anyone had run the route before us. There certainly weren’t any blogs, articles, or posts I could find about it. Hut owners on the trip later confirmed my suspicion that our 100-mile, seven-day itinerary was pretty far out of the box. Connecting the outdoor hub of Kamikochi at the southern end of the range to the Sea of Japan in the north along a single ridge line was an unheard of idea to everyone we spoke with. That made it a lot more exciting—and far from certain it would work out. If it did, however, we would get to experience all that the Northern Alps had to offer in a single push.

Because the route required a mix of trail running, boulder hopping, ladder climbing, and Class 4 scrambling, our local guide Tatsuro was adamant that we bring helmets, even if their use wouldn’t be required every day. TL;DR: he was right.

Before I get into specifics of the route and experience, let’s set the scene. The Northern Alps, or Hida Mountains, are Japan’s most primal terrain. Although lesser-known than the mountain ranges of Europe, South America, or mainland Asia, the Northern Alps are just as technical and challenging, if not more so. The range is a jagged, granite spine that defies the country’s reputation for manicured serenity. Trails in the Hida are riddled with boulders, ladders, roots, scrambling, and thick brush. Located just a few dozen miles off the Sea of Japan, the weather is incredibly fickle in the Hida, too.

Geographically, the Northern Alps lie just a few hours drive west of Tokyo on the main island and stretch across Nagano, Toyama, Gifu, and Niigata prefectures. Most of the range is inside Chubu-Sangaku National Park, which protects around 670 square miles from being absorbed by the urban centers that surround it. The Hida are widely regarded as Japan’s premier alpine terrain and feature the country’s most developed hut system, Yamagoya. These staffed huts offer hot meals, sleeping mats, water, snacks, and beer, allowing for multi-day runs and traverses with lightweight packs sans camping gear—perfect for a trip like ours.

Three years ago I ran across the Southern Alps on an ancient postal route called Nakasendo. While the Southern and Northern Alps offer remarkably different terrain and technicality, my first trip taught me much about Japanese culture and logistics that was helpful while preparing for my return.

Perhaps my biggest takeaway from that initial experience was that the language barrier is a major challenge—especially in rural places, where many people don’t speak a lick of English. While apps like Google Translate can help to order a quick meal or get assistance with navigation in a pinch, planning a trip and booking mountain huts requires someone not only fluent in Japanese, but who also understands the mountain culture. For us, that liaison was Kota.

I was connected with Kota at Japan Adventures Co. through a friend, and I honestly can’t say enough good things about him. He is an incredibly organized planner, a great communicator, and an avid hiker and trail runner. He even helped negotiate our stay with a few huts that didn’t believe our route was possible, ensuring the entire trip ran smoothly. Kota and his team lead a variety of hiking, food, and cultural trips around Japan, and are currently rolling out new trail running itineraries in the Northern Alps and elsewhere.

With help from Kota and advice from guides like Tatsuro and Paul from Nagano Adventures, I was able to refine our route to stay at unique huts, run the best trails, and find a balance between challenging and doable for each day. It’s important to note that mountain huts in Japan are warm and welcoming, but they run on rigid schedules. Breakfast is typically at 5 a.m. and dinner is around 5 p.m. If you don’t check in by 4 p.m., they will notify search and rescue, so it’s important to start early and keep an eye on your pace throughout the day.

My goal was to start in Kamikochi and end at the Seas of Japan, creating a single linkup by connecting a number of popular two- and three-day hiking routes—the Panorama Ginza Route, Mount Yari, Ura Ginza Panorama Route, the ridgeline from Mount Eboshi and Funakubo-dake, the Hachimine Kiretto, the Kaerazu no Ken (ridge of no return), and Tsugami Shindo. It’s a mouthful to say, but when drawn on a map, the routes piece together nicely, forming a (mostly) straight line running from north to south.

Getting to and from the Northern Alps isn’t terribly difficult. After landing in Tokyo (either HND or NRT), a bullet train, or Shinkansen, will take you to Matsumoto in just a few hours. From there you can take a smaller train, bus, or taxi into the mountains to begin your adventure. Returning to Tokyo is just as easy by hopping on a bullet train in a coastal city like Toyama. There are plenty of stations to choose from and you usually can find seats just a day or two in advance.

There are a few ways to shuttle your luggage from the start to the finish, but I recommend Yamato Transport. Other options include dropping bags at the post office, the front desk if you’re staying in a hotel, or even convenience stores like Lawson’s or 7-Eleven. Though this might seem risky at face value, it worked flawlessly for us. We walked into a convenience store around 10 p.m., spent a meager ten minutes filling out the paperwork, and walked out. Our bags arrived at our final hotel just after we arrived seven days later.

Despite plenty of challenges, the trip ran as smoothly as I could have imagined. We dealt with heavy rain, 50 mph winds, and thick mist for our first few days, which forced us to slow down on the scrambling sections, layer up to stay warm, and take plenty of breaks in huts along the way. Some days had tons of vert (often more than 1,000 feet per mile) and rocky trails that made running difficult, so we embraced the shuffle. On day four, when covering our most remote section, we didn’t see a single other person. Fortunately the trails are well marked, even where they are less frequented and overgrown.

The crux of the route, the Kaerazu no Ken, is a long and serpentine downclimb on Class 4 granite slabs, offering a chain for protection in some areas while others did not. This was one of the dozen or so sections that having a helmet was a welcomed addition to our kits. For those comfortable with alpine climbing, this will feel like a fun change of pace. For those afraid of exposure, it’ll be challenging. The huts themselves vary considerably from small ridgetop outposts like Funakubo to much larger and busier outfits like Hakuba Sanso. Regardless of size, every hut owner we met was incredibly kind. Japanese hospitality is something they take very seriously.

Overall, our experience in the Hida was more than we could have asked for. Steep and technical trails, unique and cozy huts, fickle yet fruitful weather, and no other Americans or Europeans along the way. It’s an undiscovered gem for anyone outside Japan. With the help of Kota, Tatsuro, and others, I’m already planning a return trip next year.

One of the lightest climbing helmets on the market, the Vapor was perfect for our trip. We frequently had sections of running between scrambles and wouldn’t leave it on because it breathes so well. The Vapor fits over a hat and under a rain jacket hood, making it great for wet days, too.

The latest from Garmin is designed for routes like ours with a solar-powered display that ran the full week on a single charge. The maps were critical on wet days when I didn’t want to use my phone, and the flashlight was perfect for early mornings trying to not wake up other guests.

The perfect size pack for a trip like ours, the Adventure was able to carry everything we needed—spare clothes, first aid, snacks, camera, and ditty—with ease, plus poles, flasks, and a phone in the external pockets. It can be adjusted on the fly to reduce bounce and chafing.

On a week-long trip you end up eating a ton of snacks—gummies, chips, gels, and whatever you can buy at the huts—but nothing hit home like GU stroops. Whether it was with morning tea, on the top of a big climb, or preventing a bonk, stroops played a big role in our success.

With major improvements from the previous version, the Speedgoat 7 was the perfect shoe for this trip, offering plenty of grip on technical scrambles and ladders, a comfortable and cushy ride for the long days, and a lay-flat tongue that kept most rocks and dirt out.

The perfect mid-layer for cool mornings or windy days, the Dawner breathes well and is quite comfortable next to skin. The exterior is stretchy and durable, which is great for running through brush and rubbing against rocks— an inevitability in terrain like the Northern Alps.

#8244. The Best Laser Rangefinders for Hunting and Shooting, Tested and Reviewed

Published Nov 4, 2026 10:29 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Most of us judge a laser rangefinder by its obvious attributes. When we peer through the lens and press the ranging button, does it deliver an accurate and consistent distance to the target. Done and done. But when it comes to sorting out the best rangefinders for hunting, we need to dig a bit deeper.

A few curious members of our community navigate the mode commands, and learn that their range-u-lator can also measure incline, temperature, elevation, and altitude and apply a prodigious amount of ballistic calculation to make us more lethal hunters.

Ours is a test of these multidimensional monoculars, those that carry ballistic software, ranging reticles, and even navigation capability. Because not every hunter and shooter needs or wants that capability, we include a few point-and-shoot units fully worth your attention. This year’s field was among the most exciting we’ve seen with both high value and the latest technology. Here are our picks for best rangefinders for hunting from our 2026 optics test.

Garmin’s entry into the laser rangefinding market has had such a seismic effect on the category that once you use the L60i, LRF monoculars that simply measure distance and spit out a ballistic solution are so two-dimensional. By adding an augmented reality display that leverages Garmin’s extensive digital mapping services, the rangefinder becomes a first-rate wayfinder.

It’s impossible to overstate the ambition of this device. Garmin has managed to pack so much mapping horsepower in this handheld unit that it is being used by search-and-rescue agencies to locate wayward folks, by explorers who want to see what’s on the other side of a blind ridge, and by hunters who want step-by-step navigation to the spot they sighted that cross-canyon buck, even if they approach from the opposite direction.

The L60i communicates its mapping capabilities via a see-through overlay inside the display that seems at times like it’s an alternative-reality headset. You can see the real world of terrain through the glass of the optical system, but the display drops over the seen landscape a digital veil of landmarks, distances, navigation arrows, and waypoints. Operationally, this means you can find waypoints from any direction. Practically, it means the Garmin’s distance isn’t limited by its laser beam but by its optical gaze. If you can see a landmark, even 20 miles away, you can drop a waypoint on it using Garmin’s onboard map.

But the unit is also a first-rate laser rangefinder. Garmin rates its ranging capabilities in two very different conditions: full sunlight and optimal conditions. Those of us who have used laser rangefinders in full daylight know that the laser bounces off all sorts of reflective objects, limiting its precision. To get the best distance readings, you want to laze objects under cloudy skies or just after the sun has set. Garmin claims the L60i can range reflective targets out to 7,500 yards in optimum conditions, or to 5,500 yards in full sunlight. We got nearly those readings in our testing.

The Garmin also has a first-rate ballistics solver onboard, thanks to its long relationship with and now ownership of Applied Ballistics. It leverages the integrated AB Elite software or AB Quantum software via the Garmin app to provide not only ballistic groupings but the specific performance of custom loads out of your particular rifle. It links to Kestrel wind meters. It includes an archery mode and an extended-range ballistics mode for ranging out to nearly 8,000 yards. But it also links to the universe of Garmin devices, from dozens of smart watches to the company’s myriad GPS devices.

The unit is among the largest and heaviest (13.6 ounces with twin AAA batteries on board) LRF monoculars we’ve tested, but that heft settles nicely in hand. To get the best out of the unit’s extended range, mount it to a tripod via the threaded adapter on the underside of the monocular. But hand-holding the unit is the best way to enjoy its mapping features, because the heads-up overlay moves seamlessly with the landscape as you pan. The Garmin is at its best with both the rangefinding and mapping features employed. Laze a distant target, acquire the ballistic solution to make a shot (or not), then drop a waypoint on the target location. Now, employ the unit’s graphic overlay to not only “see” the waypoint on a topo map, but actually navigate to it, even if you approach from a different direction. Highlighted prompts give you step-by-step directions to the waypoint. The effect is surreal, as though you are watching yourself from the perspective of an eagle. Or a satellite.

This out-of-body experience is not only useful for the pedestrian tasks of hitting targets and retrieving game, but also for exploring your world both in your boots and from far above. By harnessing the best attributes of Garmin’s mapping library, applying an excellent ballistics package to the task, and then connecting both through devices, apps, and digital ecosystems, Garmin has elevated the LRF monocular to something that approaches the first do-everything handheld device on the market.

Outdoor Life’s testers approached the Garmin L60i with a dose of skepticism. Could an LRF monocular really drop waypoints 20 miles or more away? Could its heads-up display really be visible enough to be useful? And wasn’t that $2,500 price tag simply too precious? By the end of our test, every question had been resolved to our satisfaction, excepting the cliff-hanger: Whatever in the world will Garmin dream up next?

For its astonishing capabilities, its ability to perform as a ballistics-solving LRF at a high level, and the audacious ambition of the device, the Garmin L60i is the consensus winner of Editor’s Choice as the standout LRF monocular of the year.

An 850-yard rangefinder for under $100? That’s not only about 12 cents per yard, it’s a crazy value for a starter monocular or for hunters and shooters who don’t often shoot over a quarter mile.

The Triumph HD 850 continues Vortex’s product line that provides good performance and amazing value, with full warranty coverage. The Triumph line announced itself with the very good 10×42 binocular that has a real-world street price of about $100. Like the binocular, the HD 850 will get the job done, assuming the job is mid-distance ranging, without a lot of extraneous features or particularly good optics.

Vortex claims a range of 850 yards on reflective targets and 350 yards on game. We actually got pretty close, ranging metallic targets out to 680 yards and deer at 325 yards. The LRF has the typical modes: normal, first, and last target modes and line-of-sight and angle-adjusted ranging mode, along with a fairly sluggish scan mode.

The unit has a liquid crystal display that appears washed out against some backgrounds. The ranging engine is noticeably slower than the top LRFs in our test, but it’s just fine for most purposes. Note that the Triumph HD 850 doesn’t have a ballistic solver or location pinning or any of the features you might see in a unit that links to a phone app. But its angle-compensating mode and minimum ranging distance of 6 yards makes it a good choice for bowhunters. It’s also a good unit for shotgun hunters, straight-wall carbiners, and other hunters and shooters who shoot large-caliber bullets that drop quickly, and where knowing the specific yardage inside 300 yards is the difference between a clean miss and a killing shot.

The optics are pretty tough, and the plastic unit feels a little flimsy, but its 4.6-ounce weight and compact build make it a good choice for go-light hunters or a treestand hunter who doesn’t want, or need, a heavy ballistic-calculating rangefinder.

For all its remarkable value packed in a no-nonsense build and its ability to perform the basics we require of a laser rangefinding monocular, the Vortex Triumph HD 850 wins our Great Buy award as the great bargain of the year in laser rangefinders.

Bushnell has added some tasty updates to this workhorse LRF. The Broadhead 2 has Bushnell’s very good proprietary weatherproofing coatings that boost contrast and should make the unit more usable in drippy weather. Speaking of grubby conditions, the LRF’s Brush/Fog mode, which prioritizes farther targets, has a powerful update in this generation of the Broadhead. It’s a logic that discourages the laser from picking up reflections off water droplets, and Bushnell’s works quite well.

The second-generation Broadhead retains Bushnell’s ActiveSync display that sounds on the surface like a gimmick but is a very useful feature. Sensitive to light intensity, it runs black LCD in daylight conditions but automatically turns to a red illumination in twilight. It’s a clutch attribute that allows the display to pop against any background or light condition.

We really like the overbuilt VaultLite rangefinder pouch, which has useful hardware for belts, and we like the pistol grip of the unit. The protruding outline of the rearward battery compartment serves as a “hook” that grabs the hand, whether gloved or not, and helps stabilize the very light (6-ounce) monocular.

And we like the tripod mount on the belly of the unit. That’s a nice touch for those using the Broadhead at its most-distant ranges when precision is important.

The Broadhead 2 didn’t especially wow us with its optics, ranging horsepower, or menu navigation. All are fine, and just what you should expect from laser rangefinders at this price and ranging engine.

It may take users a bit of time to get used to Bushnell’s nomenclature. “Regular” mode is line-of-sight mode. “Bow” mode is the angle-compensating mode, which Bushnell calls its “ARC” feature. “Fog” mode is called “last target” by some manufacturers and Bushnell’s “Bullseye” mode is what most LRF users know as “first target” mode.

The Bushnell R5 Broadhead 2 is a great choice for bowhunters and rifle hunters and shooters who need to reach out to uncomfortable distances. The lack of a ballistic solver holds it back from being used by shooters who require more of an LRF than just range. But it’s a solid rangefinder in the middle of a very competitive pack.

The Gen II version of Sig’s excellent Kilo8K-ABS rangefinding monocular is more powerful, brighter, and connects to a larger galaxy of mapping and ballistics apps. In other words, it’s almost a brand-new laser rangefinder.

Its engine even got an upgrade. The Kilo8K-ABS Gen II runs on Sig’s new LightWave DSP, which returns four readings a second in scan mode, even out to a mile. Its return is snappy, precise, and confident, and new coatings and optics make the active-matrix display pop. The display is worth a few sentences. Some manufacturers are so busy crowding information in their display that the result is a confusing thicket of distance, ballistics solutions, angle, temperature, and mode. Sig has done a nice job of simplifying the display to just the elements needed to make a quick shot: the range, and the come-up and wind holds. In the field, it’s fast and simple.

The lazing power of the unit is simply stunning. In extended-range mode and strapped to a tripod, I was able to range grassy hillsides at 6,200 yards without much trouble. I worked on getting the claimed 8,000 yards out of the unit, but couldn’t quite get there. The impressive part to me isn’t the distance, it’s the speed of the DSP engine.

The onboard Applied Ballistics Elite software is similarly impressive. You can tack up the data by connecting to the AB Quantum app, but you don’t need to. The entire ballistics library is in the palm of your hand, almost quivering in the 7.5-ounce monocular that’s begging to be put to work. That the unit also connects to Sig’s BDX devices, including BDX-enabled riflescopes, gives this monocular even more utility.

There are a lot of choices on the market for ballistics-solving LRF monoculars. At first glance, the price of the 8K-ABS Gen II (just under $1,500) seems excessive, but when you consider its ability to quickly and precisely range, then deliver an equally fast and verified aiming solution out to 4.5 miles … I don’t know that I’d call the Sig a bargain, but it’s a very good deal for hunters and shooters who intend to take it to its impressive limits.

We’ve seen Leupold’s RX-5000 before. Two years ago, we gushed about its ability to remotely drop onX pins just by lazing a distant spot and then pinning the location to the digital map on your phone. It’s a useful feature, but Leupold’s competitors have made it standard on so many LRF monoculars and binoculars that it’s no longer novel.

But a lot has changed with this little handheld marvel since then. Its ballistics solvers are now powered by Hornady’s excellent 4DOF software, its bow mode borrows from Precision Cut Archery software, and its mapping feature is not limited to onX Hunt. You can drop pins on maps from Deercast, HuntStand, and both Apple and Google maps. Those updates are enough to include it in this roundup of new LRF monoculars because, while the form factor and operation are pretty much the same, the guts of the RX-5000 are new and galaxies more powerful and useful than the original.

That form factor is worth mentioning. While many sub-$400 LRF monoculars feel flimsy, the Leupold has a tight, metallic heft that settles nicely in hand. We wish the unit had a tripod adapter built in, but the tripod “saddle” that Leupold ships is a good addition, and it’s necessary to get the most out of the RX-5000’s long-range chops. With the unit stabilized on a tripod, we were able to get ranges very nearly to 5,000 yards, and when you add Hornady’s 4DOF ballistic solver to that extended distance, it’s both imaginable and possible to hit targets at that extreme distance.

The optics in the Leupold are excellent. The 8-power magnification combined with the relatively large 30mm objective make this a pretty good glassing unit. But the value proposition, of course, is the ballistics paired with the fast and precise ranging engine. Given the huge amount of ballistic computations, the powerful laser, the excellent Leupold Control app, and generally clear and intuitive navigation, you could make the case that the 799RX-5000issotalentedthatitcouldundercuttheequallyimpressivebutpricey(3,900) BX-6 Range HD, Leupold’s new LRF binocular.

With this do-everything long-range LRF monocular, Leica has regained its standing at the head of the rangefinding line. The Rangemaster CRF Max not only compares favorably to peers from Sig and Leupold, but its build and optics borrow from its extensive history in the category.

But it’s the electronic guts of the Rangemaster CRF Max, introduced in 2025 but hitting retailers’ shelves now, that elevate the device. Leica has stuffed the monocular with a best-in-class ballistics solver (Applied Ballistics Elite), an interesting should-I-or-shouldn’t-I shot-probability calculator that gives you the odds of making extra-long shots, a location feature to drop waypoints on digital maps, and a tracking tool that guides shooters from the place they took the shot to the location of the target.

For just under $1,500, that’s a lot of performance packed in a tight, elegant build. The flat dark earth colorway is a giveaway to its talents. Leica has started to use device color to define its place in the brand pantheon. The base Rangemaster CRF is onyx black, the mid-level Rangemaster CRF Pro is forest green, and the top-of-the-line Rangemaster CRF Max has this handsome FDE exterior.

The unit has all the ranging features you’d expect, including three target modes, the ability to input wind direction and intensity or connect to an external anemometer, and the ability to use either onboard ballistics or import custom ballistic data from Leica’s excellent mobile app.

The 3,700-yard maximum range for the device may not compete with Sig’s 8,000-yard model or Leupold’s 5,000-yard monocular, but it’s plenty powerful for nearly any long-range hunting or shooting situation. We managed to get very nearly that distance when ranging hillsides and reflective signs.

The laser return is fast, the display is clear and bright and customizable, so you can include only the data you need to make quick, confident shots. And the glass and coatings are superior, as you’d expect from an optics company with the performance expectations of Leica.

If Bushnell’s Broadhead 2 is purpose-built for bowhunters, the 2000 AB version is similarly configured for rifle hunters. To have baked-in Applied Ballistics’ solver in a $250 rangefinder is pretty extraordinary.

The value proposition of this new R5 rangefinder is pretty appealing. Once you build a ballistic profile for your rifle load in the Bushnell Ballistics mobile app, then connect via Bluetooth, the rangefinder will give you a distance-informed hold in MOA or MIL. Note that the Ultralite version of Applied Ballistics is valid only out to 800 yards, but that’s plenty enough horsepower for most hunters and long-range shooters.

The pros and cons that we discussed in the Broadhead 2 all apply to the 2000 AB, with the exception of the display. While the archery R5 contains Bushnell’s excellent ActiveSync display, the rifle version has only a black LCD. We also note that the 2000 AB is powered by a single CR2 lithium battery. We’d like to see a CR123-sized powerplant for extended use given the amount of data the little unit has to crunch.

The R5 2000 AB retails for $250, but you can expect to see that price come down as the unit wins more fans and as more customers learn about the crazy amount of performance in such a simple and affordable rangefinding monocular.

Manufacturers’ ranging claims are as spurious as a camouflage company’s promise to elude. Most take their best distances, not their average, and discount target size and orientation. They don’t always report what we found, some inconsistent ranging on a wide variety of surfaces, from gravel to grass to 3D archery targets to trees. We test the maximum and minimum range, and use every targeting mode and menu option. We’ve provided the max and minimum ranges we were able to achieve on non-reflective targets to give you an idea of real-world capabilities.

We mount monoculars on tripods to get rock-solid ranging, and we take the units in the field, deploying them both methodically and rapidly at targets of various sizes and distances. And then we pair them to a slave rifle and a ballistic app and judge their ability to improve our shooting accuracy.

We break our 10-point scoring into four general categories: ranging performance, display and optics, features, and value. The average of these categories is the basis of our grades, detailed below.

Ranging performance includes both the maximum and minimum distances the unit is capable of ranging, but also ranging precision and ability to repeatedly range objects of various sizes and textures. The performance score also considers various targeting modes. Display and optics assesses how well the unit “sees” targets, how useful and adjustable the display is to each users’ eyesight and different light conditions, and reticle utility. The feature grade assesses whether the unit connects to a mobile app, or contains a ballistic library, or has on-board sensors. Lastly, our value grade is a measure of whether the unit is worth its price, and considers its peer group, warranty, and amenities like a lanyard or carrying case.

The laser rangefinder that gets the highest overall score wins our Editor’s Choice award for the best in the category; the optic with the highest price/value score wins our Great Buy recognition. We also assigned other awards for specific noteworthy attributes.

Our 10-point evaluation adds up to a total numeric score, but we translate those to grades for each submission. The ranging Performance grade combines the scores from ranging, accuracy, sensitivity, and processor speed. Our Display/Optics grade aggregates both display and optics scores. The Features grade considers amenities, connectivity, and versatility. And then the Price/Value grade is our assessment of whether a rangefinder is worth the money, which also considers durability.

To earn an “Excellent” grade, the average of that category must be 9 or higher, which is extremely hard to achieve. “Very Good” is an average score of 7 to 9. A “Good” grade is 5 to 7. Our “Fair” grade is 3 to 5, and “Poor” is anything under 3. This scoring system gives us a great comparative tool for the best rangefinders for hunting.

As you can deduce from the wide variety of capabilities in submission to this year’s LRF test, you can spend over $1,000 for a gee-whiz rangefinder, or you can spend $200 for a basic unit that will range your target even if it doesn’t make you breakfast.

It’s up to you to determine what you want out of a rangefinding monocular. Do you want a hand-held ballistic calculator that will give you precise ranging out to 2 miles for your pet load? Or are you satisfied with a basic unit that provides line-of-sight and angle-adjusted ranging and little else?

Of course, there are plenty of units that reside between those two poles, but the biggest differentiator for LRFs in this year’s test are those that borrow from a mobile app to provide very specific customized aiming solutions, and those that don’t allow for many inputs and instead spit out ranges for a few basic hunting and shooting scenarios.

The price between those two capabilities is immense, with Bluetooth-connected units selling for close to $1,000 and bare-bones LRFs retailing for under $300.

Beyond those basics, if you are mainly a bowhunter who wants archery-specific ranging data, look for those units that have arrow-flight dynamics baked into their software. Similarly, suppose you’re an ultra-long-distance target shooter. In that case, you’re going to want a unit with precise, situation-informed ranging results based around the specific bullet dynamics you’ve measured and plugged into the ranging software.

Check out the display of a rangefinder you’re interested in in a wide variety of light conditions. Some units have blazingly bright OLED displays while others have black LCD displays that can get lost against a cluttered background or low-light situations.

Lastly, consider the warranty. Unlike the lifetime, fully transferable warranty that has become an industry standard for non-electronic optics like binoculars and rifle scopes, most companies offer a limited warranty for electronics like rangefinders. But there’s such a wide range of protection on the market that it pays to take a close look at the details.

There are a lot of great rangefinders for hunting. To find the best one for you, you need to consider how, where, and what you hunt.

Bushnell rangefinders are popular, especially because they are affordable. But there are also other options that are better in some ways.

Yes, a rangefinder is an incredibly valuable tool for hunting.

That depends. Cheap rangefinders can work great if you only need to range shorter distances under 200 yards or so, and you won’t be subjecting them to bad weather or too much moisture. For some hunters, they will get the job done.

Most of us use only a single laser rangefinder button—the ranging button—and as long as we get fast, reliable range dope, we’re happy. That’s actually how we started our assessment, simply by punching the range button and recording the results.

But the cool thing about the best rangefinders for hunting is that they are so adaptive. The most sophisticated have on-board or off-board ballistics solvers that can guide a bullet well beyond reasonable ranges. The best units have environmental sensors and sensitive angle and directional intelligence that can inform a shot whether you’re connected to your phone, or not. And the expectation of a LRF these days is that it must have both line-of-sight and angle-adjusted ranging along with ballistically informed ranging.

If you don’t need the full-on connected unit, make sure the unconnected unit performs the basics well, with an intensity adjusted display, an ergonomic body, and enough features to enable ranging a buck deer standing behind a screen of branches. The only downside to this crop of capable rangefinders is that they’re removing our last excuse for missing that must-hit shot.

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.

#8243. South Dakota Is Losing Its Hometown Pheasant Hunters. Meanwhile, the Nonresident Business Is Booming

Published Nov 4, 2026 1:52 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

I was hunting a strip of public walk-in access across the road from a fleet of combines. As the harvesters crawled closer, pheasants kept flushing out of the standing corn and into the chest-high cover I was following my dog through. I marked one rooster that landed 300 yards ahead and, when Hatchet eventually trailed and flushed him, I was ready.

But I never shouldered my gun. The bird flushed straight toward the cab of a grain truck and veered out of range. The man sitting behind the windshield, who looked to be in his 20s, threw up his arms. Worried I might be irritating the farmers despite my restraint, I headed for my truck — the one with the Arkansas plates — with the birds I’d already killed. I know I’m a visitor here, and I don’t want to contribute to an existing problem.

This fall I drove 10 hours from my home to hunt public-land pheasants. It’s my seventh season in a row making the trip, and I can’t remember ever seeing more pickups loaded with kennels and coolers on I-29. We were all South Dakota bound.

As I’ve hunted my tried-and-true public spots and explored new ones this year, I’ve been surprised (though seldom hindered) by the number of fellow hunters getting after it. Each time I pass a truck parked in the ditch, I can’t help but clock the license plate: Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa, North Dakota. I’ve yet to spot a South Dakota plate that seems to belong to a pheasant hunter.

Anecdotal though it may be, my experience tracks with a broader trend in South Dakota. Annual harvest surveys show nonresident pheasant hunters are outnumbering resident hunters, and have every year since 2002. Last season approximately 57,100 residents hunted pheasants, while about 82,600 nonresidents hunted pheasants, according to those survey projections from South Dakota Game, Fish and Parks.

And during opening weekend on Oct. 17 and 18, SDGFP conservation officers talked with some 1,800 pheasant hunters. They hailed from 44 different states.

Many South Dakotans worry their home state is too busy courting these nonresident hunters — or more precisely, their wallets — to notice the fading tradition of resident pheasant culture.

“We love out-of-state hunters. And we want everybody to keep coming and enjoying South Dakota’s tradition,” says Brad Johnson, a South Dakota real-estate appraiser and lifelong hunter. “We just want our state government and our state tourism industry to understand the importance of in-state hunters. I think there’s a real strong feeling that we’re being taken for granted.”

Johnson, who lives in Watertown, recently wrote a column in the South Dakota Searchlight that dug into this trend — and struck a nerve with locals. He acknowledges that nonresidents are the “financial backbone” of the state’s pheasant program, thanks to higher license fees. (Residents pay $36 for a season-long small game license and a $10 habitat stamp; nonresidents pay $142 to hunt birds for 10 days, plus a $25 habitat stamp.)

“We understand that [financial dynamic] as South Dakota hunters. But at the same time, we need to start putting more emphasis on growing in-state hunting,” says Johnson. “We put so much of our advertising effort in out-of-state markets that we know where most of the hunters come from. And we don’t do similar types of advertising geared toward local residents and trying to figure out programs that are going to build new hunters within the state.”

DIY public-land pheasant hunting, especially during poor bird years, isn’t for the faint of heart. I’ve had to work for my limits of wild roosters over the seasons, slogging miles through nasty weather, thick cover, cattail sloughs, and rolling hills. Last weekend I hiked 9 miles over public ground with my dog (who covered 15 on his own four legs) and two buddies to fill our three limits. It was one of the best days of pheasant hunting I can remember.

For hunters with more cash and less interest in (or the physical ability for) such a grind, South Dakota offers hundreds of private shooting preserves. These lodges cater to businessmen, casual hunters, and the wealthy — almost exclusively out-of-staters who fly into hubs like Pierre and Aberdeen to shoot high volume put-and-take birds. Business is booming.

In the last quarter century, the number of licensed pheasant preserves across the state has grown substantially, from 157 in 2001 to a record 237 last season. Preserves must be a minimum of 160 acres (and no more than 2,560 acres). And over the past nine seasons, the harvest of released captive pheasants shot on preserves has climbed 50 percent (this excludes incidental harvest of wild birds). During the 2025-26 season, hunters shot about 400,000 pheasants on preserves — a record high.

“Everybody’s got a story about why they don’t hunt now, and all other problems that they’ve had getting access compared to how it used to be,” Johnson says of local hunters. “There’s a shift in emphasis in South Dakota toward more the commercialization of hunting — and I get it. I’ve got a lot of friends who own hunting operations … They’ve got really nice hunting operations. They’re all paid hunting and geared almost 100 percent to out-of-state hunters … Very few people in South Dakota are going to pay for that type of experience.”

Residents simply can’t afford the rates — from $2,000 to $4,000 per day at the fanciest lodges, he says — that traveling hunters are willing to pay. Meanwhile, hunting operations are leasing private land for their clients. This is more of an issue in east-central South Dakota, in the heart of pheasant country.

This steady rise in preserve pheasant hunting also contributes to access fees or the leasing of private land that could otherwise be open for permission to residents. After doing some work for a real-estate client one year, Johnson asked if he could hunt their property.

“They said, ‘Well, is it pheasant hunting? And if it’s pheasant hunting, would you be willing to pay a little bit? If it’s duck hunting, just go ahead,’” says Johnson. “So we value our pheasants quite a bit.”

While the hunter numbers cited in this story focus on wild pheasant hunting, the data they’re drawn from is murky (more on this in a bit). SDGFP explicitly says “no shooting preserve license holders were surveyed and none of their harvest is included” in wild bird harvest estimates. But these annual figures undoubtedly capture some preserve hunts, since hunters can legally shoot pheasants on preserves using their small game licenses.

The state’s harvest reports also don’t include any details on where hunters are killing pheasants or if they’re paying for access.

One lifelong South Dakota hunter, who asked not to be named so as not to upset factions of the hunting community, still puts the permission success rate at about 50 percent near the Pierre area.

“When I was a kid, it was all wild birds. We’d hop on the tailgate, the kids would walk through the [nasty cover], and adults blocked or did the easy stuff. It was opening weekend and it was a tradition. I think that tradition is still there, and I think people want to celebrate it the same way, but it has been commercialized. It wasn’t commercialized when I was a kid. It was good old landowners who let people hunt.”

South Dakota’s most recent push to ramp up pheasant license sales began in 2020 with its “Hunt the Greatest” campaign. The collaboration between the state’s game and tourism agencies spent about $662,000 that year in advertising on cable TV, podcasts like MeatEater, and in paid searches online, among other avenues. (Outdoor Life has also received South Dakota tourism funding for sponsored campaigns.) And in 2024, the campaign targeted South Dakota plus 13 out-of-state markets, including Minnesota, Iowa, Nebraska, Wisconsin, Colorado, Texas, and Michigan.

Neither agency could provide the breakdown of spending by in-state and out-of-state dollars to OL by press time.

The Hunt the Greatest campaign launched the year following the state’s final roadside pheasant counts, in 2019.

“Then-Governor Kristi Noem did away with that [roadside brood count], and that was partly because of the pressure from the tourism industry,” says Johnson. Noem’s family owned a pheasant lodge, and she also described herself as an owner and operator of a hunting lodge. “If the report came out that bird numbers were down, that sometimes caused out-of-state hunters to not come.”

Concluding the best long-running and scientific data collection on the state’s bird numbers was controversial, to say the least. As one former pheasant research biologist with SDGFP put it, the state’s current hunter survey stats are “fake news” that are “not verifiable or scientific.”

“The loss of the brood survey … means we have no accurate information on South Dakota pheasant populations for seven years,” that biologist, Larry Fredrickson, wrote in a letter to the Huron Daily Plainsman this spring. “I hope the state gets the brood survey back soon … to get South Dakota pheasant management out of the dark ages.”

The harvest numbers Fredrickson refers to — which this story necessarily relies on, since it’s the only available data on recent pheasant hunting participation and harvest — elicit limited participation from residents (25 percent responded to the survey) and nonresidents (31 percent responded), among other issues.

Given that the state has discontinued those roadside brood counts, Johnson says South Dakota would rather nonresidents not know when it’s a bad pheasant year.

“Just believe us when we tell you, ‘Oh, pheasant hunting’s gonna be great,’” Johnson jokes. “But by doing that, we lose the scientific analysis on what really is happening with our bird population.”

It’s also unfair to traveling hunters, says 73-year-old resident duck and pheasant hunter Bruce Knowlan. No matter how much money they inject into the economy, most DIY pheasant hunters still have finite time and budgets to hunt birds.

“Hunting isn’t a sport anymore, it’s an industry,” says Knowlan of the canceled roadside counts and continued marketing during down bird years. “It’s crazy, it breaks my heart.”

None of the locals I spoke with for this story felt animosity toward well-mannered visiting hunters. That includes Knowlan, who lives in northeast South Dakota. The rural community he calls home is very welcoming to nonresident pheasant hunters.

“They like people who are spending money in the towns. They like nonresident money. They like their motels busy, they like their restaurants busy,” says Knowlan. “The only thing people around here hate is nonresidents coming into the area, buying farmland, and taking it out of [crop] production to put it into some program like CREP or CRP.”

In other words, farmers and residents are happy to have out-of-staters hunt pheasants, support local businesses, and maintain the area’s farming traditions and economy.

And indeed, nonresidents spent an estimated $161.8 million statewide during the 2025 season. While visiting hunters presumably spend more on expenses like lodging during pheasant season, it’s clear: resident pheasant hunters help drive the economy, too. Last year they spent an estimated $142.7 million in the state.

To Knowlan’s mind, there are fewer resident pheasant hunters in recent decades because there are simply fewer South Dakotans living in rural areas. Even as South Dakota’s population has grown steadily in the last few decades, most of that growth has gone into urban areas.

Case in point: The population of the northeast South Dakota county where Knowlan lives has steadily declined over the past century, dropping 64 percent to roughly 5,500 people in 2025. Meanwhile, farms have been consolidated, which means there are fewer landowners to ask for permission to hunt the same amount of ground.

“It’s fascinating to me that if you take the back roads from my place into town, there used to be a farm every 80 acres,” says Knowlan, adding that families used to have more kids, too. “I would go by a hundred kids’ homes in a six-mile radius. And now, on that same road, there’s maybe four. They’re bigger farms.”

Consolidation of small farms and the rise of hunting leases and access fees are key reasons Knowlan says it’s “much, much harder” to get permission on private land than it was decades ago.

“Residents aren’t going to go out and lease the neighbor’s land so they can go pheasant hunting,” says Knowlan. “It’s still a family tradition around here, but not like it used to be, where everybody would quit working at noon on Saturday and go pheasant hunting at the neighbor’s.”

Still, he doesn’t think South Dakota is different from any other state when it comes to diminished private access. Before he bought his South Dakota farm in 2011, Knowlan was a DIY hunter from Minnesota who hunted all over North America — including South Dakota — each season. He remembers what it was like to ask for permission, and what it’s like to grant it.

“I do think a lot of guys still would allow pheasant hunting, if they don’t have relatives or family members they’re saving it for,” says Knowlan. “It used to be, I’d say, 90 percent of people would let you hunt. Maybe now, around here, it’d be 50 percent. But I would hate to be a young man, 16 to 20 years old [again], and not have a lot of money and want to do it yourself all over the country. It would almost be impossible.”

Yes, there are more nonresident pheasant hunters than South Dakota pheasant hunters, and that means they’re killing more total pheasants. But locals are enjoying longer hunting seasons and they’re killing, on average, more birds per hunter than visitors more often than not in recent years.

Last season nonresidents, who are more likely to shell out for private access, killed an average of 9.3 pheasants. Residents killed an average of 10.2 birds during their season, and most probably didn’t pay for the privilege.

For an even greater edge, Johnson would like to expand the special three-day resident-only pheasant opener that falls on the weekend before nonresidents are allowed to hunt.

“People feel that expanding that might be helpful for giving in-state residents a little bit more of an advantage.”

Resident youth license sales are also on the rise in recent years. South Dakota already has strong opportunities for new hunters — adults and kids alike — to get into pheasant hunting.

Youth and mentored hunters “have a 9-day period to themselves for pheasant hunting” prior to the regular season opening,” according to SDGFP regs. “This is an opportunity for adults to take young hunters out to experience, first-hand, the joy of hunting as well as the responsibility.”

Still, there’s at least one complicating factor to recruiting younger hunters into the fold: You must be 16 to hunt alone in South Dakota. Adjusting this age restriction for qualified teens might be another way to encourage participation.

I learned of this requirement just a few weeks ago, after agreeing to take a local 15-year-old and his retriever pheasant hunting. I assumed they were still learning the ropes and needed guidance on strategy and an extra gun for the dog. This was true enough, but the reality was he needed me to legally chase pheasants. This South Dakota teenager (whose parents don’t hunt) needed an adult alongside him to shoot pheasants. The irony is that he drove himself to our meet up. You can start driving solo at 14 and a half in South Dakota.

South Dakota has some of the best public-land access around, especially compared to other historic pheasant states like Iowa and Nebraska. There are 1.6 million acres open to public hunting across South Dakota, according to SDGFP. And indeed, I have never once thought to ask strangers for pheasant hunting permission in seven years of bird hunting here, because of the abundance of uncrowded public land. The number of private acres enrolled in public-access programs has also grown over the last decade.

Still, Johnson would like to see South Dakota invest in drivable access to its public lands. (This echoes a larger national debate around what constitutes “access” to public lands.)

“South Dakota’s got a tremendous amount of public land. I think there are things that Game, Fish and Parks can do in managing that land that makes it easier, especially for older hunters, to get on it,” says Johnson. “We might have miles of public land in one tract and the parking lot is out by the road. And it’s fenced off. And so if you wanna get access deeper into the land, you’ve got to be in good physical shape to be able to walk deeper into it.”

SDGFP communications manager Nick Harrington says the agency absolutely cares about resident pheasant hunters and its goal is to recruit, retain, and reactivate as many pheasant hunters as possible. He’s attending a women’s learn-to-pheasant-hunt event Sunday, and also cited the grand opening of the agency’s expanded outdoor campus in Sioux Falls on Thursday.

“This expansion project is important as GFP will be able to offer more programs year-round,” reports KELO-AM, “which will include archery, game processing, and classes taking students on their hunting journey from the field to the table.”

I have volunteered as an instructor at a women’s learn-to-pheasant hunt weekend in South Dakota every August for the last four years. I’ve offered sessions on everything from shotgun basics to bird dog demos to finding promising public hunting spots. These programs, and my hunt with that local teen and other new pheasant hunters I’ve taken out, reminded me of what I’ve learned from years spent reporting on the national hunter recruitment problem. New adult hunters are usually recruited into the sport only after two to three years of continuous mentorship and support from dedicated existing hunters. Youth programs typically only succeed at recruiting kids who are already from hunting families.

The best way to keep family hunting traditions alive, in other words, is to take family hunting — again and again.

There is one simple correlation around pheasant hunting that’s difficult to ignore: Both resident and nonresident pheasant hunter numbers are linked to wild pheasant numbers. When harsh weather leads to low bird numbers, fewer hunters go pheasant hunting. When winter snowfall and spring rains are mild, bird numbers shoot up, and more hunters buy licenses. This is true in recent years, which have seen excellent bird harvests.

The most dedicated pheasant hunters will keep buying licenses every year, no matter how poor or good the hunting. It’s a tradition, and the best ones, including South Dakota pheasant hunting, will endure as long as there are places to hunt and people there who welcome hunters.

On my way out of my public spot near the hard-working combines, I waved to the young farmer still idling in the grain truck. He stepped out of the cab with a broad smile on his face and, dangling on the step, hollered over the rumble of harvesters.

“I can’t afford to repair your truck!” I shouted back.

He shook his head at that and, still grinning, waved me on.

Natalie Krebs is the Executive Editor of Outdoor Life, where she tackles everything from reporting digital features to producing podcast episodes. Originally from Missouri, she currently lives in northwest Arkansas with her bird dog, Hatchet.

#8241. “We Used FFS and Were Targeting Big Bass.” Angler Breaks 76-Year-Old Smallmouth Bass Record

Published Nov 4, 2026 4:14 PM EST

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

On the morning of October 30 Austin Schiefer and his fishing buddy Ted Johnson launched their bass boat into Green Bay, a huge Wisconsin portion of Lake Michigan. They started about 7:30 working a reef area in 18 feet of water about two miles from shore. Before long, they’d go on to break a 76-year-old fishing record.

“It was a spot we’d fished previously and caught nice smallmouths on,” Schiefer tells Outdoor Life. “We used forward-facing sonar and were targeting big bass.”

The morning started windy, ideal conditions for clear water bass on Green Bay. The duo was catching bass, but about mid-day the wind died and the water got calm.

“That’s not the best conditions for Green Bay,” says Schiefer, who works for UPS when he’s not producing his own line of soft plastic lures (Schief’s Custom Baits). “There were plenty of bass on the reef, but they were finicky and wouldn’t take the lures I was casting.”

Johnson, however, was catching bass using a different type of soft plastic. He suggested to Schiefer that he try one of the lures he was doing well with, and to go lighter with his tackle.

“The bite was light and deep, so I changed to the setup that Ted suggested,” says Schiefer, from Menasha, Wisconsin.

Schiefer changed over to a Deps Sakamata Shad Soft Jerkbait, which is a 5-inch lure, and the productive hue was “champagne-pepper.”

He threaded the lure onto a 3/32nd-ounce jighead and made a long cast with the lightest 7-foot spinning rod he owns. His reel was spooled with 8-pound test Power Pro braided line with a 10-pound test fluorocarbon leader.

“I wanted to make a long cast and sort of swim the lure back as it sank, a pendulum like retrieve,” says Schiefer. “We could see fish on bottom with sonar, but they’d rise up to take lures. Except they were refusing my lures just before they’d hit – until I cast that Deps Jerkbait.”

It was about 2 p.m. and as Schiefer’s lure sank he felt a hit. But the fish didn’t fight like a smallmouth. The battle wasn’t fast and furious and there were no jumps. Just a couple minutes of it taking drag, and rugged deep pulling and rolling – so much so that Schiefer thought perhaps he’d hooked a freshwater drum.

“But as I worked it to the surface I got a look at it in that clear water about 10 feet down, and I saw that it was a huge smallmouth,” he says. “I knew it was a monster, and when I got it to the boat Ted netted it.

“I got lucky, because the hook was bent when I took the lure out of its mouth.”

Schiefer had caught big smallmouths previously, but nothing over 7 pounds, so he knew his catch was important. They put the lunker bass in their boat livewell and tried to contact Wisconsin’s Department of Natural Resources. But it was Friday afternoon before Halloween, and no one from the DNR was available.

The anglers quit fishing and trailered their boat to a grocery store where the bass was weighed at 9 pounds, 11ounces on certified scales. It measured 23.75 inches long. The smallmouth easily topped the 1950 Wisconsin record smallie weighing 9 pounds, 1 ounce. That fish was caught by Leon Stefonek in Oneida County’s Indian Lake.

To qualify as a state record bass, the DNR required the fish to be weighed and examined by state biologists. That didn’t happen until the next day, when DNR fisheries staff weighed and inspected the fish.

They discovered the bass was a male, not a female – which usually are the larger of the two fish genders. Additionally, Schiefer’s 9.70-pound smallmouth had nothing in its stomach, again unusual as most bass in autumn are feeding heavily for the coming winter.

Schiefer will have a skin mount made of his smallmouth bass record, which he says has been officially recognized by DNR as Wisconsin’s heaviest bronzeback of all time. He’s also considering having replica mounts made of the fish.

Read Next: 7 Forward Facing Sonar Tips: Settings, Mounting, and Techniques Explained

“I think a replica mount of the bass would be nice for the National Freshwater Fishing Hall of Fame in their Hayward museum, and maybe one for Bass Pro Shops, too,” he says.

“My only regret in all of this is I didn’t release the fish alive. I couldn’t with the DNR requirements for weighing and inspecting the fish for the record… I’ve had some sleepless nights because of that. I did everything in my power to keep from killing that bass.”

#8240. Old Town Sportsman PDL 120 Pro Kayak Review

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

The Old Town Sportsman PDL 120 Pro is a beast. I tested this boat on a 6-mile fishing trip, standing, pedaling, and accessorizing the kayak to see what it can do—and I was impressed. If the name Sportsman PDL 120 Pro sounds familiar, that’s because it’s been in the Old Town lineup for some time. But this year Old Town completely redesigned the top half of this kayak and re-released it. The new model features horizontal rod tubes, a deeper and wider tankwell and cockpit, pre-set grommets for mounting motors and anchors, and more. The seat’s mounting system is different, too. Basically, everything from the water line up is different—and better. Here’s a closer look at the redesigned Old Town Sportsman PDL 120 Pro.

The top half of this boat has been completely redesigned with thinner walls and deeper wells to create more room for storage and operating space. The Sportsman PDL 120 Pro has a combined 150 inches of track, pre-cut through-hull wiring ports, pre-set holes for mounting motors and shallow water anchors, and three access hatches to get down into the hull. That means you can modify this boat however you want. Plus, the front hatch is twice as big as the previous design, and there are four horizontal rod tubes.

Old Town also redesigned the seat so the angler sits higher and has a better paddling angle. The seat sits on adjustable tracks, so you can slide it forward or back for a custom fit. Four knobs beneath the seat can be loosened and tightened from the seated position, so you can adjust the seat even on the water. A large rudder at the rear of the boat deploys with a lever to the right of the angler and is controlled with a knob to the left. Overall, the seating and controls are top-notch. The Sportsman PDL 120 Pro retails for $3,599.

I tested the Sportsman PDL 120 Pro on Thurlow Reservoir while targeting bass and catfish. I laid my bass rods in the rod tubes, with the reels to the sides of the seat. I put my tackle under the seat, my phone and keys in the little waterproof hatch on top of the PDL Drive console, and a large cooler and 14 floats in the rear tankwell.

I peddled about 6 miles during that trip, targeting bass for the first 5 hours. I liked being able to control the boat relatively hands-free with the PDL Drive while still actively fishing. I had to turn the rudder control knob, of course, when moving from spot to spot. But while fishing, I found I could backpedal if I drifted too far forward, and I could stop or correct myself when needed. The PDL Drive let me cover significantly more water than my traditional paddle kayak.

I stood up a couple of times and found the boat extremely stable in both scenarios. I was also really impressed with how sturdy and powerful the PDL Drive is. I could scoot along pretty well with this pedal drive system, and it didn’t rock back and forth like some others I’ve tried in the past. Towards the end of the trip, I baited up 14 floats and tossed them in the lake to try to catch catfish. That ended up being the most fun I had all day. As the floats started bobbing, I chased them down with the PDL Drive, giggling as I got close. I landed three solid fish and tossed them in the cooler to clean up for a buddy.

What really impressed me was how sturdy this boat is. I weigh 260 pounds, and leaning over to grab something out of the water is enough to topple many kayaks. But even when I stretched as far as I could to grab the float, the Old Town PDL 120 Pro didn’t budge, with the top of the gunwale staying several inches above the water. And, using the rudder and control knob, I was able to slip right up within inches of the floats, once I got the hang of it.

Installing the Minn Kota Kayak Terrova trolling motor on the Old Town 120 PDL Pro elevated this boat to an entirely different class of vessel—quite literally, since I had to register it at the courthouse after adding the motor. But practically speaking, the troller put this boat into a whole other league. While I’m not the biggest fan of installation projects like this, I found some great tutorial videos on Old Town’s website and dove in headfirst.

Mounting the motor itself was super easy, with pre-set mounting hardware built into the bow, specifically for the Kayak Terrova. Just line the Quick Release MKA-21 Bracket up and screw in the four bolts. This bracket is sold separately, but I recommend it so that you can take the motor on and off when loading the boat, to lighten the load. It’s also good to have it so you can detach the motor and set it in the truck or hotel room when on the road.

With the motor mounted, I bought a 6-gauge marine wire to run the length of the boat from the trolling motor to the battery—I put the battery in the stern to disperse the weight. The kit includes an optional relay board you can use to add a safety switch. I highly recommend doing this, even though it’s a little bit of a headache. The safety switch acts like the kill switch on an outboard motor and stops the Terrova instantly should you fall off.

After installing the safety switch near the seat and connecting all the appropriate wires to the relay, I was ready to hook up the battery, pair the motor to the included Micro Remote, and test it out. To test the motor, I took the boat to a local lake on a windy day. It blew 15 miles per hour, sustained throughout most of the day—the type of day I just wouldn’t have fished from a kayak if all I had was a paddle. Even the pedal drive would have been brutal. But with the motor, I could set a course into the wind and set my speed using the AutoPilot feature, or hit Spot-Lock and sit in place while I fished a point, brushpile, or dock. I even used the AutoPilot feature to slowly drift backward in strong current under the dam; I plowed my way upstream with the motor on high, then pointed my motor into the current, set it to about 40 percent, and slowly drifted backward to where I could fish without the motor raging at full bore.

The Terrova is phenomenal, plain and simple. It was a bit of a headache to install, but if I can do it, you can too. Stowing and deploying can be a bit cumbersome at first. I saw people use a rope around the shaft to lower the motor slowly and raise it back up, so I did that, and it worked well. I found my paddle to be the best tool in the boat for pushing the locking deploy/stow lever to send the motor out or lift it back up. The Lift-Assist feature also helps with deployment and stowing.

All things considered, the redesigned Old Town PDL 120 Pro is a great boat. It’s sturdy, has a fantastic layout, and the PDL Drive system is top-notch. If you’re into accessories, you can trick this boat out a hundred different ways. Stability is my biggest concern when kayak fishing, and this boat is among the most stable I’ve ever set foot in. I really value a good seat and seat positioning, too. The higher seat and better angle make it much easier to stand, stay seated longer, and fish all day. Being able to slide it forward and backward to find the sweet spot for pedaling was great, too. The bottom line is that the redesigned PDL 120 Pro is more comfortable, stable, and better equipped—which means more time on the water and more fish in the net.
