#8210. My 99-Year-Old Grandmother Built a Hidden Empire Around Flannel. Then She Lost It All.

When I was a child, visits with my Korean grandmother always began with the same ritual. She would place my left hand on her lap and trace the lines in my palm with her index finger, before delivering a prophetic verdict about my future. She’d tell me that when I became an adult, I would be a cheapskate. Apparently, the so-called “money lines” on my left palm were unbroken. “Your pockets won’t spill money, unlike your grandfather,” she would say.

After reading my palm, my grandmother would turn her attention to my shirt. Starting with the threads, she’d run her fingers along the seams and the stitches, analyzing the fabric for some soothsaying quality. Her hands would rub the material, and she would look at it closely. After pausing for a few seconds, my grandmother would announce her findings: “This shirt has good cotton!” or “I’ve never seen this weave!”

I lived with my family in Arkansas, worlds away from Seoul, which is where my parents had been born and my grandmother lived. Sometimes my grandmother would visit us in the United States, and sometimes we’d fly halfway across the globe to see her in Korea. I remember thinking that her fixation on fortune-telling and garment analysis was normal. I assumed that, across the U.S., grandmothers were greeting their grandchildren by gifting them candy and presents, before sitting down and studying the microfibers in their sweatshirts and blouses.

As I got older, I learned that my grandmother’s hyperfixation on fabric was the product of her younger adult life in Korea. According to my family’s fuzzy family lore, Grandma had once managed a textile factory. Well, no, maybe she had actually owned it. Did she simply work at the factory? Facts were hard to come by. Different family members visiting from Korea would tell pieces of Grandma’s life during their stays in Arkansas. And over the years, Grandma’s history in the garment industry became a source of my curiosity.

I’m now in my early forties, and my grandmother is 99. After years of hearing these mysterious stories, I set out to discover the truth of her connection to the garment industry. During one of my trips to Seoul, as we sat on her couch watching professional wrestling on TV—her favorite pastime—I asked my grandmother questions, in my second grade–level Korean, about her career in textiles.

More than half a century ago, she told me, she and my grandfather had owned a textile factory in Seoul that employed more than 50 people. They had helped pioneer the industrial production of a fabric that stills defines the style and culture of the outdoor industry: cotton flannel.

I wanted to know more, but my lack of Korean fluency kept me from truly interrogating this history. So, I enlisted my cousin, Spring, who speaks fluent Korean and English, as well as my sister, Mary, and my own mother to uncover the real story. Over the course of two years and a half dozen interviews, we interrogated Grandma, full name Sonia Shin, but whom we affectionately call “Hal-money” (grandmother in Korean). She told us stories, recounted memories, and helped us understand what her life was like more than half a century ago. We pieced together the tale of how she and my grandfather built a small empire of industrial flannel production in postwar Seoul. And then, how she lost it all.

Flannel is one of the most popular fabrics amongst outdoor enthusiasts—just try walking into an outdoors store without spotting a flannel shirt at any time of year. Over time, the soft, plaid, button-down shirt has become the unofficial uniform for those of us who work in the outdoor recreation industry. It’s the stuff of cozy pajamas and warm camping blankets, the foundation of the lumbercore fashion movement. Its cultural significance extends far beyond the campfire: flannel is synonymous with Kurt Cobain and grunge rock; with Snoop Dogg and nineties hip hop; with ranchers, tech bros, and city dwellers seeking blue-collar authenticity.

Despite its ubiquity, few wearers of the material ever stop to consider what flannel actually is. Most people associate it with colorful plaid designs woven into wool, but not all flannel is plaid, nor is it wool. The term “flannel” refers to any woven fabric, usually cotton or wool, that’s been brushed until it becomes fuzzy and extremely soft.

Imagine taking a metal brush and scrubbing down a spot on your khaki pants until a thin layer of fuzz forms on the surface. That layer is called a “nap,” which is made up of loosened fibers that, due to the brushing, now stand on end as a soft and warming tuft. The process of creating flannel makes garments warmer and softer.

Industrial textile factories use machines affixed with fine metal bristles to scratch fabric as it passes through the device, raising the nap evenly across thousands of yards of material. The technique used to make flannel is centuries old. Flannel’s origins have been traced to 17th-century Wales, where textile workers brushed fabric made from sheep’s wool into a material that was warm enough to survive the region’s wet, cold winters. Originally done by hand, the technique eventually became mechanized, and it spread across Europe during the industrial revolution. Cheap cotton from North America eventually flooded the European market in the 19th century. Mills quickly swapped out wool for cotton. Amid this evolution, cotton flannel became a fabric for working-class Europeans.

In the U.S., flannel’s connection to the rugged outdoor lifestyle came from Woolrich, the Pennsylvania-based company founded in 1830. The company introduced its red and black buffalo check shirt in 1850. The brand was a hit with hunters, loggers, and trappers, and the design became the official shirt of the lumberjack.

Steven Kurutz, author of American Flannel: How a Band of Entrepreneurs Are Bringing the Art and Business of Making Clothes Back Home, grew up 25 miles from Woolrich headquarters. Flannel was the uniform of the town, even on dressed-up days. His grandfather, a sheet metal worker and fisherman, owned a fancy flannel coat that Kurutz still wears today. “Everyone had one,” he told me.

Kurutz’s explanation for its popularity is that flannel lends a quiet humility and authenticity to those who wear it. The style, he says, has never belonged to any one kind of American. “Flannel cuts across races,” he reminded me. “It’s American, but not necessarily a white person’s garment.”

America’s production of flannel garments shrunk as the textile industry increasingly sought cheaper labor abroad. In 1980, approximately 70 percent of the clothing Americans wore was made in the U.S.; today, it’s about 2 percent, Kurutz wrote. The lion’s share of our garments is instead woven in massive factories in China, Vietnam, Bangladesh, or India.

The Woolrich mill, the oldest continuously operating one in the country, closed at the end of 2018 after the brand moved production overseas. Kurutz calls this a “quiet tragedy” in his 2024 book.

“It’s a deeply American brand, and now it’s not made here, not headquartered here,” he lamented. These days, the brand’s corporate headquarters are located in Italy.

As I spoke with Kurutz, my grandmother’s connection to flannel echoed in my mind. Her story seemed to become more compelling with every historical data point he explained. Decades before American textile manufacturers shipped their operations overseas, my grandparents built a flannel empire out of a half-burned factory in Seoul.

My grandmother is exhausted. Spring and I have just completed a two-hour-long interview session, and Hal-money is lying sideways on her favorite sofa in her apartment in the Apgujeong neighborhood of Seoul. She ignores us while we wrap up our camera gear for the day. I’ve turned on the TV to drown out the noise so she can sleep. WWE wrestling is, of course, playing on the screen.

“If I was just a little younger, I could do it again,” she mumbles before nodding off for a nap.

Spring and I have been aided by a sizable trove of documents, photos, and records from my grandmother’s career in the textile industry. While searching through her belongings, we found the incorporation documents for her business, as well as photographs of the factory, of the looms, of past employees.

These photographs and documents jog Grandma’s memory. She recites exact dates, locations, names of old friends, measurements of fabric. She describes scenes as clearly as if they’d just occurred.

Sonia Shin was born in the northern city of Pyongyang in 1928, back when Korea was under the colonial rule of Japan. Her father worked as a court clerk for the Japanese colonial administration, while her mother was a homemaker. She had an older sister who was academically astute and would eventually marry into Pyongyang’s elite class. Sonia, however, was, in her own words, “naive and mediocre. Obedient.” She found a supporter in her own grandmother, who would say, “The little one has it better in the end,” when referring to her. Sonia has repeated this phrase under her breath for 90 years.

In 1947 Sonia was married off by her father—a traditional custom at that time—to my grandfather, KwangDal Suh. Kind and gentle, KwangDal was from the city of Incheon, in the south of Korea, and had traveled to Pyongyang to work on a railroad project connecting the two cities. They spent the first year of their marriage in Pyongyang so he could be closer to work, but eventually, they decided to move to Incheon in 1948 to be closer to his family.

The move came at a pressing time in Korea’s history. The Korean peninsula was politically fracturing in the post–World War II years, as communism and democracy tore the population in half. Armies from the Soviet Union occupied the north half of the country while American troops were in the south, and the 38th parallel created the de facto border. The dividing line was supposed to be temporary.

Sonia had one child and was visibly pregnant with her second at the start of her journey to Incheon. Before she left, her mother sewed cash into her clothing, should she need it. Her father also hired a travel broker, whose job was to help her complete the journey without being arrested or stopped. As she and KwangDal awaited a train to take them south, Sonia had just a few minutes to say goodbye to her mother and father. She told them she didn’t want to go, that she would miss them.

“I had no idea what was ahead of me,” she remembers.

Her father turned and gently pushed her back onto the train. She would never see her parents, or her home, again.

The journey to the south was treacherous. The first leg, from Pyongyang to Namchon, was by train. From there, Sonia, her husband, and a group of refugees, led by the broker, traveled by foot. She strapped her toddler son, JungDuk, to her back. They hiked along ridgelines and through dense forests to a ferry on the Ryesong River, which they caught after crossing quicksand-like mudflats. They had to complete the muddy crossing in the dark, and bullets from border guards whizzed by her head as they trudged through the muck. Sonia nearly drowned in the crossing.

“My foot got stuck in the mud and I thought my baby and I were going to die,” she says. “Someone in the group heard me crying and pulled me out by my shoulder. I still remember how painful it was.”

They evaded border guards who lined the roads, ready to shoot at anyone seen moving across the boundary. They completed the final leg to Kaesong, in modern day North Korea, on foot, and then traveled by train and car to Incheon. They were safe.

But they weren’t entirely happy. Sonia and KwangDal found work in his family’s herbal medicine shop. Sonia performed the daily manual tasks of grinding roots and other plants into medication. She did not like the work. After six months, she told KwangDal that she wanted a different life away from his family.

“My husband [had] told me his parents were pharmacists. This wasn’t a pharmacy, it was a traditional medicine shop where they wanted me to pound roots all day long,” she says. “I was not about to spend the rest of my life doing that kind of physically demanding work for my in-laws.”

After weeks of arguing, KwangDal relented. They moved into a boarding house where they rented one room to sleep in and another for work. Their first job was to repair sewing machines and other mechanical equipment. KwangDal was a natural tinkerer, and he loved disassembling machines, fixing their broken parts, and reassembling them. He even innovated with the leftover parts, building prototypes, including a makeshift loom and a cotton candy spinning machine.

Eventually, KwangDal and Sonia started a repair business. They added a secondary business selling cotton candy from the machine KwangDal built by hand.

But being business owners came with its own stresses. KwangDal was terrible with money, often donating his time to clients without charging them enough for his duties. Undercharging customers frustrated Sonia. But with the cotton candy machine, she got an opportunity to run her own business selling sweets to kids.

“That was the pivotal point,” Grandma says. “A young naive woman became a business-minded woman. As it turned out, I had a business mind that had been hibernating.”

It’s dinnertime in Seoul, and the three of us sit at a small table and attempt to finish off the fish my grandmother has made for us. In Korea, when an older person places food onto your plate, not only are you supposed to eat it, you also have to show immense gratitude that they gave it to you. In previous generations, when food was scarce, this is how the older family members treated their kin, by picking out the best pieces of meat, or the most symmetrical looking pieces of kimchi, and placing it on your plate—or even onto your spoon. But Spring and I are too full to finish the meal. Grandma spoons more fish onto my plate. “Yellow croaker is good for your brain,” she tells me.

“Hal-money, you didn’t eat enough, you should eat this last one,” I say as I move the fish to her plate. Eventually, Spring finishes off the meal. Throughout dinner, Spring has shown Grandma old photos on her iPad. Grandma had recited addresses of the old factory and names of people she hadn’t seen in decades. I wonder: maybe if I eat enough yellow croaker, I’ll have a memory like hers when I’m 99.

Sonia and KwangDal’s first factory was located in Seoul, which, in the early fifties, was a city of transition and turmoil. War between North Korea and South Korea officially broke out in 1950, and during three years of battles and bloodshed, Seoul changed hands four times and was decimated by bombs and shells.

Sonia and KwangDal departed Incheon for Seoul in 1951. Millions of Koreans had been displaced as the city tried to rebuild during and after the war. Using their earnings from selling cotton candy and repairing machinery, plus some of the cash that had been sewn into her clothing years before, my grandparents purchased a partially burned, two-story textile factory in the heart of Seoul.

“We saved enough from the cotton candy business to buy the property, all while supporting our fast-growing family,” Grandma said. By this time, they had four children.

Inside the burned-out factory sat several metal looms for weaving cotton. KwangDal set to work repairing them. Cotton had been the fabric of Korean society for centuries, ever since the Chinese had introduced it to the peninsula in the 14th century. Most garments were made of simple, loom-woven cotton.

Ever the tinkerer, KwangDal iterated on his original loom design from Incheon. He wanted a device that could make cotton garments have the softness of cotton candy. Instead of spinning sugar, he used metal bristles to scratch tightly woven cotton fabric. The cotton strands, when pulled apart, would stand on their ends, making the piece of fabric fuzzy, soft, and warm. This process is still used today to manufacture cotton flannel.

Building the machine took several months, but after KwangDal finalized his design, he took it to a metalworking shop and had three identical devices built. In 1958, he installed the four machines in his factory and set to work producing brushed cotton flannel fabric. The textile was a hit.

“We made so much money that the bank had to drive to our factory and load the cash into their vehicle and count it at the bank,” Grandma said.

Within a year, the looms were pumping out 4,800 yards of cotton flannel every 24 hours. They stored the fabric on massive rolls in the factory. And, as quickly as they could churn it out, it was purchased by clothing makers across the city.

Sonia and KwangDal named their company Baeekyang Gimo, which loosely translates to “White Lamb Flannel.” While KwangDal operated the machinery, Sonia ran the business. She became the bookkeeper and inventory clerk, the quality-control manager and logistics coordinator, as well as the HR department. Perhaps most important, however: Sonia was head of the company’s sales department. She processed every order, negotiated contracts with clients, and signed off on deals.

“I had to see things for myself,” she said.

As the company grew—by 1959 it employed 50 people—Sonia also took over the finances. While KwangDal was a brilliant engineer, he was terrible with money.

“He spilled money everywhere he went,” she said. “He couldn’t walk past a beggar without emptying whatever he had on him.”

Sonia, now 31 years old, blossomed as a business owner and entrepreneur. Most of Baeekyang Gimo’s customers were wholesalers and garment manufacturers throughout Korea. Sonia took orders from small businesses in Seoul’s Pyeonghwa Market in the Dongdaemun district and sold large orders to garment factories in Daegu. Even the Korean military was using their flannel in standard-issue uniforms. Baeekyang Gimo was profitable in its first year. By the societal standards of the time, Sonia’s work was almost unheard of. Women in postwar Korea worked hard, but they toiled in the background: in fields, markets, or family shops where a husband or father was the face and the owner. Confucian tradition places a woman at the bottom of a social pyramid: under her father, her husband, and even her son, for life.

Placing a woman at the head of an industrial operation violated social traditions. The only reason Sonia was tolerated in her position was that, on paper and in the public eye, the business belonged to KwangDal. Sonia could run everything as long as everyone agreed that Baeekyang Gimo belonged to him.

My grandmother’s story has had a tremendous impact on my own sense of identity in the outdoor industry, where I’ve spent most of my professional career. I first attended Outdoor Retailer (OR), the official industry meetup for outdoor industry professionals, in 2010 in Salt Lake City. I was employed by an e-commerce company in the outdoor space, and was eager to get to know an industry I had long been wanting to join. I wore a three-piece suit—attire that would have been fine at a normal trade show. But at OR, I stuck out. Nobody wore formalwear. Everyone was clad in flannel.

That wasn’t the only reason I stood out. As I walked the showroom floor, I saw very few people of color, aside from the show’s director, Kenji Haroutunian, who later became a mentor and, now, colleague in my current venture.

Over the years, I came to understand many truths about the industry. Industry leaders love to talk about diversity and inclusion, and in many cases, they do follow these guidelines. These days, the people who are featured in marketing campaigns are diverse. The entry-level ranks are finally starting to get more diverse. Even the crowds you see at trailheads are less white than they were decades ago.

But the leadership in the outdoor industry and the people owning these brands haven’t really changed. For 15 years, I’ve been asking myself if I’m crashing a party I wasn’t invited to. So in 2015, I launched my own event, an outdoor conference called Outdoor Media Summit (OMS). Since then, it’s become the largest gathering of media in the outdoor industry. It turns out my grandmother’s prophecy was spot-on: bootstrapping a business has required me to become extremely frugal. It’s been a grind, and I’ve only recently been able to pay myself a livable wage.

But money was never the hardest part. My face was. Once, at a fly-fishing industry trade show, someone made a highly offensive racist joke to a group of people, and everyone in the circle laughed at me. To this day, I still consider changing my public-facing name to “Ian” in hopes that my email response rates improve.

Not long ago, the industry’s leadership decided that OMS didn’t belong on its list of recommended trade events. We’ve earned the right to be on that calendar. Yet these are the kinds of things that make me wonder if I can survive in an environment that is so overwhelmingly white-run, if I can overcome the structural barriers ingrained in our industry.

My perspective changed after spending time with my grandmother and unpacking the details of her history. I learned how she spent nearly three decades building a business in a country that didn’t want women at the helm. My grandmother didn’t have the luxury of asking whether she belonged—she just worked, because stopping was never an option. Yes, my grandmother lived in a different time, in a different country, and faced deeper discrimination than anything I’ve encountered in the outdoor industry. But hearing her story instilled in me a sense of perseverance that, otherwise, I may not have developed on my own.

Learning my grandmother’s story also taught me that I indeed do belong in this industry. I no longer view myself as an outsider, the one guy in a suit in a sea of flannel shirts. You see, those shirts—worn by almost everyone walking the showroom floor—are made from a fabric woven into my own family history. My grandmother produced countless yards worth of brushed cotton flannel, which made its way into thousands of shirts across the globe.

My grandmother’s sedan rolls through the streets of Seoul’s Sindang-dong neighborhood, past soaring apartment high-rises and modernized commercial buildings. Inside, I sit packed into the car next to my cousin, mother, sister, and grandmother. We’ve come to Singdang-dong to try and find the old factory that Hal-money and her husband operated. Our mission is to snap a photograph of the five of us in front of the building. But alas, we cannot find it.

We circle the crowded city blocks, driving past throngs of people and modern buildings. It’s been 30 years since my grandmother was last in Singdang-dong, and the neighborhood has completely changed. The factory has been enveloped by a city that no longer resembles the one that she and KwangDal helped rebuild from rubble 70 years ago.

“Just drive around,” Grandma keeps saying. “There’s an entrance somewhere. Circle the block.”

We park, look at the map, and then continue driving three different times. Each time, we get out of the car and wait for Grandma to follow us. But each time, she finds a reason to stay in her seat. No, this isn’t the correct block. Let’s check another street. She won’t get out of the car.

After a few stops, our situation becomes obvious: We’re not lost. My grandmother is simply stalling.

But we are persistent, and my grandmother realizes that we aren’t going to give up. Eventually we coax her out of the car and into her wheelchair. And as she settles into the chair, she looks deep into my eyes. “It’s because I’m embarrassed,” she says.

It takes me a few minutes to understand her emotion. Decades ago, these city streets had been the site of my grandmother’s lifelong triumph. She had been the boss. Everyone walking the sidewalks had known her, respected her, and worked with her. Now, she is an old woman in a wheelchair, pushed along by her grandchildren. To her, everyone was staring at her, and not in a good way.

The turning point in this transition had occurred in 1982. That year, KwangDal had turned 60 and decided he was ready to retire. Per Korean cultural norms, he handed Baeekyang Gimo to his eldest son, KwangDuk, and walked away to tinker with his next project, an electric car endeavor commissioned by the South Korean government.

There was no discussion about whether or not Sonia would simply take over the business from her husband. KwangDuk was the eldest male of the family and the only boy among nine children. By societal rules, he was the next in line.

Instead, Sonia retired the same day as KwangDal, but not because she was tired or ready to walk away from her position. She simply gave up the oversight, the management position, and her job inking contracts. This was despite the fact that she had financed the business in the early days with her money from selling cotton candy and with the money sewn into her own garments.

Baeekyang Gimo did not last long under KwangDuk’s direction. Eventually it shuttered amid tough financial times, and he sold the building.

I ask my grandmother how the business would have continued, had she stayed at the helm. She tells me that a woman approaching 60 deciding to run her husband’s business would have been considered “unsightly” by Korean society.

“I haven’t even thought about it,” she says. “What’s lost is lost.”

After some searching, we eventually locate the address of the old factory. The building was long ago transformed into residential real estate that blends seamlessly into the neighborhood. It’s just another apartment, housing some of the 10 million people who live in Seoul.

I stand behind my grandmother’s wheelchair in an effort to get a photo of us in front of the old factory. My sister and I are trying to get her to look at the camera, but she’s unable to hear anything we’re saying. The memories of this place are flooding her attention. Eventually my sister gives up and snaps a photo of just my grandmother. In it, she is reliving the years when all this was hers.

Spring B. Han, Mary Kim, and SangHyun Kim contributed to this story.

This article is from the Fall 2026 issue of Outside magazine. To receive the print magazine, become an Outside+ member here.

#8209. The 7 Items That Got Me Through October (and the Rest of Fall)

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Oh October, the month of mystery. Here in Boulder, Colorado, it’s when you wake up in the dark not knowing if it will be warm, cold, raining, or windy. The only thing you do know every morning is there will be even more much-larger-than-life-sized skeletons poking out of peoples’ lawns. (Why has this become a thing? As my friend Clare said on a run the other day, “people are desecrating their lawns with plastic trash!”)

Anyway, it’s a tricky time of year for running. Head out the door overdressed and you will end up a puddle of sweat that, depending on the weather, ultimately makes you cold. Leave underdressed, as I did for a tempo run two weeks ago, and your limbs will feel like they’ve been cursed by a witch who’s turned them to immovable ice.

But tricky conditions can be solved with treats. My trusty associate editor is, in his words, “going to the desert to do something stupid.” (Go Cade!) That leaves just me to round up our gear of the month. Here are the five items I kept packed in my Janji Ultrahauler (another piece of gear I can’t live without!) so I was ready for whatever I woke up to:

Kilian Jornet’s fledgling shoe and apparel company has stuck to relatively technical alpine equipment—until now with the Nnormal Cadi. This do-everything trail shoe is exceptionally comfortable thanks to a padded heel collar and tongue and a cushy midsole with 37 mm stack in the heel, 31 mm in the forefoot. It’s got a nice wide toe box (an obsession of mine as I work on my foot strength and toe splay). And with a Vibram Megagrip outsole it’s tacky on all terrain and in all conditions. I also appreciate the mesh upper, which is breathable on hot days and dries quickly on wet ones. It’s the only shoe I brought on a trip recently, which means I found myself wearing it for a 12-mile run around the Charles River in Boston—definitely not as energetic as your typical road trainer these days, but it got the job done just fine. It’s just a solid, dependable shoe.

It’s rained A LOT in Boulder this month. And by a lot, I mean more than zero times. I know I’ve lived here for too long because I’ve gotten soft and the only thing that got me through more than zero very dark, very wet mornings was this rain jacket from Arc’teryx. That’s because it’s actually waterproof. But it’s also super lightweight and breathable, meaning you don’t incinerate in your own body heat and end up wet anyway. Plus one for the cinch on the hood so you can actually keep it on your head while you’re running and another bonus for the vents under the armpits, which help moderate body heat. I know $450 is an obscene amount to spend on anything, but this is definitely a case of you get what you pay for.

When it comes to running pants and tights I am very, very picky. They can’t suffocate my waist, but they also need to stay put. They can’t bunch around the knees, but they also can’t be so baggy that the pant legs rub into each other. The Janji Altas Multi Pant is one of the few pieces that passes my stringent test. They are supremely comfortable thanks to a wide elastic waistband, and a drawstring lets you dial in the fit. They’re loose enough to allow for full range of motion, but they’re streamlined enough that I can wear them for harder efforts without getting annoyed. Why I really love them for this time of year is they are lightweight and breathable, providing just the right amount of insulation. And even better, they have nearly knee-length ankle zips so I often wear them for the warm up and zip them off for intervals—no shoe removal required.

There is something so comforting and luxurious about tucking into a comfy vest for a fall outing. Enter this fleece-lined vest from 7Mesh. It’s super breathable yet cozy thanks to a soft, woven outer layer paired with the light and ultrasoft fleece lining. I’ve been loving it for colder runs when a jacket feels like too much but a long sleeve isn’t quite enough. And I’ve also been loving it on the bike—especially because the vest folds into itself via a big back pocket, revealing little straps that let you fix it to your bike frame when you’re not wearing it.

Not too cold and not too warm, snug but not tight, these gloves are  a shoulder-season star. They’re so lightweight that I don’t think twice about wearing them for the start of a run before the sun rises and stashing them in a pocket as I warm up with the ground. I can use my phone with them on, carry my ballot (the midterms are on Tuesday!), as well as maneuver zippers and, if desperate, tie shoes. Plus the colors and patterns instantly boost my mood. (They came in so many fun options!)

One-star review for the name. Zero stars for the logo branded on the top of the collar. And yet, five stars for these socks. They are just that comfy and moisture-wicking. I am pretty skeptical of overengineered gear, but CEP has me thinking maybe there is something to developing stuff in a lab. These socks provide a gentle amount of compression and arch support while also being ventilated in all the places you want it. In other words: they stay put, and they keep my feet comfortable for a wide range of temperatures—perfect for fall running. Most importantly, my feet do not slip in my shoes. I repeat: no slippage here. My friend saw me running in them the other day and he said he also loves these socks so much that he ordered five pairs. Oh and they come in approximately one billion colorways.

I know, I know, it’s a crime to spend more than $50 on a hair product—much less two products. But hear me out: Colorado is savage on my wavy hair. When left unchecked, the dry air and harsh sun leech out every last drop of moisture, turning my hair into a wiry mess. Add in the rainy days of October (or my annual pilgrimage to Hawaii) and in years past I am ripping out chunks of matted hair every time I shower. Enter this fancy shampoo and conditioner. I am not exaggerating when I say this stuff has revolutionized my hair’s life. For the first time in 13 years since I moved here, my hair feels soft. And I can actually get a brush through it when I get out of the shower! You better believe I will be buying it again.

#8208. 5 Wellness Trends We’d Like to See Go Away

Fitness tracking can help take your training to the next level, but know when you're taking things too far. (Photo: SimpleImages / Getty)

Calin Van Paris has been writing about wellness for more than a decade. Here, she breaks down a handful of wellness hacks and trends that, though beneficial for some, many of us could do without.

Let’s talk about wellness trends. More specifically, let’s talk about our collective penchant for “optimizing” the human experience.

Being a person is not always easy. We’re all in bodies that are designed to decay, with minds that tend to run amok and emotions that can seem like they have brains of their own. It’s only natural to try to control what we can—and self-care provides what can seem like an ideal platform for the pursuit.

Routines that can support physical, emotional, and mental well-being fall under the ever-growing umbrella of “wellness.” But many wellness trends begin in a beneficial place and spiral out of control from there.

A growing corner of self-care fads is overly focused on tracking, streamlining, and pushing extremes. And anything that makes you feel inadequate or anxious is one we’d love to fade into the background.

Take what, if anything, really works for you from the below trends and then notice when it’s time to let it go.

The concept of “sleepmaxxing,” or maximizing the quality of your sleep, began swirling around social media a couple of years ago. Sleeping better is a trend we can get behind—but you don’t need expensive gadgets or high levels of anxiety to do it. More importantly, putting too much focus on your sleep habits has the potential to backfire, transforming a restful part of your day into a stressful one.

Good sleep is essential. Nicole Moshfegh, MD, clinical psychologist and author of The Book of Sleep, notes that proper (or inadequate) rest can affect your physical health and cognitive function, not to mention your mood. Sleep is meant to be restful. Relaxing. Restorative.

Your sleep routine should not be causing you additional stress. If habits like evening restorative yoga, breathwork, or less blue light after dark improve your sleep quality, maxx on! But should you find yourself agonizing over a sleep score or lying awake calculating how many minutes of rest you’re losing—both examples of orthosomnia, an obsession with achieving the optimal sleep score—know that you’ve lost the plot.

Dunking your body into cold water might sound refreshing—and for some of the population, it is! Cold plunging is a Nordic tradition that some say boosts mental clarity and resilience (again, you are willingly submerging yourself in cold water) and is thought to reduce post-workout muscle stiffness, fatigue, and more.

Still, you may want to pause before adopting the cold plunge as your new cure-all. One study suggests that using cold baths for muscle recovery may be more of a placebo effect than anything else, as parsed by longtime Outside columnist Alex Hutchinson. And for those in female bodies, some research suggests that over time, exposure to cold water can adversely affect the reproductive system, and there is no proven boon to female muscle recovery.

Between phone apps, smartwatches, and Bluetooth-connected rings, it’s never been easier to know exactly what’s going on in your body, at least on a biological level.

Certain smart gadgets, like the Pulse Mindfulness Ring, can act as a little buddy, helping you breathe deeply, commit to daily meditation, and focus. And when used correctly, the Oura Ring can also be a mindful companion.

The issue isn’t the tracking devices themselves, but how they’re being used. Just as putting too much stock in sleep scores can be considered an obsessive condition (again, orthosomnia), too much preoccupation with the information provided by wearable devices may negatively impact psychological well-being. For some—including those with eating or health disorders—this sort of constant tracking can serve as a trigger, increasing rigidity and anxiety around otherwise healthy habits.

In short, try taking your smart accessories off sometimes, just to see how you feel.

We live in a world where the breaking news about what’s going on in our minds and bodies—and, usually, what we’re lacking—is practically non-stop. And usually, there’s a supplement for that. According to one report, the global supplement market is projected to be worth $300 billion by 2028.

Supplementing becomes an issue when you’re adding to your stack before looking at your diet and other habits. Studies have shown that supplements and weight loss pills offer a perceived sense of invulnerability, ironically leading to poorer choices in nutrition and fitness habits.

Another more obvious issue is supplements offered with no scientific evidence to back up purported benefits. Not all supplements on the market are even FDA-approved; in fact, many are not.

But if your supplements are thoughtfully chosen and supplementing an existing healthy lifestyle, you’re probably on the positive side of this trend.

The internet can make your life feel like a reality show. And if you make your living as an influencer, maybe it sort of is. But even with audience perception, brand deals, and showmanship at stake, your health and wellness routine can and should make you feel good.

At its core, self-care is for you. If sharing your journey feels beneficial for you and for them, go ahead. But when your wellness practices become more about the performance of tending to yourself and less about actually doing things that bring you peace and healing, you may want to reconsider your approach.

#8207. The Dean Fidelman Interview: 6 Photos, 6 Decades

A portrait of Dean Fidelman in 1971, the year he arrived in Yosemite. (Photo: Warren Shelton)

Dean Fidelman arrived in the Yosemite Valley in 1971 as a teenager. Yosemite has been his home ever since—except for a blip in the ‘80s, when he set aside his passion for climbing to become a fashion photographer in New York City and Los Angeles. But a phone call saved him from what was, for him, soulless commercial work.

It was Lynn Hill who called, asking Fidelman to start making climbing photos again. She invited him to come shoot her on some climbs in Europe, where he also first met Chris Sharma. From there, he doubled down on his life’s mission to show “the art of rock climbing,” in his words.

Fidelman spent the first half of his career shooting in black and white on film cameras, including a Pentax 6×7. He processed his own film and developed his own photos—sometimes by night in the historic Yosemite darkroom of Ansel Adams. Eventually, he caught up with the times when filmmaker Renan Ozturk gave him a Sony a7R II mirrorless camera and he made the switch to digital—and full color. “In my viewfinder, I set the preview to black and white, but the capture contains full color,” Fidelman told Climbing.

Now, 55 years after arriving in Yosemite, Fidelman still calls the area home and continues to shoot climbers around Camp 4. Perhaps best known for his work capturing the Yosemite Stonemasters and Stone Monkeys, Fidelman has also sat down for interviews in a couple documentaries released this year, including The Dark Wizard about Dean Potter, and a film about the weed plane that crashed in Yosemite, enriching many of his friends.

Fidelman is also known for his Stone Nudes, nude portraits of climbers bouldering or free soloing. He started the series in 1999 and now estimates it runs 300 images deep. At least a few times a year, he still receives requests from climbers to shoot a Stone Nude—a phrase which he has tattooed on his hands.

We caught up with Fidelman to discover the changes and throughlines he’s observed across six decades of Yosemite photography, the challenges of revisiting his relationship with Dean Potter for The Dark Wizard, and the next iteration of the Stone Nudes project. For this retrospective interview, we also asked Fidelman to select one photo for each decade of his work, which you’ll find below.

This interview has been edited for clarity and concision.

Dean Fidelman: As the decades have progressed, the way that I think about making a photograph has changed. But the people haven’t changed as much. With the Stonemasters, I was just making photographs of my friends doing cool things in the desert. I wasn’t really thinking about anything besides trying to make the best photograph I could—and finding out what a good photograph was.

With the Stone Monkeys, from the late ’90s until 2010 or 2015, I was simply living in Yosemite in the meadow, sleeping down by the river. So I fit in financially with this group of people really well. When I asked someone to make a photograph with me, there was no hesitation.

Recently, I’ve done some photographs for Summit Journal of people on YOSAR [Yosemite Search and Rescue] and at Camp 4. The first thing someone would say when I asked if I could make their photograph was, “I’d be honored.”

That kind of put me on the back foot in a weird way. If I ask to make a photograph of you, it’s because I respect you, or there’s something about you that I really enjoy being around or seeing. So it’s more like you’re honoring me, because you’re going to be vulnerable in front of my camera for a moment. Once we get over that, it’s just like working with the people I’ve always worked with.

Fidelman: When Lynn reconnected with me, it was pretty much immediate—”there it is.” You think of your path in a linear way that leads to being the best at something, but that’s not how it works. I was doing my photography much more personally than commercially. When Lynn connected with that, I thought, “Oh yeah, the personal aspect of photography, I can do that.” She definitely sponsored me and opened that world back up.

Fidelman: Charles Cole at Five Ten and John Bachar at Boreal both used me for ads. But Charles especially would say, “Here’s $500, here’s $1,000. Here’s my camera. Just give me some photos, but make what you’ve always made—no pressure.”

When I got back into Yosemite, one of the first people I met was Dean Potter. He was super open to me. I met him through Bachar because they were giving him shoes at the time and wanted to make some photographs. We had an immediate kinship, and that brought me deeper in with the Stone Monkeys. Then you had Cedar Wright, who was just starting off at that moment in time, and everyone else just came out of that.

With the people who survived—and the people who didn’t—I realized I was making this visual record of friends, trying to express them in the moment. That’s what I’ve hopefully continued to do.

Fidelman: Honestly, my opinion hasn’t changed since the ’70s. It wasn’t like I just happened by when Bachar or Yabo [John Yablonski] or somebody was doing a solo. Sometimes Bachar would say, “Hey, I’ve got this thing figured out now and I’m going to do it. I want you to make the photographs.” Three or four of us would jump in his van, go down to wherever the solo was, and make these photographs.

Even back then, climbing magazines did not want to publish [free soloing photos]. I didn’t take it personally. The first publication that published my work was the National Enquirer. It was a picture of Bachar soloing with a headline like “Man Climbs Rock” or “Daredevil Climbs Rock.”

So I experienced both ends of the spectrum early on. I realized that what you’re making isn’t going to be universally accepted. But you’re doing it for the people who are doing these solos and the people who appreciate it. I wasn’t making all this stuff happen; it was happening in front of me and has continued across generations.

Fidelman: When film crews called 10 years after Dean Potter died to make a film, I was really kind of conflicted, but I approached it as professionally as I could. They showed me a rough cut of all four episodes. After I watched, I went into this horrible depression that I just got out of in the last couple months.

Fidelman: It made him very real again. Suddenly, I still think he’s alive. He’s existing. I can feel his presence, trying to come up really close to me and intimidate me—his voice and everything. Obviously, it’s storytelling, but it’s made me really question a lot of what happened and a lot of who I was. I think hopefully I’ve gotten that straightened out.

Fidelman: It means having a high respect for unspoken boundaries—how you carry yourself in that moment, what your objective is, and what you can ask of the person in front of you. With Stone Nudes especially, they are naked and vulnerable. There’s all kinds of trust going on there. You respect unspoken boundaries by observing someone to see how open they are to direction. But I’ve also found women have been mansplained with men trying to tell them how to climb.

And then with your friends, you’re on an intimate level because they know you, but suddenly there’s a camera up. They’ve seen your work and they’re honored. So you need to try to get rid of that awkwardness by bringing your energy back and refocusing.

Fidelman: I’m still working on the Valley Muse book. I made some new Stone Nudes this March that I really like, so I’m looking at calendars or possibly a book, gathering for another five or six years, traveling to favorite spots and places I’ve always wanted to go to.

Fidelman: There are a couple of photographs I want to make in Patagonia. It’s just a boulder in the middle of nowhere—and there was so much nowhere. There’s also a cool volcanic place in Venezuela. But next, I’m heading to Spain to work on deep-water soloing nudes in Mallorca.

Fidelman: Probably 2018, right when I stopped with the Stone Nudes calendar and Renan [Ozturk] gave me that camera. That’s probably the last time I went into a darkroom, unless the darkroom had a scanner in it and I was scanning my negatives. With a lot of my original black and white photography, I would process the film myself. I used to find these traditional photo labs up and down the coast.

After the last lab closed, I used Ansel Adams’s darkroom in Yosemite. They would let me use the darkroom from 10 at night until midnight. What was left of it was just a long sink and a heavy dark curtain. I’d be rattling cans at midnight and I look over and there’s a portrait of Ansel looking at me like, “What are you doing in my darkroom?”

Fidelman: Once I was shooting in the middle of the Merced River by the 120/140 junction. A friend was on top of the boulder posing while I was waist-deep in the river. Suddenly, a big tour bus pulled over and a bus-load of tourists piled out, pushing each other trying to take photos with their phones.

One time I was making photographs in Eldorado Canyon on that boulder right in the middle of the river with my friend Anora, a hippie. I went back to Yosemite and processed the film in Ansel Adams’s darkroom. I’m hanging out at the lodge and this person comes up to me—obviously a climber, but very clean-cut. He goes, “Excuse me, are you Dean Fidelman?” And I go, “Yeah.”

He sticks his hand out, with this big smile on his face and goes, “I want to shake your hand. You were in Eldorado Canyon about a month ago and you were making some photos. We were on the Bastille and oh my God, she is so beautiful. That was the most amazing day. My partner went home and bought a calendar even though he knew she wasn’t going to be in that one. But is she going to be in the next one?”

Then I made a Stone Nude of my friend Brian Ludovici, who’s a wonderful human and a super cool boulderer. He asked if I would make a photograph of him on Midnight Lightning (V8) with his clothes on. So I show up there and he’s just got this pair of short shorts on, right? This is his favorite boulder problem. He loves it. He worships it. And he goes up it and down it. I say, “Hey, man. You think you could do it nude?” Maybe four or five of his friends are there, all egging him on. He gets to where he’s pressing out the mantle, but he couldn’t do it. He put his shorts back on.

Then there’s this guy running full blast toward me from 100 yards away. He looks really closely at Brian. Then he stops and goes, “Dude, this was the most amazing day of my life. I looked from over there by the kiosk and there was a beautiful nude woman doing Midnight Lightning, so I started running to get a closer look. But it’s a dude.”

Fidelman: One fall. My friend Joey was like, “Let’s make a photograph.” I first met her when she was 16. She goes, “I want to make a photograph.” I go, “No, no.” Same with [Chris] Sharma. I go, “No, you have to wait until you’re 18.”

A couple years later, she’s in Joshua Tree and wants to climb the White Rastafarian (V2). First, I tell her she has to do it with her clothes and shoes on, so I can see that she can do it. She does it perfectly. But she can’t do it barefoot. So, she took her clothes off and we had a bunch of pads down, hidden by the bushes. Three of her friends were spotting.

She gets up to the crux and starts to bring her hand up and she blows. Her friends didn’t even touch her. She hit the pads, but sprained her ankle fairly badly. I felt really horrible, but I did put it in [a calendar]. I always make certain that [climbers] can do it at least with their clothes on first. Now I always tell the spotters, “If you’ve got to get in the photo, don’t even worry about it. Put your hands on them, even though they’re naked!” Unless somebody wants to solo something, but it’s not going to be outside the limits—ever.

Fidelman: I’m working on two books. One is a history of the Nose with John Long, Hans Florine, Ed Hartouni, and Sarah Conley. The other is a book on the Stone Monkeys with James Lucas. We’re getting the manuscripts and photo selections organized, with plans to publish over the next couple of years.

Fidelman: I’ve been working on archiving all the stuff from the ‘60s and Glen [Denny] was a huge influence on me, as well as Tom Frost and and a few others.

I understood two things very early on. One is if you’ve tied into a rope with people who have climbed with people like John Salathé and Royal Robbins, you’ve tied into a rope with all those other people, too. I tied into a rope with [Jim] Bridwell and lots of people that probably go back all the way to Salathé.

When John Long and I made the Stonemaster book, it was a fulfillment of my dream to make a book, but also of the understanding that if we allow those stories to die, we have no magic. All our beliefs are based on those stories and those legends.

I’m hoping maybe someone shows up, and I don’t care who they are. If I can see that passion and they’re really looking to provide that rope that we can all tie into, then my work would move forward.

#8206. ‘Please Help Me.’ A Hiker’s Desperate Text Led to Her Dramatic Rescue on a Famed Colorado Trail

A Black Hawk helicopter. (Photo: patty_c / Getty Images)

A desperate text to 911 turned into a dramatic rescue in the Colorado high country after an early-season storm trapped a 37-year-old solo hiker in thigh-to-hip-deep snow on the Four Pass Loop on October 30.

The Four Pass Loop is a popular but rugged 27-mile route that travels through the Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness while gaining about 8,000 feet of elevation. Most hikers tackle the route as a backpacking trip over the course of two to four days.

According to a release by Crested Butte Mountain Rescue (CBMR), the ordeal began when Pitkin County Emergency Dispatch received a text to 911 that read “please help me.” Before calling for help, the hiker had texted a family member that her phone’s battery was down to 10 percent. Shortly after that initial call for help, emergency services lost contact, leaving them with only a single coordinate to guide their search. With temperatures dipping into the teens, CBMR reached out to CareFlight of the Rockies to coordinate air support. The team also dispatched a ground team, reasoning the elevation and mountain conditions could make landing a helicopter impossible.

By 11 p.m., the helicopter team located the hiker attempting to climb over Frigid Air Pass, but they were unable to make a safe landing to extract her from the scene.

About four hours later, the first two party members of the CBMR ground team reached the pass and located the hiker struggling to make it over the pass near where the helicopter had spotted her. But neither air support nor ground support could reach the hiker: “The steep terrain, deep snow, and darkness presented legitimate avalanche concerns,” CBMR wrote. “The first two rescuers initially attempted to descend toward the subject but encountered concerning conditions. Recognizing the potential hazard, they made the decision to wait for the remaining team members before committing to the descent.”

When the remaining members of the CBMR ground team reached the pass at about 5:30 a.m., two team members descended somewhere between 300 to 400 feet to reach the hiker. Upon their arrival, they realized that her condition was potentially life-threatening since she was no longer ambulatory, she had cold-related injuries, and was showing signs of hypothermia. The rescue team placed the hiker in a bivy before realizing that the best way to extract her would be via a helicopter hoist rescue.

CBMR coordinated with the Colorado Search and Rescue Association (CSAR), who contacted the Colorado Army National Guard to dispatch a UH-60 Black Hawk helicopter from Gypsum. A helicopter lowered a rescue technician to the hiker, then hoisted both party members into the helicopter.

After the hiker was successfully transferred to the airport and flown to the UCHealth Burn and Frostbite Center in Aurora, the National Guard returned to the Frigid Air Pass to remove the remaining rescuers due to the pass’s dangerous conditions.

In the wake of the incident, CBMR reminded hikers to take extra precautions before heading into the backcountry since high-altitude rescues can be dangerous for rescuers, too. (“So throw that extra puffy in your pack!” the team wrote.)

The team noted that rescue came at the end of a particularly challenging week for CBMR, which responded to three incidents, two of them fatal.

#8205. How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September. He guessed he’d be maybe 20 or 30 minutes behind in the early miles.

But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.

“That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner. “But I told myself that maybe he went out at more of a race effort, while my pace was better for a multi-day FKT.”

McConaughy, known by his thru-hiking trail name, “Stringbean,” has more than a few multiday FKTs to his name. He’s set records on the Pacific Crest Trail, Appalachian Trail, Long Trail, and Arizona Trail. And he had two prior record attempts on the JMT, one of which earned him an unsupported FKT.

“I thought my experience could help me beat him,” McConaughy said.

As he chased the ghost of the JMT’s past, McConaughy drew from his many multi-day FKTs and races. All of the miles and mistakes, successes and failures, and lessons and growth along the way helped him ultimately establish a new FKT of 2 days, 16 hours, and 15 seconds, taking nearly three and a half hours off a time that had stood for nearly a decade.

In rock climbing, climbers talk about “flashing” a route. It’s when they successfully climb the whole thing on their first attempt—without any practice or “beta” to help. McConaughy’s JMT effort was pretty much the opposite of flashing. The 33-year-old Seattle-based endurance coach was incredibly familiar with every mile of the JMT. Prior to his record setting attempt this fall, he’d covered the trail four times—the first in 2014—including the two prior FKT attempts. He’d also spent five summers guiding backpacking trips in the Sierra.

So when McConaughy ended up in a blizzard on Muir Pass with snowflakes landing in his eyeballs, it didn’t really stress him out or slow him down. If anything, it helped him move faster as he wanted to get up and over to warmer ground.

“I’ve seen the worst that the Sierra can throw at you,” he said, citing thunderstorms, blizzards, and rugged terrain. “I didn’t have to do a bunch of mental gymnastics, worrying about things I hadn’t experienced before. Instead, I could devote all of my energy to things that actually were issues.”

Most of McConaughy’s issues during the record attempt were ones he expected to occur, was prepared for, and could handle. “The long climbs were long climbs and some of the descents take decades,” he said. But after numerous JMT attempts he knew “it could feel much harder.” A little over a day into his attempt he was two hours ahead of D’Haene’s splits.

The JMT is far from the only goal for which McConaughy’s persistence has paid off. He took seven swings at earning a Golden Ticket into the Western States 100 before clinching one at the Black Canyon 100K on his eighth try in 2025. He’s also raced the Cocodona 250 three times and has a trio of Barkley Marathons starts.

“I like to think I’m more fun than a project-er, but when I look back, that’s pretty much my entire running career,” he said. “I feel like it gives me purpose. I want to do routes that inspire me and motivate me and take what I’ve done wrong, or what I feel like I could improve on, and continue to experiment, tinker, and optimize.”

He’s not as intense as a rock climber going after a seemingly impossible objective like the Dawn Wall, he swears. Rather, it’s about finding the sweet spot where he’s pushing himself to grow but having fun doing it. He’s not training to be the best at any given race or record attempt; he’s training to be the best version of himself for years to come.

“I get a lot of joy from sticking with the process, training with a smile, putting in the work to make a difference, and looking for opportunities to rise like a phoenix and perform the best that I can,”  McConaughy said.

Caroline Himbert, who is coached by McConaughy and set her own unsupported FKT on the JMT this July, helped pace McConaughy on the JMT this fall. “He goes back to things he’s failed at and tries to continuously learn and grow; he loves the science and spreadsheets and takes things seriously,” Himbert said. “But at the same time, he doesn’t take things too seriously and he keeps things fluid and fun.”

As evidenced by the fact that it stood for nine years, the JMT record was stout. D’Haene is known for bringing a newfound level of professionalism to FKT attempts, with a full support staff, set of pacers, and film crew. But rather than seeing the competitive level of the record as a deterrent, McConaughy saw it as part of the draw.

“It’s the granddaddy of FKTs,” he said. “More people have attempted the JMT FKT than pretty much any other premier route that exists—and the fact that François [D’Haene] and Darcy [Piceu] were the [previous] record holders is an ode to the level of attention and competitiveness that it’s gotten.”

On his first attempt in 2022, McConaughy set an unsupported record of three days and one hour. But Jeff Garmire beat it by 13 minutes just 25 days later.

McConaughy knew he could do better, so he tried to reclaim the record in 2024. But he hallucinated in the final miles and wound up off-trail on a class-four scramble, much closer to life-and-limb-threatening risk than he’d anticipated. It was a wake-up call for McConaughy, who always considers what he’s asking of others when he chases a big goal. He’s now the father of a 6-month-old and knew he couldn’t end up in a similar situation—or worse—if he went back.

“That experience made me really rethink what the record meant to me and ask myself if I wanted to do it again,” he said, adding that it felt reckless to go for another unsupported record. But after much reflection, and many conversations with his wife Katie, he decided he had to go back.

“I knew I couldn’t exist as an athlete without trying to put my stamp on the JMT,” he said. “This was my third time [attempting the FKT] on this trail and I wanted to give it my all, and use my best tips and tricks from every other effort to get the record.”

McConaughy showed up with a 12-tab spreadsheet and 12 years of beta to guide his effort this fall. He thought some of the greatest opportunities for improvement lay in fueling, pacing, and recruiting an all-star crew to help him out. In his unsupported-style attempts, he’d had to carry all of his own food and gear with no supply restocks along the way.

At Cocodona in 2025, McConaughy hit a wall that no amount of carbs could fix. He thought he knew how he needed to fuel to compete for the win. He’d done sweat testing and was experimenting with high-carb fueling. But he ended up with GI distress and struggled to breathe. He still finished in a respectable fourth place, but it was far from the finish he wanted.

He started working with nutritionist Meredith Terranova, who suggested he was likely hypernatremic—too high of blood sodium concentration—during Cocodona. He wondered if trying to optimize his performance through a data-driven approach with high carb fueling and sweat tests meant he’d stopped listening to his body.

So on the JMT he turned to real food like trail mix, purees, and waffles, especially on the big climbs—of which there is no shortage with 38,000 feet of elevation gain to cover. He also used recovery drink mixes and fat- and protein-based fuels from his nutrition sponsor, Näak.

“I feel like sticking to more whole food was the biggest learning and the biggest difference maker in my performance,” he said.

He also made up ground through a smarter sleep strategy. In his 2022 attempt, in which he finished six hours behind D’Haene’s record time, McConaughy slept for six hours. He knew there was an opportunity to trim down time spent resting while still sleeping enough to avoid dangerous hallucinations.

He settled on taking a mere 40 minutes of sleep beneath a pine tree on Bear Ridge—around 28 hours in. He thought it might be prudent to get at least an hour but he decided to push it a little with 40 minutes, figuring he could always nap later if he needed it. When he got to his third night out on the trail he was still running strong, cracking jokes, and appreciating his surroundings, Himbert said.

“You could tell he was having a good time and he was a ball of energy,” she said. “I was with him more towards the end, and he was still moving so well. I think that’s the key with this trail; it’s so challenging but if you can still move well towards the end then you can crack these times. I think Joe really nailed it, and it went close to perfect.”

McConaughy’s crew was one of his greatest assets. He learned some things about crewing the JMT after his crew missed him at Kearsarge Pass during his Pacific Crest Trail FKT in 2014. The PCT overlaps with the JMT for about 170 miles. He had to keep going on the PCT for two days with no sleeping bag, only a half-day’s worth of calories, and nothing warmer than a thin windbreaker. “We didn’t really know what we were doing,” he said. Hence the 12-tab spreadsheet this go-around, which was largely for the benefit of his crew and the complicated logistics of supporting a record-attempt on the JMT.

Part of the beauty of the JMT is that it offers an uninterrupted tour of backcountry wilderness. The trail only crosses the road twice over the course of the entire 223 miles. That’s also what makes it a bear to support. Meeting McConaughy on the trail required hiking several miles and thousands of feet of climbing to deliver food and gear. Pacers ran monster sections—usually around 40 miles at a time. But his crew of pacers was up for the challenge, with a collective résumé that boasted JMT FKTs, podium finishes, and 200-mile runs.

“Tara Dower talked about being a vessel on the Appalachian Trail, and I certainly had a similar experience on the JMT,” McConaughy said. “I was able to appreciate the beauty of where I was and the excitement of doing this absurd endurance thing because my crew was always filling my cup instead of making me pour things out to keep going.”

One thing that McConaughy has learned time and time again, is that he runs best when his cup is full.

“Gratitude and joy are the greatest performance-enhancing drugs,” he said.

While he was running, he thought about Katie, who was home solo-parenting so he could acclimatize to the altitude and run for 64 straight hours. He thought about his parents, who enabled him to get outside and run cross-country from a young age. He thought about the people who have supported his running career, and the friends who traveled to the Sierra to help him through the 223-mile journey. And he thought about the Sierra themselves, the mountains that have kept him coming back time and time again for the last 12 years.

“I run my worst when I’m thinking about how far behind someone’s splits I am,” he said. “When I caught myself doing that on the JMT, I thought, ‘This is doing more harm than good. You need to move forward at your own pace, and focus on the things that really matter.’”

After shaving over three hours off such a long-standing record, McConaughy hopes that he’s reached an end with his JMT FKT attempts. With all of the time and effort he has dedicated to the JMT, it feels a bit like a fairytale ending: “The princess was saved,” he said.

Now, he’s ready for a new goal, one he’s ready to chase to fuel his performance and fill his cup

“It’s one of those moments where I realize I’m maybe more capable than I thought I was,” he said. “And that makes it exciting to go back to Cocodona, or Western States, or another FKT, or any number of things to see what I can do.”

#8204. The Best Rain Jackets for Hikers Who Always Overheat

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Picture this: You’re halfway through a 20-mile day when the sky opens up, dumping sheets of rain on you and your hiking partners. You pull out your shell, zip it up, and keep crushing. An hour later, you notice you’re starting to feel awfully damp. Your shell isn’t leaking, but it might as well be: Your exertion has turned it into a sweatbox.

The best rain jackets are next to useless if you end up sweating them out. If you’re the kind of hiker who always steams up your shell, picking one that has the breathability and venting options to keep you cool and dry is a must. We went through our testers’ favorite rain shells of 2026 and chose the best picks for hikers who always overheat.

Weight: 15.3 oz (men’s) / 13.9 oz (women’s) Sizes: Men’s S-XXXL / Women’s XXS-4X

Pros and Cons + Very breathable + Slightly stretchy + Certified carbon neutral – Too slim for layering

Our favorite rain jacket on the market today is also the most breathable we’ve tested: After wearing the Aspire (the Foray is the men’s equivalent) on a steep, 7-mile hike into a cabin in Alaska’s Chugach National Forest, tester Kate Paskievitch reported that she stayed dry the entire time—even with 40 pounds on her back. Outdoor Research’s AscentShell Dry, a 40-denier, 100-percent recycled three-layer nylon fabric, helped, but credit mostly goes to the full-length side zippers, which helped us bleed off heat quickly.

Weight: 10.9 oz (men’s) / 9.9 oz (women’s) Sizes: Men’s XS-XXL / Women’s XS-XXL

Pros and Cons + Excellent adjustability + Superior breathability + Dialed-in details – Expensive

Let’s acknowledge the elephant in the room first: Any rain jacket that costs $600 had better be really good. Fortunately, this model from Canada-based 7mesh delivers. Diagonal pit zips kept us from sweating out the Guardian Apex, even when our testers’ arms were down. And the nylon face fabric was both surprisingly breathable and tough enough that it remained snag-free, even after a long bushwhack through brambles.

Weight: 5.8 oz (men’s) / 5.5 oz (women’s) Sizes: Men’s S-XXL / Women’s XS-XL

Pros and Cons + Very light and packable + Partially plant-based – No hand pockets

At just 5.8 ounces for a men’s medium—roughly the same as the ever-popular Frogg Toggs Ultra Lite—the Marmot SuperAlloy Bio takes up barely any space, making it an ideal just-in-case piece to tuck into your pack. And it performs, too: The 2.5-layer NanoPro fabric kept our tester dry even after she wore it under a heavy pack in 50-degree temperatures, but was still tough enough that it didn’t fray after heavy use.

Weight: 25.4 oz (men’s) / 25.0 oz (women’s) Sizes: Men’s S-XXL / Women’s XS-3XL

Pros and Cons + Soft and supple + Lots of venting options + Easy to repair and actually recyclable – Heavy and bulky – Too warm for summer weather

The Velez Adventure Smock is not the lightest jacket in our test: The jacket, which eschews a waterproof-breathable membrane for a DWR-treated polyester face backed by wicking fabric, is better suited for colder-season temperatures. So what makes it a good jacket for hikers who run hot? In shoulder-season conditions, it breathes and maintains its waterproofing better than most traditional three-layer rain shells. Venting helps, too: Biceps zippers and a horizontal front flap across the torso make it easy to dump heat quickly before users get too steamy.

Weight: 1.8 oz (men’s) Sizes: Men’s XS-XXL

Pros and Cons + Ultralight + Surprisingly durable + Surprisingly weatherproof – No hood or chest pocket – Tight fit

At 1.8 ounces, this gossamer hoodless jacket is a reliable friend for mountain runners, fastpackers, and anyone who values velocity. The 10-denier recycled nylon exterior packs up to (literally) pocket size, and while we wouldn’t bet on it to keep you bone-dry through a multi-day storm, it handled surprise desert downpours without batting an eye. Breathability is exceptional, which our tester confirmed after a full day of biking along the Grand Canyon’s South Rim.

First, understand you may have to compromise. While waterproof-breathable membranes are almost ubiquitous, most jackets prioritize waterproofing over breathability, or vice versa. Jackets that can weather a downpour without so much as wetting out may not breathe well, and those that breathe well may be better for scattered showers than the kind of rain that makes you start thinking about building an ark.

Pay attention not just to the breathability of the jacket itself, but to the venting options, too. Even the most breathable fabrics can’t dump heat as well as a set of pit zips or mesh-backed pockets that expose your underlayers to fresh air. Packability is more important than you might think, too: If you’re consistently hot, having a jacket that you can ball up and stick inside your pack without a second thought is a better move than carrying a heavy, bulky one.

Our lead testers for men’s and women’s rain jackets are Drew Zieff and Elizabeth Kwak. Our gear editors pulled these recommendations from their original testing notes and scores to recommend the best rain jackets for hikers who overheat.

#8203. Forget the Florida Trail, These 6 Hikes Reveal The Wild Variety of The Sunshine State

The jungle foliage can get thick along many of these Florida Trails (Photo: Boogich via Getty)

Florida may be best known for its beaches, theme parks, and sprawling wetlands, but if you are willing to venture inland, you will find a surprisingly diverse set of hikes in an equally varied landscape. Trails along sandy ridges, shady hardwood hammocks that shelter wildlife, and deep ravines providing a welcome escape from the subtropical heat are scattered across the state. And you don’t even have to commit to a months-long thru-hike to experience them.

From ancient dunes to forested ravines, these six all-season, pet-friendly trails offer a reason to lace up your hiking boots and explore the wilder side of the Sunshine State. They are open from dawn to dusk, and some even allow camping for a small fee if you want to make your hike an overnight trip.

Mileage: 2.5 miles Location: 1600 Twigg St, Palatka Entrance fee: $5 per vehicle, $2 for pedestrians and bicycles.>Highlight: The trail is especially beautiful during azalea season, from late January through March, when the park’s flowering shrubs explode in splashes of pink, red, and white.

This part of Florida is unlike anything you’ll find along the coast, with steep paths covered with ancient root systems of Azalea bushes. The 2.5-mile Azalea Trail at Ravine Gardens State Park is a short but challenging loop that takes hikers along narrow dirt paths, over exposed roots, and down historic stone staircases. There are two suspension bridges over a spring-fed creek that flows through a shaded forest of ferns, mosses, and native trees.

Mileage: 39 miles Location: 13208 SR 72, Sarasota Entrance fee: $6 per vehicle, $5 camping permit per night.>Camping: Three campgrounds with 90 sites with water and electric hookups (check water conditions before camping) and six primitive campgrounds with three sites each Highlight: You may spot wild turkeys and alligators, so be sure to stay on the trail at all times, especially through the open prairies.

Myakka River State Park, just east of Sarasota, is one of Florida’s largest and most ecologically diverse state parks. The Myakka trail is a roughly 39-mile loop. It winds through pine flatwoods, oak and palm hammocks, open prairie, and wetlands. Several shorter day hikes like the 5.4-mile Bee Island and 8.7-mile Honore branch out from the main trail. Those are great alternatives if you don’t want to stay overnight.

Mileage: 5.8 miles Location: 13201 San Felasco Parkway, Alachua Entrance fee: $4 per vehicle, $2 for pedestrians and bicycles; dogs are not allowed in some sections frequented by birders.>Highlight: Birding is very popular here as species like the Wood Thrush and Red-headed woodpecker thrive in the park’s varied ecosystems.

The San Felasco Hammock Preserve State Park is home to one of the only remaining hardwood forests in Florida. The Spring Grove Trail is a 5.8-mile loop that passes through a variety of habitats and ecosystems within the park and is a great reminder that Florida’s natural diversity isn’t limited to its famous swamps and coastlines. This trail passes through shady hardwood hammocks, pine forests, and sandy hills. There are also both dry and water-filled sinkholes, adding interesting terrain features along the way. You can also hike a shorter 2.8-mile loop up to the Hammock cutoff.

Mileage: 7.1 miles Location: 5298 Michigan Ave, Sanford Entrance fee: None. Highlight: Explore a swampy jungle that is teeming with Florida wildlife of all shapes and sizes.

If you’re looking for that classic, marshland, jungle Florida experience, with rugged hiking and tons of wildlife, look no further than the Black Bear Wilderness Area. This 7.1-mile loop trail takes you deep into lowland habitats like wet prairie, hydric hammock, and cypress swamp. The trail is challenging in spots, due to roots, boulders, and muddy sections. Bugs and humidity are to be expected, but it’s worth putting up with those for the chance to see some wildlife. Hikers often encounter river otters, alligators, white-tailed deer, tons of bird life, and, if it’s quiet enough, even black bears.

Mileage: 5.8 miles Location: 4335 Firetower Road, Haines City Entrance fee: Free; $5 camping permit per night.>Highlight: It is home to 21 rare plants and 31 animals, some of which are not found anywhere else in the world. You might see scrub morning glory, pygmy fringe tree, and cutthroat grass, along with protected animal species including the Florida scrub-jay and gopher tortoise.

The Allen David Broussard Catfish Creek Preserve State Park is located along the Lake Wales Ridge. It includes Florida’s most unusual ecosystems—an ancient shoreline and sandbar dating back almost 350,000 years. The park protects more than 8,000 acres of scrub, sandhill, and flatwoods habitat. The Catfish Creek Trail is a 5.8-mile loop that is mostly exposed with little to no shade. This trail crosses a lot of sandy terrain, which can make even a relatively short walk feel strenuous. Be prepared with plenty of water and consider bringing your own shade.

Mileage: 7-13 miles Location: Torreya State Park Loop Parking Lot, Bristol Entrance fee: $3 vehicle entrance fee; $5 backcountry camping feeHighlight: Striking cliff formation and primitive camping for backpackers.

This hike follows the Apalachicola River and offers some of the most challenging terrain in this part of Florida. It can be completed as a 7-mile single loop if you want a shorter dayhike. Or, extend the hike by adding the second loop. It connects with the first and nearly doubles the distance to 13 miles. In total, you’ll gain a whopping 1,646 feet of elevation. If you want to make this an overnight adventure, there are three different primitive campsites along the trail. Campsites require a $5 backcountry camping fee and must be reserved at Torreya State Park or by phone at 850-643-2674.
