#8196. In His Own Words, a Czech Alpinist Describes How He Survived a Nightmare on Peru’s Highest Mountain

Honza Špička on Huascarán (Photo: Courtesy of Matěj Žák)

My name is Jan “Honza” Špička. My climbing partner, Matěj Žák, and I are two alpinists, climbers, mountaineers, skiers, and endurance athletes from Nove Straseci, a small town in the Czech Republic. Although we have known each other since childhood through our families (and the local ice hockey team), our climbing paths only crossed a few years ago. Since then, we have spent three seasons together in Peru’s Cordillera Blanca and two seasons in Argentine Patagonia. We have roped up together a few times on Czech sandstone as well. We are no professionals, though; rather than extreme lines, what we have behind us are moderately difficult routes climbed in our own style: clean and fast.

Our speciality? Long days in the mountains and a fast, lightweight approach. We take nothing on an expedition that we cannot carry on our own backs.

Huascarán is the highest mountain in Peru and the highest point in the entire tropics. Its south summit reaches 6,768m and the north summit 6,655m; the two are separated by a broad col called La Garganta (“the Throat” in Spanish) at roughly 6,000m. Huascarán lies at the heart of the Cordillera Blanca, the most heavily glaciated tropical mountain range in the world, and it gave its name to the surrounding national park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985. Because the Earth bulges slightly at the equator, the gravitational acceleration on the summit of Huascarán is among the lowest anywhere on the planet’s surface; a person there measurably weighs a little less than at sea level, by a matter of grams. The summit of Huascarán is also the second most distant point on Earth from the planet’s center, right after Chimborazo.

The mountain is named after Huáscar, the Inca ruler who fought his half-brother Atahualpa for several years over control of the Inca Empire. Atahualpa eventually defeated his brother and had him executed. The American mountaineer Annie Smith Peck, then over fifty years old, climbed the north summit in 1908. The higher south summit held out until 1932, when a German–Austrian expedition made the first ascent.

Huascarán, however, also has a darker side to its history. In 1962, a huge mass of ice broke away from the mountain, and the resulting debris avalanche swept down onto the towns of Ranrahirca. Then, on May 31, 1970, an earthquake off the coast triggered a far larger and more extensive avalanche from the north summit, which within minutes buried, among other places, the entire town of Yungay. The earthquake and avalanche combined took the lives of approximately 67,000 people. It was the deadliest single avalanche disaster by death toll in recorded history.

This tragic event unfortunately also carries a strong Czechoslovak mark. It was right here, in the valley between Huascarán’s north summit and Huandoy Sur, that a Czechoslovak expedition was camped—and the whole expedition became a victim of this mountain.

If we take into account the victims of 1970 and all the climbers who have died on its slopes, it is probably the mountain responsible for more human lives than any other in modern history.

The ascent itself, via the Normal Route, is not particularly difficult, but Huascarán’s glaciers are retreating fast, and so today some routes that were relatively straightforward climbs just a generation ago involve significant objective hazards. In the six years that I have lived in Peru, I cannot remember a year when Huascarán did not claim another victim. There have even been years when it allowed no one at all to reach its summit.

The start of our trip began on Friday, July 11, in the evening in our favourite “pollo a la brasa” restaurant. Our whole group, which we called the “Cayesh crew,” met for a shared dinner to load up on a solid dose of protein before what was to be the main climbing objective of the season for all of us: Huascarán Sur. It has to be said, though, that for none of us was Huascarán the center of the universe. We all had it in “one day, maybe, I’d like to, if it comes to it…” mode, but there was certainly no obsession with this “fat one.” I already had three unsuccessful attempts behind me, but even so I wasn’t insisting on “bagging it.” Yet somehow the appetite, the motivation, the hunger for it arrived. And essentially by coincidence it arrived not only for Matěj and me but also for our friends from Peru. In the end we formed three teams of two.

I have known Saul—formally, Freddy Saul Mendoza Lizana—since 2021; he was essentially my first climbing partner here in Peru. Since then we have been through a lot together—in the mountains, on the crags, at home, and in the pub. He was like my Peruvian brother. We were so close that my wife Alča and I were already counting on a little room for Saul for when we one day return to the Czech Republic and settle down somewhere.

Agnieszka is a Polish “machine” with several 8a/5.13b sport routes to her name. She had seen plenty in the mountains, too. Definitely no lightweight.

Alejandro “Chicho” Ugarte Jordan was a professional photographer from Lima. His main interest was unique mountain images captured with his DSLR or his drone. We had known each other since 2022 through the Skiing Peru project, which we were both part of. We often spent time together with our girlfriends in Lima outside the season, too.

Artidoro “Arti” Salas Gaitan was a pure Huaracino—someone who comes from Huaraz. He was born in the town at the foot of the Cordillera Blanca and lived there his whole life. He ran the Big Mountain hostel, well known among climbers. I personally have known him since 2021, when I spent my first season in Huaraz at his hostel.

Our expedition began on the morning of Saturday, July 11, when we loaded the van with heavy packs. Under the watchful eye of—as Matěj called him—our adoptive father Paul, our friend and the owner of the cozy Cayesh Guest House bed and breakfast, we set off for our starting point, the village of Armapampa in the Yungay area. From Huaraz, it was about a two-hour drive. Besides the six of us, Alenka came along, too, having arrived from Lima that same morning, as did Míša, a Czech woman living in Nepal who had just popped over to Peru to see friends. The girls, however, were only going on a day trip to the hut and back down the next day.

On the edge of the beautiful village of Armapampa, we unloaded our gear from the van, ate the last gluten-free cinnamon rolls that Alenka baked for the trip, and shouldered our heavy packs. Matěj took a group photo and we set off towards Refugio Huascarán, our base camp. We reached the refugio at 4,650m spread out over quite a wide time range (Matěj first, at 2 hours 45 minutes, and Saul and Aga last at a little over 6 hours). Who knows where and why they lingered; apparently they were finishing off their avocados. Either way, the trail was easy and there was no rush, so everyone went at their own pace.

There was no one at the hut apart from us, so we enjoyed it immensely. The evening was a very friendly affair: dinner, beer, guitar, and singing in four languages mixed together. And, of course, planning the climb.

This is where the first, relatively pivotal moment came. Aga wasn’t feeling well—to be precise, she felt pretty crap—so she decided to walk down with the girls. That left the five of us Mohicans. Saul immediately arranged with the lads to form a three-person team. At the time, it seemed to me a good idea. Saul is the most experienced of the three, and the team would only be stronger for it. In hindsight, I blame myself that we didn’t tell him to stay with Agnieszka; Aga was his big “project.”

After breakfast at the hut, we packed our rucksacks, took a group photo, and set off. The girls headed down; the lads headed up. None of us had any idea that this would be our last photo together, and that the girls would never see Saul, Chicho, and Arti again. Just writing this sentence brings tears to my eyes.

The second day of the climb up Huascarán was easy going. A few hundred vertical meters led up to the glacier, then a few hundred more traversed over a gently angled and relatively safe glacier to the spot where Camp 1 is set, at about 5,300m. Matěj and I arrived first, and shortly after us Arti and Chicho, with Saul behind them. We pitched the tents, melted water, cooked food, took photos, rested, and fine-tuned the details for tomorrow’s summit push.

Huascarán is normally climbed via the Garganta col, where Camp 2 is placed at 5,950m, and from there climbers make for the summit. All of us, however, were heading for the El Escudo (“The Shield”) route, which is technically harder but objectively safer,and of course more fun. It is a roughly 600-meter long ice face at 60 to 70 degrees. Thanks to its shape, there are no seracs hanging above you, no cornices, and far fewer things that can come down on your head. Unfortunately, there is little room for a Camp 2 there, so the Escudo is usually climbed from Camp 1 straight to the top, with the descent via the Normal Route.

We set our departure time for 10 pm. While the sun was still up, we crawled into our sleeping bags to get at least a little sleep and recharge the batteries a bit. We all knew that brutally hard work lay ahead.

This was it: summit day. Matěj and I got up at 9:30 p.m. so that we could leave at 10. We could hear the lads sometime before 9. In the end, we left more or less together: the lads at about 10:15 pm, we a few minutes after them.

Given the profile of the route over the Escudo, the plan from the start was to climb in pairs. Later, we became a pair and a three. You cannot climb this with five people on one rope, and none of us ever suggested it. The same applies to the descent.

The first part of the route was probably the most dangerous section of the whole ascent. It was a zone of crevasses and seracs of a size you will not encounter in Europe. There were a few sections of steep ice, but it wasn’t outright hard; it was just that something could come down at any moment. This section was shared with the Normal Route, which then branched off to the left towards Camp 2, while we headed right towards El Escudo.

We reach the bergschrund in less than two hours, with the lads following an hour or so behind us. Here we re-tied onto the full length of the 60m rope and racked up all our gear. In the process, I dropped my radio somewhere into the bowels of the glacier, and Matěj set off upward. The terrain wasn’t hard, so we simul-climbed on a single rope. Matěj climbed three to four pitches this way until he ran out of ice screws. On his last two snow pickets, he built a belay and let me through. My section was more hard snow than ice:easier climbing, less fun, but with correspondingly worse protection. I had three snow pickets on my pack, but I wanted to save those for later, for the belay anchors. After climbing some six pitches on just a handful of screws, I topped out over the lip of the Escudo, where I brought up Matýsek. (Editor’s note: “Matýsek” is a Czech nickname for “Matěj.”) By then, we were at 6,300m. It was cold as hell, with the sun still nowhere in sight. I dropped a glove and started feeling properly ill from the altitude. From this moment on, I suffered like an animal. The section from the top of the Escudo to the summit was endless; it wasn’t as steep any more, but it was long, and the soft snow did nothing to help our progress.

Sometime before 9 a.m. on Monday, July 13, though, we stood on the summit of Huascarán Sur. We didn’t really feel much joy, because we knew the worst was still ahead of us: the way down. On top of that, the summit was a completely flat plateau. You could play soccer on it, only you’d have a long way to go for a stray ball. Even so, weakness came over me and I cried. It was my fourth attempt, with my partner and childhood friend, and exactly a month to the day since our dog, Pisco, was poisoned. I cried again just remembering him. But the joy was there, too, although the main part of it was supposed to come down below. And it did come. But only for a moment.

We didn’t linger on the summit. There really was nothing there. After a snack, a little tea, and the summit photo, we headed down. No one had been on the summit for about two to three weeks, so there were no tracks and no trail. Our only guide was the offline mapy.cz app, which traced the Normal Route. But it was the route that was walked an unknown number of years ago, so we treated it as a rough indication only. We re-tied into classic glacier-travel mode, roughly 15–20 meters apart, with the rest of the rope coiled around each of our bodies.

A few minutes from the summit, on the empty, white, flat plateau, I saw something that looked like the windblown hint of a trail. Before I even got there, something happened and I was falling through the air into an icy hell.

A crevasse. With no sign whatsoever of its existence, it had been waiting there silently for its victim. I remember precisely the feeling of flying into the void. It was as if I were falling for an eternity. Suddenly, I felt the rope come tight, and I knew that was Matýsek. But I keep falling. In that instant, I was certain that in a moment, Matýsek would come flying in after me and we’d both be dead.

But a miracle happened—a miracle called Matěj. The rope bit again and I stopped. He bloody well caught me. I was hanging about 12–15 meters down in a crevasse that runs 100m in each direction and could easily be 50m, 100m, or 300m deep. Who knows? Below me, I saw nothing but icy hell. The crevasse was completely covered with a cap of fine snow. Zero chance of seeing it.

To my own surprise, I didn’t panic; I knew exactly what to do. My only connection to our world was the rope I was hanging on and whatever Matěj had rigged up there to keep me in this world. I clipped a Micro Traxion onto my harness as a self-belay and climbed up the vertical ice wall towards the surface as far as I could. I felt so OK that I even took three photos inside the crevasse. When the line of the rope stopped me from climbing any farther, I swung out into space. I ascended the rest on prusiks.

In a little under half an hour, I was out, back on the surface, back in the world. Only now did I breathe out.

Matěj and I fell into each other’s arms and began to grasp what we just survived. It would have taken very little for him to come in after me, and no one would ever have found us. In hindsight, I see it as an enormous miracle and a measure of enormous skill on Matěj’s part. He saved our lives. And maybe it was at this very moment that we realized this really was no joke and that things were getting serious. We continued the descent very cautiously, and we were genuinely scared.

We reached the edge of an ice wall where the Normal Route was supposed to be, but there was nothing there—nothing at all. There was no question of searching for a way through this labyrinth. The wall looked to be about 20m high, with a ramp below it along which we hoped to traverse off left toward the Normal Route.

We rappelled off two snow pickets into a relatively safe spot surrounded by seracs. I remember looking at the leaning towers next to us and thinking that one deep breath would be enough to bring the whole lot down. Still, we felt a certain safety in our little hollow. Finally, we had a bit of time to catch our breath, eat and drink a little, and get in touch with the lads.

Before I could do that, they called me. They said they were about 200 vertical meters below the summit. But it was already late, around 12 to 1 p.m., so their plan was to traverse off towards the Normal Route and descend by it.

I told them to try to find our tracks and our rappel, and to really watch out for crevasses, because I had just fallen into one. We confirmed that everything was OK and that we would meet in the evening at Camp 1, or if need be, at base camp, depending on the time and our energy. If I had known that this was the last time I would speak to them, I would have told them so much more.

A little later, while searching for the route on the map, my phone slipped out of my hand and vanished somewhere below. But I didn’t dwell on it. I knew we had other worries. It was just a shame to lose the photos from inside the crevasse.

Another unpleasant rappel off a 25-meter serac, and we were on the slope leading towards the Garganta. By now the weather had turned and visibility had dropped to a few tens of meters. But we were already in the Garganta, at 6,000m. All we needed now was to find Camp 2, which was just a flat patch where tents stood two days ago. From there, there should be some tracks and a route down.

We wandered about a bit, but eventually we found Camp 2 and there really was a hint of tracks. Shortly before that, the summit shook off its cloud, and we saw the lads above us at about 6,300 or 6,400 m. It even looked to us as though they were closer to the Normal Route than we were. We were really relieved.

The route from Camp 2 to Camp 1 is the most dangerous crux of the climb. It is a zone of avalanches, collapsing seracs, and crevasses. Later, Matěj and I agreed that we both felt as if we were living in some kind of virtual reality, outside our bodies, just waiting for the video game to end. Maybe that was why I didn’t really register the risk.

We arrived back at Camp 1 at sunset. With our last reserves of strength, we packed up and continued down to the refugio. A hot dinner and a bed was, after all, a big draw. And it was only a little under two hours more.

We reached the hut sometime before nine in the evening, after 23 hours on our feet. We asked for something to eat and a beer, then went to sleep. We thought about the lads and somehow had no doubt that they were fine and that they were at Camp 1. After all, we saw them a short way above Camp 2.

In the morning, we woke up at the hut completely wrecked, but suddenly also happy with what we’d achieved. We expected the lads to turn up any moment, and then we’d race down into the valley. The news from the lads, however, was different.

Saul wrote that they couldn’t find the way down and had to bivouac somewhere above Camp 2. But they were OK, he said; they survived the night up there without any camping gear. They were tired, Chicho was apparently feeling ill, but all were OK. They would try to find the descent route. From then on, we were to communicate with Chicho, as Saul’s battery was dead.

We still had no idea that things were bad. But neither did the lads. Because things weren’t bad yet. We managed to download our GPS track onto a phone and send it to the lads as a mapy.cz link. Up above Camp 2, there was occasionally a signal, so we communicated with the lads via WhatsApp.

At 9:10 a.m., Chicho wrote asking us to send our route. At 9:15 a.m., we sent the mapy.cz link and it was delivered.

At 10:16 am, Chicho sent a photo and a video from where they were. They sounded fine; Camp 2 was visible below them. At 10:18 a.m., we sent them a crib sheet of roughly which way to go down, including a sketch drawn onto their photo. This was delivered. At 10:21 a.m., we asked Chicho whether he had our route on mapy.cz. This was the last message delivered to Chicho. After 10:21 am, no further messages were delivered. From then on, there was no communication from them.

Since the weather was beautiful, the lads were fine, and there was no signal lower down towards Camp 2, it never occurred to us that the lads might be in trouble. We were certain they had descended lower, lost signal, had flat phones, and so on—but were descending. There was essentially no reason to think anything else. They werebujacos”—tough guys. They had survived a night without sleeping bags at 6,400m, and now they would just run down to us, to the girls, to lunch, to a beer.

Given these assumptions, we knew we had several hours of waiting before they would appear above Camp 1, which could be seen from the hut. Meanwhile, we tried to contact them by radio and by phone, in case they happened to come into signal. But still, we were completely calm.

When about 3 p.m. came and there was no sign of them, though, it seemed odd to us. It had gone on too long. We decided we would go up and look for them. They were probably tired and frozen, and another night up there would be truly critical.

We ate, brewed tea, and took all the clothing we had. In the meantime, I called a friend, a guide, down in town so that he knew something was going on and could start rounding up help if needed. But there was still a chance alive in us that they were at Camp 1, asleep in the tent, and simply had no way of letting us know. Down in town, a group of volunteers was already getting ready to set out to help. There is no organized professional mountain rescue in Peru.

But there was no one at Camp 1. By then we sensed that things were bad; we just didn’t know how bad. On top of that, a snowstorm was moving in.

The message we sent down was clear: It was official, we needed help. The lads were somewhere up there. We were going up for them. We knew that down in the valley things were already under way and would keep going without us. But we had a different task: to find them and bring them down.

We pack all their sleeping bags as well and set off up into the gale. Matěj created a Garmin messaging group and made our position trackable online. He realized more than I did that we were heading into real trouble.

I have friends up there – my “churaks,” my “hermanos.” I registered nothing.

For the first time in my life, I was faster than Matěj. In my head, I knew they were up there, frozen and exhausted but alive, and that we were their only chance.

In these conditions I would turn around on any climb of my own; I would never go on. But now it wasn’t about me. It was about the lads. The moment we gave up, they would have no chance.

We got as far as above Camp 2, to 6,000m, but there was nothing anywhere. That was shortly before midnight. Just gale, snowfall, a temperature I’d estimate at around minus 30 degrees, and not a trace of the lads.

By this point I knew things were very bad. In this weather, no one survives up here for even an hour. Matýsek was very afraid of going down because of the avalanche danger and pushed for us to stay at Camp 2 and somehow sit it out with all those sleeping bags. I knew that if we stayed, we would be dead within the hour. In the end, I convinced him that we had to go down. That was about 50/50. But staying up there felt to me like 90/10.

The descent was horrific. Avalanche terrain was everywhere we looked, with giant seracs over our heads almost the entire way. Visibility was near zero, and our tracks drifted over with snow. Nevertheless, our guardian angel was on duty again and guided us down. We get back to Camp 1 sometime around 3 a.m. on Wednesday, July 15. There I well and truly collapsed, mentally and physically. We crawled into the tent for a while and waited for the first group of volunteer rescuers, who, as we already knew, were on their way from the refugio.

Even in the tent and in a sleeping bag, 700 vertical meters lower, the weather was terrible, and it was here that Matýsek told me we were one–all. He had saved us above that crevasse, and I had by insisting that we go down.

The first rescue team reached Camp 1 just after first light, sometime after 6 a.m. It was five people in all, three guides and two aspirant guides, and among them my good friend Szymon, who was the only one closer to me than Saul. That was all. We handed over all the information we had and let them go up. We would head for the refugio, where further teams were supposedly bound: one to set up a support base at Camp 2, another at Camp 1. Supposedly lots of people were coming.

Unfortunately, we were in Peru, where everything does not quite work. We met the Camp 1 team below the glacier—five lads, all friends, climbers, and volunteers from Peru, Colombia, Spain, and the Czech Republic. No Camp 2 team ever came, and in fact, there never was one. The five lads up above had packed late in the evening and set out from Huaraz to help friends in need. In a single push they climbed to over 6,000m. But because of the lack of support and the conditions up there, they had to turn back in the afternoon and descend to Camp 1. That essentially ended any realistic chance of finding the lads alive. I personally had known already at Camp 2, which we had climbed to in our attempt to find them, that there was almost no chance left.

From then on, great chaos set in across the whole organization of the rescue and search. As I already mentioned, Peru has no mountain rescue service; there are no rescue helicopters, no rescuers, no system, no protocol, no designated person to take charge of any coordination. Everything happened through the WhatsApp group that Matěj created when we set out for the lads. Everything was done on the basis of volunteers, friends, guides and family members.

Eventually, the police, the high-mountain police (Policía de Alta Montaña), and apparently even the army joined in to help. But their help consisted solely of transporting volunteers by helicopter from the town of Caraz to the refugio at 4,650m, and the first helicopter took off 24 hours after the official call for help. What’s more, it flew up empty, to assess the situation, only to find that another police helicopter had been sitting on the “helipad” by the refugio for several days, badly parked, and that its pilots were afraid to take off in it.

In the end, some transport up did take place, but effectively only on the following days. If someone down below had been able to coordinate it, they could have sent the line of volunteers towards base camp on foot, with a herd of donkeys, on the very first day of the search (July 15), and they would have been there far sooner than waiting until the next day to see whether anyone would get a place on the helicopter.

The entire rescue, and subsequently the search, was run by volunteers and the families. It was they who hired private companies with advanced drones, they who coordinated everything, mainly with the police, they who did everything they could. I myself went back with two volunteers a few days later to a point just above Camp 1 to attempt a further search with drones—without success. The zone where all the clues ended—GPS signals, the location of the last photos, the hint of the last tracks, and so on—is at around 6,500m. Camp 1 is at 5,300m, and most drones simply cannot fly that high and that far. Only the advanced police drones can, and they in turn lacked experienced pilots willing to risk it. Going higher wasn’t possible because of the conditions on the mountain. So, a stalemate. In the end footage from the suspect zone was obtained, but there was not a trace of the lads.

After almost detective-like work by many friends—using the GPS signal from their watch as requested from Garmin headquarters, footage from private and police drones, plus footage from the guides who went all the way up during the search, information from us, and the lads’ last photos—it appears that the lads missed our belay station by literally a few meters, and that while crossing a snow bridge over gigantic crevasse systems it collapsed beneath them.

When I first wrote this report, it had already been more than three weeks since I last saw the lads, since I last spoke to them. Still nothing has been found today, and in my view it will be hard for anything to be found. The scale of everything on Huascarán is utterly absurd: crevasses several hundred meters wide and deep, seracs the size of apartment blocks… Sure, this isn’t the Himalaya, and it doesn’t look like it, either. Huascarán looks like two lazy fat blokes lying side by side. But beware of it. That mountain is mean and hostile, and although on paper it isn’t hard—the Normal Route was reportedly graded only AD/AD+, the Escudo D—it is no game. You are playing for your life at every single step.

I don’t think that either we or the lads made any fundamental mistake; it was simply that Matýsek and I had a large dose of luck, while the lads had a little less of it.

I am not writing this story for sensation. It is just one real story with a tragic ending. If at least a few of you take something from it—ideally some kind of lesson—it will have served its purpose. As we all know, the mountains give, but sometimes they also take away. We unfortunately now know that this is no empty phrase but the hard truth.

Editor’s note: This trip report has been translated from the original Czech into English with permission of the author. Place names and local terms (La Garganta, El Escudo, refugio, Huaracino, pollo a la brasa) have not been translated from the original Spanish.

#8194. From Trail Access to Hunting Rights, Here’s How America Voted on Public Lands

A bull elk stands in an alpine meadow in Colorado's Rocky Mountains. Colorado voters rejected Amendment 83, which would have established a constitutional right to hunt and fish and designated those activities as preferred methods of wildlife management. (Photo: Mark de Leeuw/Getty)

Trail access, hunting rights, and how to spend gear sales taxes are just a handful of the public lands topics Americans voted on during the November 3, 2026, midterm election.

Colorado voters rejected a proposal to protect hunting and fishing in the state constitution, while Massachusetts approved a plan to use existing sporting-goods tax revenue for conservation. Elsewhere, voters weighed in on funding for parks, wildfire prevention, protected open space, and public access to waterways.

Here are seven election developments that could affect how Americans use the outdoors.

Colorado voters rejected Amendment 83, an effort to establish a constitutional right to hunt, fish, and harvest wildlife using “traditional methods.” The amendment did not define what “traditional methods” meant. However, if approved, Amendment 83 would have designated hunting and fishing as the state’s constitutionally preferred methods for managing game species.

Rejecting Amendment 83 preserves the state’s current regulatory system, keeping wildlife policy decisions under the authority of the legislature and the Colorado Parks and Wildlife Commission.

As of this publication, Colorado voters are still waiting on final counts for Proposition 137, a measure that would raise an estimated $175 million in annual conservation funding. If approved, the decision would redirect existing sporting-goods sales tax money toward wildfire mitigation, watershed protection, wildlife habitat, state parks, and trail maintenance.

Colorado limits how much tax money the state can keep, and it generally refunds any excess to taxpayers. Proposition 137 would also allow the state to keep sporting-goods tax revenue for conservation, which could mean smaller refunds in some years and less money for other state programs in others.

Official results have not been published yet. Outside will update this article accordingly.

Massachusetts voters approved creating the Nature for All Fund, which would tap existing sales tax revenues from sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and golf courses.

The fund could receive up to $65 million a year to protect forests, waterways, and wildlife habitat, and to improve parks and trails. Any money left over at the end of the year would stay in the fund rather than return to the state’s general budget, and state lawmakers would still decide how much to spend each year.

Charleston County voters in South Carolina backed extending a half-cent sales tax projected to generate up to $4.25 billion over 25 years.

The measure sets aside $690 million to protect open space, split equally between urban and rural areas. The money could help the county buy land for parks, preserve farmland, and create more places for people to access the water, according to the ballot language. The tax will also fund bike paths and pedestrian improvements through its separate transportation budget.

County officials will still need to approve specific land purchases and projects.

In Sarasota County, Florida, voters supported two complementary measures to protect natural areas and public parks. The first extends an existing property tax through 2049, while the second allows the county to borrow up to $250 million to buy and maintain conservation land.

The county will use money from the extended property tax to help pay back the loans. Together, the measures will help protect wetlands, forests, wildlife habitat, and public parks along Florida’s Gulf Coast.

California voters in Napa County favored a half-cent sales tax that would raise an estimated $23 million annually over 18 years, dividing proceeds between wildfire preparedness programs and the Napa County Regional Park and Open Space District.

The funding could help clear brush and other vegetation that fuels wildfires, protect water supplies, and maintain parks and natural areas.

Official results have not been published yet. Outside will update this article accordingly.

Rhode Island voters cleared the $55 million Green Economy Bond, which will help pay for improvements to state parks, beaches, campgrounds, and other outdoor spaces.

The funding includes $12 million to improve parks, beaches, and campgrounds, $7 million to restore Narragansett Bay and nearby waterways, and $3 million to protect open space. Additional money will support local recreation areas and boating facilities, while $25 million will help communities prepare for flooding, coastal erosion, and other climate-related damage.

#8193. After an Accident Left Her Paralyzed, Brittany Chadbourne Found a Way to Keep Climbing

“I'm the giant asterisk at the end of ‘climbing is dangerous.'" —Brittany Chadbourne (Photo: Maya Silver)

For some climbers, campusing—climbing with only your upper body—is a training strategy. For Utah climber Brittany Chadbourne, it’s her only choice.

I met Chadbourne in early October at Momentum Millcreek, one of the gyms she regularly visits in the Salt Lake Valley. She pulled onto a V3 boulder problem angled at least 45 degrees, working her way to the top and back down in about a minute. Then she eased herself into her wheelchair, hardly out of breath.

Bouldering carries particular risks for Chadbourne. Because she can’t control how she lands, a fall could cause additional injuries, including damage to the rods in her spine. These days, she saves harder climbing for ropes and sticks to boulder problems she knows she can safely descend. Afterward, I belayed the 28-year-old on a 5.11c. Her powerful shoulders, arms, and back carried her up the route without the use of her legs or lower abs.

Four years ago, a routesetting accident left Chadbourne paralyzed from the belly button down, so she had to find a new way to practice the sport she loves. “I’ve always wanted to be in Climbing Magazine,” Chadbourne told me. “But I thought it would be for something way cooler than a V2 boulder. I’m still proud that I’m continuing with it and being positive, or at least as positive as I can be.”

Chadbourne discovered climbing while in school at Weber State University in Ogden, Utah, and really got into it in 2020. But before she started climbing, while growing up in northern Utah, she was a gymnast who had heard plenty of stories about gymnasts breaking their necks and becoming paralyzed.

“It was something that I always feared and tried to avoid,” Chadbourne says of paralysis.

On November 22, 2022, that fear became reality.

When Chadbourne began working as a routesetter in September of that year at The Front in Ogden, routesetters used a pull-through system of static lines, an alpine butterfly knot, and quickdraw anchors to access the wall. Chadbourne says the setup made her nervous from the start. She worried the knot could slip through the quickdraw carabiners. And the system differed from the one she’d used while routesetting at Weber State University.

“I was pretty new to all of it. So I was just like, ‘If this is what you guys have been using, obviously it’s safe. I’m sure it’s fine.’ Obviously, it wasn’t fine.”

Not long after she started, Chadbourne and The Front have stated that another routesetter reattached the wrong side of the rope when they were lowering and fell from the wall. According to both The Front and Chadbourne, the climber wasn’t seriously injured. After the accident, The Front retired the system and hosted trainings to get all routesetters up to speed on the new standards. Eddie Morillas, the gym’s director of routesetting, told Climbing via email that an updated fall-protection plan took effect on October 18, 2022, removing the alpine butterfly setup.

Under the new standard, Morillas explained that routesetters “are only permitted to gain initial access to anchors and remove working lines while on belay or connected to an autobelay unit, where applicable.” He added that Chadbourne attended two training sessions on the new standard before her accident.

According to Chadbourne, the head routesetter that day instructed her to use the alpine butterfly setup. The Front confirmed this, stating in an email to Climbing: “Our understanding is that the routesetter in charge let Brittany use the alpine butterfly system, which went against The Front’s fall protection plan and the training every setter on the team had completed.”

The precise cause of Chadbourne’s fall remains uncertain. Morillas told Climbing that The Front’s investigation found her knots were tied correctly, but that she pulled the rope in the wrong direction, preventing the knot from cinching around the anchor. According to The Front, the knot temporarily caught in the anchor before slipping through as Chadbourne moved up the rope.

Chadbourne says she followed the head routesetter’s instructions when setting up her static line correctly and had a coworker double-check it. Near the top of the wall, as she slid her ascender upward, she felt the rope go slack. She believes the knot slipped through the quickdraws, just as she’d feared.

“I immediately knew that I was falling,” she says. “So I just closed my eyes and fell 30 feet.”

When Chadbourne hit the ground, her left leg took most of the impact. She shattered her tibia and fibula, and suffered a burst fracture of her T12 vertebra and compression fractures at her C7, T5, and T7 vertebrae. The fall left her paralyzed from the belly button down.

Chadbourne says she receives workers’ compensation benefits that cover her medical expenses and equipment, including wheelchairs. She has chosen not to pursue a lawsuit, saying she was already overwhelmed by the aftermath of the accident and didn’t believe legal action would change what had happened.

Initially, Chadbourne felt embarrassed that her accident happened in a gym rather than outdoors. She’d spent years caving, exploring abandoned mines, and climbing outside without serious injury, only to suffer a life-altering fall inside a gym.

But that embarrassment didn’t diminish her desire to climb.

“I pretty much knew immediately that I would go back into climbing,” Chadbourne says. “Even as I was being loaded onto the helicopter to go to the hospital.” She didn’t know a lot about paraclimbing, but she figured there must be people out there climbing without their legs. “Campusing is a thing, so I’m sure somebody’s doing it,” she recalls thinking.

After two months in the hospital and another month adjusting to her new normal at home, Chadbourne’s doctor cleared her to climb. But her first time back on belay was “pretty rough.” She made it about 10 feet off the ground, partially hoisted up by her belayer. At first, she couldn’t climb high enough to experience the fear she’d felt during her fall. But as she grew stronger and began climbing higher, Chadbourne admits some of the fear came back.

Chadbourne still has days when she cries about her injury, sometimes even while climbing.

“Day to day, my life is just as hard now as it was four years ago [when I was first injured],” she adds. “I’m just doing more.” And she is. She’s traveling more, training more, and trying things she once thought were out of reach, including becoming an ambitious competitive climber.

Before the accident, Chadbourne loved technical slab climbing. Now, without the use of her legs or lower abdomen, she competes in the AL1 paraclimbing classification, also known as seated climbing.

In 2024, just two years after her injury, Chadbourne made Team USA. She earned bronze in the women’s AL1 competition at the 2025 Paraclimbing National Championships and silver in 2026.

But she found herself in a small competitive field. With so few women in the AL1 category, Chadbourne often faced just one or two other athletes. She and fellow paraclimber Carlie Cook advocated for mixed-gender AL1 competition, which would allow women and men to compete against each other. In March 2025, the International Federation of Sport Climbing released updated paraclimbing guidelines permitting mixed-gender competition in the category.

Competing against a larger field has made the sport more exciting for Chadbourne. “If it was just women, it would be like three or four of us in the entire world,” she says. “So to be able to compete against 20-plus people is really exciting. And it makes me want to beat the men!”

Now, Chadbourne has her sights set on making a World Cup final one day. She’s also working to bring more athletes with paraplegia, especially women, into the sport. One day, she hopes there will be enough female competitors to support a separate women’s category.

But there’s another stage Chadbourne hopes to compete on someday: the Paralympics.

“When I had heard rumors that [paraclimbing] was going to be in the LA Games, I got really excited,” Chadbourne recalls. But like many paraclimbing categories, AL1 was excluded from climbing’s Paralympic debut at the Los Angeles 2028 Games.

Chadbourne hopes that will change for the 2032 Paralympics in Australia. In the meantime, she’s also training in Nordic skiing and biathlon, with ambitions of making Team USA in both sports.

For Chadbourne, staying busy is one way of coping with the difficult days. “The busier you are, your brain just forgets to be sad,” she says.

“Continual motion builds on itself,” she adds. “I don’t really have any other choice but to just keep on going.”

Chadbourne’s momentum has carried into her work with other climbers. Between competitions and training, she teaches climbing and continues to set routes at Weber State University.

There, she’s become an advocate for safe routesetting and climbing practices, encouraging climbers to ask questions about systems before trusting them.

“I’m the giant asterisk at the end of ‘climbing is dangerous,’” Chadbourne says about teaching college students. “I want to prepare them that this is a possibility, but then I prepare them to avoid it in as many ways as they can.”

The most important lesson Chadbourne underscores is to always speak up if you don’t understand how something works. No matter their experience level, Chadbourne wants all climbers to feel comfortable raising concerns and asking questions.

“I want them to feel like they have a voice.”

#8191. Avoid California’s Crowded Trails With These 5 Quiet Coastline Hikes

There’s no shortage of spectacular hiking in California. Big Sur, Yosemite, and Redwoods have achieved international renown––and for good reason. But if you want to escape the crowds, the less congested San Luis Obispo coast offers scores of trails, uncrowded wilderness, and stellar vistas along Highway 1.

These routes invite you to hike on hills turned gold by spring flowers, spot seals in coastal reserves, and explore both long and short routes near cozy coastal towns—all without fighting for a parking spot at the trailhead. Integrate these hikes into a road trip along the iconic Highway 1, or just visit for an active getaway. San Luis Obispo’s landscapes are beautiful, the food is delicious, and, for the nights you’re not camping, there’s great lodging.

Named for the abundant yellow wildflowers that paint the hills gold every spring—namely bright yellow poppies, Deerbrush, and wild mustard—this unique park along the Morro Bay estuary is home to riparian environments, coastal scrub, and pines.

Scores of trails weave across 8,000 acres of wilderness and offer views of Morro Bay. But for epic views of the coast and a solid taste of all the park has to offer, start at the Hazard Peak Trailhead on Pecho Valley Road and hike out on Hazard Trail to the peak. From there, you can retrace your steps back to the junction with Canyon View Trail. Take that and descend a series of short switchbacks to Islay Creek Road, which will spit you out just down the street from the Hazard Peak Trailhead. You can also extend the hike by doing the full Hazard Peak loop, which is about 11 miles.

Located in the Lopez Lake Recreation Area outside Arroyo Grande, this trail climbs up and along the western ridge of the county park. Wildlife sightings of deer, birds, even black bears, aren’t uncommon. The last section of trail involves a steep climb to the peak, but the 360-degree views of the Oceano Dunes and coast to the west and surrounding Santa Lucia, Caliente, and Sierra Madre Mountains are worth the effort.

Start on Wittenberg Trail at the end of Lopez Dr. and branch off onto Duna Vista Loop Trail. Duna Vista Spur Trail will lead you to the peak. Hike directly back on the southernmost part of the loop for a slightly shorter route (8 miles) or split off onto the northern section for the full 8.8-mile trek. A day-use fee of $12 per vehicle is required.

This beautiful coastal walk isn’t a challenging one, but give yourself plenty of time to complete it: You’ll want to stop and soak in the wide ocean views, sea stacks, and wetlands. Most of the hike is along bluffs, but opportunities to descend and explore intertidal areas at low tide abound. Expect to see plenty of sea lions and bring your binoculars to try to spot an endangered snowy plover.

Start at the North Ocean parking lot on the edge of Cayucos and take Estero Bluffs Trail along the coast to the end of the park and back.

There’s more to this hike than classic California coastal scrub. In fact, as you climb over rolling hills, you’ll score views of Morro Bay and jagged Morro Rock, a volcanic plug in the estuary, and even drop into shady live oak groves. Volcanic peaks pepper the periphery, and opportunities to spot wildlife abound, including any of hundreds of bird species that follow the Pacific Flyway.

The state park’s trail system is extensive, but this route is a nice loop that touches a lot of the trails on the east side. Start at the parking lot on S Bay Blvd. and take Quarry Trail to Canet Trail, followed by Chumash, Crespi, Park Ridge, and Live Oak Trails. That leads you right back to the parking lot you started in. You can customize the length by combining various side trails, including to the top of Portola Trail, a small summit, which adds about a mile. A state park pass or $8 day-use fee is required.

This rugged trail leads into the Santa Lucia Wilderness within Los Padres National Forest, finally reaching an 80-foot waterfall that streams into an azure pool. Much of the trail slowly climbs through the woods alongside a creek and lush riparian zone in Big Falls Canyon. However, if you continue onward past the trio of falls, your efforts will be rewarded with sunny views of the surrounding Coast Ranges.

Start at Big Falls Trailhead on Upper Lopez Canyon Road and hike to the junction with Hi Mountain Trail. Return the same way. The last section of Lopez Canyon Road to the trailhead can be rough, so 4WD is recommended.

Eat: Gardens of Avila, located within Sycamore Mineral Springs Resort and Spa in San Luis Obispo, offers elegant dining, homegrown ingredients, and garden paths for after-dinner strolls.

Sip: Wineries abound. Oenophiles who appreciate organic and regenerative farming should visit Chamisal Vineyards in Edna Valley.

Explore Town: Los Osos offers welcoming coffee shops, local art galleries, and fine boutiques. Avila Beach is worth exploring for sunny waterfront vibes. Cayucos is home to classic seaside tourist scenes complete with souvenir shops and antique stores.

Campgrounds are in no short supply along Highway 1, and the San Luis Obispo area is no exception. Most of the state parks, like Montaña de Oro, Morro Bay, and Estero Bluffs, have their own developed campgrounds. Morro Beach also has a campground along the coast. Those can be booked online or in person, but they fill up quickly, especially on weekends. During the winter, these campgrounds are closed, so you’ll need to seek out dispersed camping or other lodging options.

Dispersed camping is strictly prohibited along Highway 1. However, some nearby mountain areas allow it. Check out TV Tower Road, Carrizo Plain National Monument, or Williams Hill Recreation Area.

Want to break up your nights outside? You have options. San Luis Obispo and nearby towns have plenty of hotels, BnB’s, and more luxurious accommodations. For a splurge, check out La Lomita Ranch, a chic and colorful former stable with painted tiles, terracotta, and horses in San Luis Obispo.

#8187. 3 Expert-Approved Exercises to Build Power in Your Climbing

There’s a famous quote by Wolfgang Güllich, the German climber who invented the word “redpoint”: “There’s no such thing as too much power.” As a coach, I often see and hear this in the climbing community. I agree with the sentiment, but I think that by and large, power has been misused, misunderstood, and poorly trained by the vast majority of climbers.

Firstly, I think it’s misused and misunderstood because the general climbing population doesn’t grasp that strength and power are not the same thing. Secondly, as a result of this, the training methods climbers use when they’re trying to improve their power are often wrong.

So let’s start with a very simple explanation of strength and power. I’m also going to have to bring speed into the equation, as this gives context for how these all sit on a spectrum. Afterwards, we’ll look at some of the main things I think climbers are getting wrong when doing their own power training, how to solve these issues, and some examples of simple but effective ways to train power.

The reason that power matters so much in climbing is because not all moves are possible—or most efficient—when executed at a slower pace without speed and power. Trying to just use strength (slower movement) could mean that you’ll either fail on the move or you’ll climb inefficiently using excess energy, which ultimately means no send!

An easy example of this is completing a super long hard move. With just strength, we’re only able to lock to a certain depth of shoulder position and throw or deadpoint to a limited distance. Add in power and you’ll cover way more distance and end up latching that hold.

One additional note on the “power endurance” term: This one is a bit of a misnomer which caused us many issues over the years at Lattice, mainly because power endurance does not actually use power. It should have been named “strength endurance,” as that’s what it really is.

Strength is how much force you can produce. Think of a max hang on a small edge, or a heavy weighted pull-up. The movement is slow, but the force is high.

Speed is how fast you can move when there’s very little resistance. Think of how quickly you can move your hand from one hold to the next with only the weight of your own arm to overcome.

Power sits between the two. It’s force multiplied by speed, so you only have lots of it when you can produce a relatively high force quickly. Dynos, band-assisted pull-ups, and latching holds at the end of a deadpoint all fit into this category.

Think of it as a sliding scale. Heavy and slow climbing is at one end, light and fast climbing is at the other, and power is in the middle. You can’t produce your maximum force and your maximum speed at the same time, so where you train on that scale matters and I think climbers are continually getting this wrong.

None of this means strength doesn’t matter. Strength is the foundation of power. A stronger and bigger muscle can produce more force at every speed, so if you’re relatively weak, getting stronger will improve your power more than anything else. This is a really important point to grasp, for those of you who haven’t yet developed a foundation of high strength. Once you’re reasonably strong, though, specific power training starts to give you more benefits. As a rough guide, if you can’t do a pull-up with an extra 35-50% of your bodyweight, strength should be the main focus still (even though power training in addition is still useful). Once you’re above this threshold, power training should become increasingly important.

This is the big one. Power is extremely sensitive to fatigue and it drops well before you actually feel tired. Despite this, many climbers I see at the gym do their “power work” at the end of a session, after an hour of board climbing or a set of endurance drills. Unfortunately, if every rep is slower than your best, you’re practicing being slow. Power work goes at the start of the session, straight after a thorough warm-up, when you’re fresh. Prioritise this timing over everything.

Linked laps on the campus board, long sets of explosive pull-ups, and circuits of “powerful” moves can be useful, but they’re all mostly power endurance, not power. Power training means low numbers of high-quality reps. Stop the set as soon as a rep is noticeably slower, shorter, or messier than the first.

Ninety seconds between sets isn’t enough. You need at least three minutes, sometimes more, for the systems that drive maximal efforts to recover. If it feels like you’re resting way more than you should and you’re slightly bored, you’re probably resting the right amount.

The intention to move as fast as possible is a large part of what drives the adaptation, even when the movement itself ends up slow. So remember, if you’re doing a power pull-up, even if only the first 20% of the pull is fast, that’s ok. You should put in full intent, with complete focus on speed for each pull, and you’ll find that’s what really counts.

Some climbers only hang, push, squeeze, and lift heavy. Others love to campus, jump, spin, and dyno. The best results come from working across the scale. Heavy strength work (for the foundation of power and speed) and explosive power work should be included in the same training block, with the emphasis shifting depending on what you need for your goals.

Below are three power exercises that work well. Pick one or two for a session, do them first, and remember to stop as soon as speed or quality reduces.

If your 1RM pull-up is greater than 160%, you may be able to do this at bodyweight.

Pull as fast as possible, aiming to get your chest as high as possible, almost as if you’re trying to roll into a muscle up. Do four sets of three, resting three minutes between sets. The faster you can complete each rep, the better, so generally use more assistance than you might think.

Always learn how to do this session on a comfortable hold and using your preferred grip type.

Using a hangboard edge (or a load cell, if you have one), pull as hard and as fast as you can for two to three seconds. Do four to eight reps, resting at least three minutes in between. This trains your ability to generate high force quickly, which is exactly what deadpoints need.

These can be done on holds, a hangboard, or a pull-up bar. The critical part is getting the height of the starting position right.

Using your chosen hold, you want to jump from the ground into the middle range of the pull-up motion, using the momentum from your lower body to assist in generating speed and power in the upper part of the pull. You’re jumping into the pull-up with your legs, and your arms and back are finishing off the pull at high speed as you’re already carrying momentum. Do four to eight reps, resting at least three minutes in between.

Train power like this two to three times a week when it’s your focus, and once or twice a week to maintain it the rest of the time. Don’t forget that power fades faster than strength when you stop training it, so it’s worth keeping a small amount in your plan all year round.

So back to Güllich: Is there such a thing as too much power? Probably not. But there’s definitely such a thing as too much fatigue, too much volume, and too little speed and intention when you’re trying to train it. Get strong first, train power fresh in mind and body, keep the quality high, and stop before it drops. I think you’ll be pretty happy with how you feel on the wall after just a couple of months of this.

#8185. Two Hikers Dead in Bear Attack in British Columbia, Leaving Officials to Look for Answers

A young grizzly in British Columbia (Photo: Colleen Gara / Getty Images)

Two hikers are dead after a suspected bear attack on Indigenous lands in British Columbia, provincial wildlife officials say. The incident comes just a year after a bear encounter in the same area left four people seriously injured.

Rescuers discovered one body on the afternoon of Nov. 2 near the Snooka West Trail in Bella Coola, leading to a search for a second, missing victim.

That search concluded late Tuesday night when searchers found the second hiker dead. Officials with the B.C. Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) believe both were attacked by a grizzly bear, and efforts are ongoing to locate and trap any bears in the area for assessment.

Authorities and family members have since identified the pair as 48-year-old Jennifer Balcarras and her daughter, 20-year-old Selah Reed.

“It is not yet clear whether more than one bear was involved,” BCCOS Investigator Jeff Tyre told Backpacker. “Any captured bear will be assessed. If it is determined to have been involved in the attack, it will be dispatched in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety.”

Family members first reported Balcarras and Reed overdue on Sunday, Nov. 1. Police and SAR operators found the first human remains on Monday afternoon, and called BCCOS due to evidence that suggested an animal was involved.

The victims’ remains have since been returned to their families, and the Snooka West Trail remains closed.

In the wake of the deaths, tribal authorities of the Nuxalk Nation, the First Nations people who live in the Bella Coola valley, expressed their support. Samuel Schooner, elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, said in a statement that the tribe understands firsthand the trauma this incident will inflict on the victims’ family members and on the survivors of last year’s attack.

That incident occurred near Highway 20 on Nov. 20, 2025, when a grizzly attacked a local school group taking a lunch break. Adults were able to repel the animal with bear spray and a bear banger, but not before it severely injured four people, including three children. The four individuals were rushed to the hospital in varying conditions, and seven others required care at the scene.

No one died, and investigators continued to search for grizzlies in the area, eventually determining three bears could have been involved. Over the following two weeks, officers captured eight adult and juvenile grizzlies for forensic testing. All eight animals were eventually collared and relocated after they could not be forensically connected with the attack.

A total of 24 officers were involved in the response to that attack. Some reportedly drove 14 hours overnight to hand-deliver samples to the Alberta Wildlife Forensic Laboratory. BCCOS described both the response and the incident as extraordinary.

“In my 34 years of experience, I have not seen an attack like this with a large group of people,” Kevin Van Damme, with BCCOS, told Global News at the time. “So this is extremely rare and I think the public needs to understand that part.”

As 2025 field operations concluded, the Conservation Office reported decreasing bear sightings and pointed out that grizzlies in the area typically transition from hyperphagia to denning in or around December.

It’s unclear how long the current search will continue. A spokesperson for BCCOS said investigators were unavailable for comment due to heightened field activity.

“Our thoughts are with the family of the victims during this tragic time,” the agency said. “We are in contact with the family to offer any support we can as we continue to investigate this incident.”

#8182. A Blizzard Did Not Kill Two Missing Colorado Climbers. A Broken Anchor Did.

Colorado Mountain College students Kaden Matsuda, 19, left, and Jackson Donlon, 20, died in late October after a climbing anchor failed during their descent of West Apostle Mountain in Colorado's Sawatch Range. (Photo: Courtesy of Chaffee County Sheriff's Office)

The two Colorado Mountain College students found dead in Colorado’s Sawatch Range last week fell to their deaths after a climbing anchor failed on West Apostle Mountain, authorities announced November 3.

Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20, died instantly from multiple blunt force injuries, according to a November 3 joint statement from the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office and Coroner’s Office.

“Kaden and Jackson lived life at the highest peaks chasing freedoms and panoramic views that most of us only see in pictures,” Chaffee County Sheriff Andy Rohrich said in the statement. “We hope their families and friends find strength in the memories of their vibrant spirits.”

The findings provide the first official explanation of what happened to the two friends, whose disappearance prompted a dayslong search involving multiple agencies working through heavy snow and treacherous mountain terrain.

According to the release, investigators pieced together what happened on West Apostle Mountain, the 13,597-foot peak where the students were climbing after leaving Colorado Mountain College’s Leadville campus on October 23.

The pair were descending the mountain when Donlon began to rappel, using a rope secured to an anchor in the rock to lower himself down the steep terrain. Matsuda was clipped into the same anchor system through his personal anchor device.

The setup appeared to have two backups, including a piton—a metal spike driven into rock—and a second rock anchor. But despite those apparent safeguards, the anchor system suffered what investigators described as a “catastrophic failure,” sending both climbers falling down the mountainside.

Authorities have not determined why the anchor failed or exactly how far the students fell.

Search crews discovered their bodies on October 28 in a snow-filled basin below West Apostle Mountain. A helicopter recovered them the following day.

“There are no right words to family and friends for a loss this heavy,” Rohrich said in the statement. “Know that whenever we explore our backcountry in the future we will think of them as young men who didn’t just look at the world; they climbed it.”

As Outside previously reported, a powerful early-season snowstorm dumped up to two feet of snow on the mountains, complicating the search and raising questions about what happened to the climbers.

Investigators now say the storm was not a direct contributing factor in the students’ deaths.

In his November 3 statement, Rohrich also praised the students’ preparedness, saying his staff had found no obvious mistakes to point to.

“Kaden and Jackson will certainly be remembered by my staff as an example to others of what preparation looks like,” Rohrich said. “In most similar cases that have led to a devastating conclusion we find it easy to pick apart what was done wrong. That was not the case with Kaden and Jackson.”

#8178. Baby Sign Language 101: Baby’s First Signs

Well before they utter their first words, infants as young as six months can learn to sign. Baby sign language is thought to reduce baby’s frustration levels, boost self-esteem, and bolster language development. And you don’t need to be an expert. Begin with three to five signs, saying the word as you sign it. Encourage other caregivers and siblings to join in. Then repeat, repeat, repeat. Your little one’s motor skills may not allow them to perfectly mimic the sign, so watch for hand gestures that indicate she’s trying, usually within two months of being introduced to it. Here are some great baby sign language starter signs.

Show your little one the sign for a person they know, like mommy, daddy, brother, grandma, or baby. It doesn’t matter if you plan to use mommy, mama, mother, or mom; the sign is the same — using an open palm with fingers spread, tap your thumb on your chin. For “daddy” and its variations, use the same hand position; only tap the forehead. Remember to point to the person as you sign.

Food is a great motivator. Teach your little eater the sign for their favorite food or the ones for eat, milk, or bottle. When Baby’s plate is empty, “more” and “all done” allow them to set the pace for the meal. To sign “more,” press the thumb and fingertips of each hand together, and then tap the fingertips of the two hands together several times. Look for baby to put their fists or palms together as they start to get the hang of this sign.

Animal signs are fun because they often mimic some aspect of the animal. Baby will love learning the signs for her beloved pet or for the animals around the neighborhood. Dog, cat, fish, and bird are all good candidates. You can even have a favorite stuffed animal act out the motions for its sign. The baby sign for “dog” is patting your hand to your hip, as if calling a dog. This is a slight modification from the American Sign Language version, which includes a snap that is too difficult for emerging motor skills.

It’s never too early to introduce your little bundle to being polite. “Please” is a great word to start with. Try this technique when it’s clear your baby desires something specific, like a toy or a drink, and he’s not upset or in any distress. Say that you will get it and ask if they can say “please,” demonstrating the sign as you do so. Then give them the item, regardless of whether they do the sign or not. Eventually the concept will begin to sink in, and they’ll be doing it on his own. With a flat hand and thumb extended, sign “please” by moving the palm of your hand in a circular motion in front of your chest.

Use the repetition of baby’s routine as an opportunity to teach her the signs of daily life. Learn “sleep” for naptime and bedtime. Let baby know it’s playtime by signing “play,” and then show her the sign for whatever you are playing with, be it a ball, blocks, or a book. The sign for “bath” mimics the act of washing. To do this sign, simply move both your fists up and down in front of your chest as if scrubbing it.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8177. The Best Nonprofits That Support Dads and Fatherhood

The best nonprofits that support dads and fatherhood.

Research has shown that when dads are engaged and present, kids do better. We celebrate dads on Father’s Day because we should celebrate everything that makes children’s lives — and outcomes — better. When children have close relationships with father figures, they tend to avoid high-risk behaviors; have higher-paying jobs and healthy, stable relationships; and have higher IQ test scores. The benefits go on, but one thing’s for sure: Dads matter in the lives of children, and so we should support and celebrate their presence in their kids’ lives.

Here are just a few organizations that champion dads and understand the integral role that fathers play in the lives of their children.

All Pro Dad is a program of Family First that provides tools and resources to dads that allow them to be more present in the lives of their children. Spearheaded by former NFL coach Tony Dungy, NFL player Benjamin Watson, ESPN personality Dan Orlovsky, and many other prominent sports figures, All Pro Dad hosts a yearly interactive get-together for kids and dads at an NFL or NCAA stadium and a monthly school program where dads meet up with their children at school to spend time bonding and relationship building.

The Center for Family Policy and Practice is a nonprofit organization that advocates for fair and equitable laws and policies that affect low-income families and fathers. Focusing on child support, family safety and security, and financial and economic security, the CFPP acts as a think tank to develop solutions to barriers experienced by low-income fathers and fathers of color.

The Child & Family Blog provides research-driven content on the impact of family on social, emotional, and cognitive child development. In addition to covering topics like race, divorce, and inequality, the Child & Family Blog covers research on the importance of fathers and the role they play in both the family dynamic and the development of children.

The Family Equality Council works to ensure that members of the LGBTQ community have the ability to create families and provide support, education, activism and advocacy, and the resources they need to become parents and foster loving, healthy family relationships. The FEP also tracks national and state legislation that affects the ability of LGBTQ couples to become parents and maintain parental rights.

Fathering Together provides anyone who identifies as a father with tools and resources to uplift and support them as they work to create a “more equitable society.” The organization hosts different communities so that dads from every walk of life can reach out to peers for help, support, and advice while working to make the world a better and safer place for their children.

The Fatherhood Project is a Massachusetts-based program that empowers fathers to become more “knowledgeable, active, and emotionally engaged with their children.” Through research-based principles and curricula and programs like Dads Matter, Dads in Recovery, Teen Dads, and Divorcing Dads, the organization aims to help all dads be more present and engaged with their children while focusing on dads in marginalized and underserved communities.

Fathers Incorporated is an Atlanta-based nonprofit that works with federal lawmakers and leaders in the responsible fatherhood movement, faith and business leaders, and family law practitioners to advocate for legislative and community changes that promote fathers’ involvement in the lives of their children. The group focuses on co-parenting, domestic violence, incarceration, child development, child support, and employment and financial stability. Fathers Incorporated provides resources and programs for fathers to engage with their children healthily and raise awareness through programs like the Million Fathers March and Black Dads Count.

Fathers’ Uplift is a one-of-a-kind organization that provides fathers with the tools they need to overcome trauma, addiction, racial barriers, and emotional issues to help them fully engage with their children and families. Fathers’ Uplift provides therapy, coaching, training opportunities, and youth enrichment with the aim of reducing the number of children raised without positive father figures in their lives. It is the only organization in the United States that offers therapy, counseling, and addiction support specifically geared toward fathers and their families with the aim of reuniting families and providing them with the framework to thrive.

The National Fatherhood Initiative is the country’s largest provider of research on the involvement of fathers and the impact fathers have on families. It provides communities with resources and training to increase father engagement with the goal of ensuring that communities and human service organizations have the tools and training they need to be father-inclusive so fathers can be more involved in the lives of their children.

The Native American Fatherhood and Families Association is an Arizona-based nonprofit focusing on nourishing family relationships through its Fatherhood Is Sacred/Motherhood Is Sacred (FIS/MIS), Linking Generations by Strengthening Relationships, and Addressing Family Violence & Abuse programs. Employing culturally sensitive curricula and materials, NAFFA is able to address the specific concerns of the Native American community to reunite families and empower fathers to become family leaders.

The National Partnership for Women and Families understands that families benefit when dads are present and actively engaged. One way the NPWF is creating a more equitable world for women is by spearheading programs, legislation, and calls to action that support fathers by promoting active fatherhood and gender equality.

Established in Brazil in 1997, Promundo has worked globally to engage fathers in the care economy, promote active fatherhood and promote gender equity and justice by engaging men and boys with women and girls. The organization is currently undergoing a rebranding to be more inclusive of all genders. Its new name, Equimundo: Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, “reflects our commitment to fostering gender equity and our roots in social justice. The name change also captures our approach of collaborating with and never overshadowing our diverse partners worldwide.”

This article was originally published on June 7, 2022

#8176. The Origin of "Dad" And Why Some Men Prefer to Be Called "Father"

The nicknames we use for parents go in and out of fashion, age to age and era to era. At one time, men preferred “Sire.” Other times, “Father” was preferable. What we do know is that the most agreed-upon way to refer to dad these days is by calling him, well, ‘dad.’

But why have we ditched ‘father’ for dad? The short answer is that things have gotten a little less formal. But the reason we’ve moved away from formality is that we’ve embraced what’s more linguistically natural for children and parents. ‘Father’ comes from the Proto-Indo-European “pəter” and Old English ‘fæder,’ meaning “he who begets a child,” reflecting the baby-talk sound “pa” as well as a phonetic shift from ‘p’ to ‘f’ in Middle English.

However, ‘dad’ did not evolve from ‘father.’

“It’s from ‘dada,’” says Professor John H. McWhorter, a professor at Columbia University, “a natural sound from children’s mouths as a second stab at consonants after they try the most natural ‘mama.’ Next is often either ‘dada, ‘tata,’ ‘baba’ or … ‘papa.’ Upon which, ‘father’ starts in Proto-Indo-European as “puh-TAIR,” and the ‘puh’ part is this same thing: what started as ‘pa’ in ‘papa.’ The words for Mommy and Daddy are the closest thing to linguistic universals because they are about mouth anatomy in infants rather than thought.”

There are also another key reason why this is reinforced over time. Emie Tittnich, a specialist at the University of Pittsburgh, speaking to Live Science, noted that parents generally refrain from using pronouns like ‘I’ or ‘you’ to avoid confusing their kids with abstract concepts early on. “‘Parents will use [‘mommy’ and ‘daddy’] to help their children learn the role names and also to indicate the relationship, ‘mommy and me,'” says Tittnich. “It usually takes the child awhile to understand that the same person can be called two different names.”

The agreed-upon naturality of these linguistic principles mean that as American society has become more colloquial and secular over time, we move (at least in this instance) away from a term that’s reflective of a status quo based in rigid concepts of class and religion—one of the meanings of ‘fæder’ in Old English is ‘supreme being,’ according to the Online Etymology Dictionary. As a result, we’re generally caught off guard when we hear a child refer to a parent as ‘father.’

However, this is not the case unanimously. We spoke with six dads who prefer — or simply stuck with — ‘father’ instead of ‘dad.’ Some do it as an homage to their own fathers; others do it to sound more authoritative. Others do it because it’s what their kids like. All have their reasons and, maybe, deep inside, some are just big fans of Proto-Indo-European language. Here’s what they say.

I sometimes worry that it sounds a little austere out loud, but it’s just what my father always asked us to call him, and it felt like it was important to me that we carry that on. No one in my family has had a problem with it. I think you can still be a ‘dad’ and be called ‘father,’ if that makes sense. It’s basically semantic, in that way, but it’s also more than semantics. — John, Baltimore, MD

It’s less of a request or a demand or anything, but when we were teaching my oldest what everything is called, we always just said ‘this is your mother’ and ‘this is your father,’ and he liked to say that, too. So we’ve kept it. I’d be lying if I said I didn’t think it was just adorably proper to have our little man coming up to us and saying, “father, mother, may I use the bathroom,” or what have you. But as with everything, I don’t mind anything that seems to feel natural for my kids and makes them happy. — Eric, Austin, Texas

My son didn’t start until he was older. I think he thought it sounded more respectful, or just more professional. We’ve always been a more traditional family, in how we carry ourselves, I guess you would say. So perhaps this was his way of taking that in stride, or contributing to that. My wife teases me about it sometimes. I should clarify, it’s generally him introducing me to other people that way. ‘This is my father, have you met my father?’ etc. — Patrick, Twin Cities, MN

In the past two years, my older daughter, age 21, began calling me ‘father’ and as strange as I found it, I didn’t mine it at all. Now, my four-year-old calls me “father” and I guess I now have a new title. As long as I am not being called ‘Henry,’ I am okay with it. — Henry, Boston, MA

I have eight children—three boys and five girls. I’ve always asked that they call me ‘father’ not to be domineering but because the house could get a little chaotic, as you can imagine, and my wife and I felt that it was a label that was more authoritative and kept things from being too chaotic. ‘Please don’t touch your father’s golf clubs’ just has a better ring to it, I guess. — Elliott, Charlotte, NC

I love that my children call me ‘father,’ because of the sense of responsibility it instills in me. Your ‘dad’ or ‘daddy’ is there to lend you the car, your ‘father’ is there to raise you, and protect you and make sure that you have the tool you need to succeed in life. When my kids call me ‘father,’ it reignites that sense of purpose for me every day, and reminds me it’s up to me to make their world a great place to grow up in. — Sam, Alachua Country, FL

This article was originally published on May 17, 2019
