#8142. Disney+ Has Adapted Your Favorite 'Goosebumps' Books — But Which Ones?

The new Disney+ Goosebumps has 10 episodes in this series, all with links to the original R.L. Stine books.

For over 30 years, Goosebumps books have scared children silly. A gateway for children to step into the world of horror novels, this R.L. Stine mega-franchise has maintained its spot as one of the best-selling book series of all time. These books combined just the right amount of kid-friendly spookiness with a dash of humor, complete with twist endings that always left readers demanding more.

Goosebumps is no stranger to screen adaptations, including a four-season live-action series on Fox Kids in the mid-90s, and a pair of movies with Jack Black from a few years ago. This Halloween season, Goosebumps is back with an all-new live-action show streaming on Disney+ and Hulu, promising more mature frights while remaining faithful to the original material. This series follows five small-town high-school kids investigating the death of a teen from three decades prior, whose home the new English teacher has just moved into.

As opposed to its 90’s counterpart, this modern adaptation will be a spine-tingling 10-part mini-series, with the first five chapters dropping on October 13, and subsequent episodes added weekly. Instead of transforming a single book into a self-contained 30-minute mini-movie, the new series takes inspiration from them, inserting those elements into the overarching narrative across the duration of the show.

According to an official press release from Scholastic, the show draws elements from five of the books, but the recently revealed titles for the episodes show nearly all of them evoke fan favorites from across the 62 original books, with links across the entire 230+ books in this expansive franchise.

Which Goosebumps books can viewers expect to see in the new show? Readers beware – you’re in for a scare!

Official trailer for Goosebumps on Disney+ and Hulu

Throughout the trailer, we see Miles McKenna as James and Zack Morris as Isaiah causing trouble with a Polaroid camera. The story that develops is taken from the fourth Goosebumps book, which shares the same name as the episode (a trend throughout most of these titles).

A group of friends discover a cursed camera in a rundown house, but instead of snapping a pic of the moment, it predicts a grim future for whoever is photographed. Scary movies and cameras are always a bad mix, no matter if it’s for photos or videos. It’s also a reminder – never take things you find in decrepit abandoned houses, unless you want to be a character in an R.L. Stine book, and you know how they tend to end up.

Seen briefly in the trailer is a lifelike human face attached to a slab of wood. It’s a mask, but just any kind. It’s a recurring haunted object seen throughout the Goosebumps franchise. These self-aware parasitic masks were created by a mysterious shopkeeper, hungry to be worn so they can completely take over the body of the wearer.

“The Haunted Mask” was the 11th book in the series and is among the most popular for adaptations into different media. In addition to being one of the few books to have a direct sequel (“The Haunted Mask II”), the masks made an appearance in the recent live-action movies, were an item found in the 2015 video game, and returned to the books over a decade later in “The Scream of the Haunted Mask.”

What tied them all together was Carly Beth Caldwell, the child who defeated them in the first entry of the saga back in 1993. Don’t be shocked if that name comes up once again in this new show!

Cuckoo clocks are a classic trope in horror, loud pendulous machinery that lulls the audience into a false sense of security, right on time for a jump scare leaping out of the furniture. In the 28th Goosebumps book, “The Cuckoo Clock of Doom,” flipped that cliché is flipped on its head by instead becoming a sinister time-travel device that could go years into the past, and even undo the existence of people.

In the trailer for the new series, James and Isiah were seen playing with the cursed camera, but the repercussions of that might not have been revealed. The following scene shows a cluster of those two characters in a cave, meaning those two might be involved in some time-altering dilemmas thanks to the clock.

Ana Yi Puig as Isabella from “The Cuckoo Clock of Doom”

The 21st Goosebumps book was a play on the 1973 classic kids’ book by Thomas Rockwell, “How to Eat Fried Worms.” The exception was that the main character in Stine’s version wasn’t paid $50 to devour the wriggling bugs, and instead “supernaturally” found their way into clothing and food.

While the true cause of this ruckus wasn’t actually revenge-seeking worms, the book ended with an enormous worm erupting from the ground, one of the more surreal third acts in the franchise. The trailer doesn’t show much in the way of insects, but get ready for some potential gross-outs if the show follows any scenes from the book, unless you don’t mind finding a half-bitten worm in your sandwich.

The fifth and seventh episodes of the new series aren’t named after a specific edition, but an entire sub-series in the Goosebumps literary universe. “Reader Beware” – besides being what R.L. Stine used to introduce some of the live-action ’90s shows – was the tagline for the “Give Yourself Goosebumps” imprint.

Totaling 50 volumes, these were interactive books that offered readers multiple ways to control the outcome of events. Imagine “Choose Your Own Adventure” books, but with titles like “Welcome to the Wicked Wax Museum,” “Escape from Camp Run-For-Your-Life,” and “Secret Agent Grandma.” A screenshot from this episode shows the kids enraptured with glossy, darkened eyes while listening to a mysterious figure read from a mysterious tome, so perhaps the teens will unwittingly be pulling the strings of some events unknown to them. Speaking of strings...

There can’t be anything made under the slimy Goosebumps umbrella without Slappy the Dummy making an appearance!

The sixth and ninth episodes of the 2023 TV series share titles, with the latter being Part 2 of this story. All of the “Night of the Living Dummy” books star Slappy, the de facto face of the Goosebumps franchise. He debuted in the seventh book of the series in 1993, and returned multiple times over the years to torment more hapless children, including the movies and the 90s TV series. Slappy was so popular that this malevolent ventriloquist’s dummy even had his own series of books, “SlappyWorld.”

Puppets can often be a scary thing for kids, and Stine admitted in his autobiography that this character originated from his own aversion to puppets, specifically Pinocchio. He later took back control of that fear by using his own dummy to scare his brother, a formative moment for Stine en route to writing horror books.

The 15th book in the original series, “You Can’t Scare Me” has one of my favorite Tim Jacobus covers, giving readers a sneak peek at the terrors lurking inside its pages. This one features the Mud Monsters, reanimated corpses of town residents from yesteryear who drowned in a flood in Greene Forest, and rise up once a year to seek revenge on those who refused to help.

There are no murky dirt zombies to be found in the trailer, so this one may be in name only, but I wouldn’t be disappointed if I saw these turbid golems rampaging in the woods once during the series.

The cast of high-school kids entranced in something sinister from the episode “Give Yourself Goosebumps”

The finale for the 2023 series brings us to another mainstay in the Goosebumps universe, HorrorLand!

This ghoulish theme park debuted in the sixteenth book in the series back in 1994 and is another popular part of the franchise. Run by the HorrorLand Horrors, sadistic monsters who can only be defeated by pinching them, this is far from the happiest place on earth. Their motto is “Where Nightmares Come to Life!” and features rides like The Coffin Cruise, Ferris Squeal, and Wheel of Misfortune.

Besides a direct sequel, this volume has been adapted over the years into a board game, comics, three different video games, a two-part episode in the 90’s show, and spun off into its own series that concluded by bringing notable characters from past books together to take on this haunted establishment. This marked the first serialized tale in Stine’s Goosebumps franchise, a fitting title to close out this new series, which also follows a single narrative amidst the disparate scary events these five high-schoolers contend with.

Earlier this May, a different R.L. Stine series, Just Beyond, was pulled from Disney+ along with many other shows and films during a period when many streaming platforms were culling their content. It seems like Disney is hedging their bets on this one, with a rollout that includes the first two episodes being shown as part of Freeform’s “31 Nights of Halloween” the same night it launches online. It’s possible the new Disney+ Goosebumps could be 2023’s version of Wednesday — a scary good time of destination TV with the right amount of nostalgia, ready to scare and entertain audiences of all ages.

This article was originally published on Oct. 9, 2023

#8140. The Best Back-to-School TV Episodes For Every Age

Timeless back-to-school episodes for kids, from toddlerhood through high school.

All good things must come to an end, or so the saying goes, and when you’re a kid that’s never more true than when late August rolls around and summer vacation draws to a close. Going back to school means an end to unscheduled days of fun in the sun, but it can also be the start of something good. The first day of school can be the first time a kid meets their new best friend, or it can kick off an important semester of learning and discovery. It can also be, well, not so good. Sometimes, back-to-school is hard.

This is why families sometimes turn to our greatest TV shows for guidance. TV isn’t the perfect teacher, but it can help families reflect on their own experiences in cathartic ways. Here are 10 of the best back-to-school episodes, an assortment that captures the highs and lows of stepping back into the classroom — or stepping into a new one for the first time. These episodes are listed here roughly in how young the target audience is for each. So, we’ll start with toddlers and end with high schoolers!

As one might expect from a series based on Mr. Rogers’ Neighborhood, “A Visit to School” showcases the same gentle understanding and straightforward communication the beloved children’s show host excelled at. If you’re feeling scared about doing something new — like going to the first day of school — talking it out and preparing for the new experience is a great way to feel more confident. It’s actionable advice.

These two Arthur episodes, from the very start and very end of the long-running PBS series, show how every back-to-school comes with its own challenges — and how all of them can be overcome. In the first episode, Arthur and Buster are nervous about their new third-grade teacher, Mr. Ratburn, until they learn he’s not actually scary at all. Then, 15 real years later, Arthur’s excited to be moving on to 4th grade, until he realizes his best friend Buster won’t be in his class anymore. But, that doesn’t mean that they’ll stop being friends.

The Disney Channel series Recess is focused on a group of elementary school friends, but not every member of “the gang” was in the first episode. It’s not until the second episode that Gus Griswald shows up at school. Recess has a great way of heightening normal playground politics and Gus’ struggle to escape the “new kid” label is one that anybody who has transferred schools probably empathizes with — and there’s a very happy ending. Not only does Gus get his actual name back and ditch the “new kid” moniker, but he also gets a group of fast friends.

The first episode of the Netflix kids' show Karma’s World has the titular character excited about her first day of middle school, only to initially be met with a bully who makes fun of her name Things end up all right, as she makes a friend and the bully eventually apologizes, and the episode offers a more representational take of the back-to-school story.

DJ Tanner’s first day of junior high does not go well, and not just because she’s accidentally dressed just like her teacher, which is just about the least cool thing you can do. She’s also feeling less developed than her classmates, and she only has one class with her friend Kimmy. But, “Back to School Blues” knows that a first day of school is always followed by a second day of school, and DJ (with some guidance for Danny) returns the next day with a good attitude and a little more age-appropriate outfit.

Cory and Shawn’s first day of school is exactly as melodramatic as you’d expect from Boy Meets World, but’s also a pretty heavy look at bullying and brotherly bonds, as Eric stands up for his younger bro even though the “cool” politics of having a younger sibling in the same school as you are fraught, at best. And, Boy Meets World gets to keep the sitcom status quo while also shaking things up with the reveal that Mr. Feely has been promoted to be the principal of their new school.

Most back-to-school episodes are focused, understandably, on the kids who are stepping back into the classroom. But, it’s a big day for parents, too, and this Season 5 episode of Modern Family focuses more on parents Phil and Gloria as they come to grips with the fact that Luke and Manny are growing up!

OK, chances are the average student doesn’t need to list “vampires” as one of their concerns on the first day of school. But, even if Buffy the Vampire Slayer’s premiere episode isn’t as relatable as some of the other entries on this list, it’s still a great back-to-school episode. Sometimes school sucks, and sometimes it sucks blood.

This article was originally published on July 24, 2023

#8138. Want Your Halloween Decor To Feel Like A Scary Movie? It’s All About the Lighting

My youngest child is obsessed with decorating our house for Halloween, to the point where we now have several boxes in the basement that contain life-sized plastic skeletons and scary clowns. And while I love making our house look festive around the holidays — from our every-expanding lawn graveyard in October to cozy accents and twinkly touches for a winter wonderland — each year I’m reminded that the homes with the most impressive displays are all about the lighting. You know what I’m talking about: they’re the ones your kids excitedly point to, eyes glazed over with awe-struck longing, and sigh, “Why can’t we do that?”

Well, now you can — and you don’t have to be a professional lighting tech (or even close!) to do it yourself. Govee teamed up with horror icon Sarah Michelle Gellar as part of its “Turn Up The Spooky. Slay Halloween” campaign, helping you to transform your home into a delightfully haunted house using colorful lighting and atmosphere — they even co-created a short film, Turn Up the Spooky, on the subject. The crux of Gellar’s advice? Don’t feel like you have to go overboard in order to have the most festive house on the block.

“Instead of covering every inch of the exterior in light, choose one architectural or landscape feature to be the focus, such as the roofline, a tree or the front facade,” Gellar advises. “Leaving some areas darker will make the lit areas feel more dramatic.”

That same focus on contrast and shadow comes to life in Last Light, an original short horror film made with Ryan Connolly, founder of the DIY filmmaking channel Film Riot. Featuring narration by Doug Jones, the acclaimed actor known for bringing some of Hollywood’s most unforgettable creatures to life, the film uses Govee outdoor lights to turn an ordinary home into a perfectly eerie movie set.

“Cinematic spookiness isn't about throwing up as many lights as possible,” Connolly shares. “With smart lighting, you don't need a film crew budget to give your home a high-end, haunted movie aesthetic.”

And here’s the best part: Film Riot doesn’t just show you the finished movie magic. In a companion how-to video, Connolly takes viewers behind the scenes of Last Light, breaking down the practical lighting tricks and creative techniques used to build its haunting atmosphere. From playing with color and contrast to using shadows for dramatic effect, the video offers inspiration for bringing a little Hollywood-style Halloween magic to your own front yard — no professional crew required.

Inspired to give your own home the Hollywood horror treatment? Both Gellar’s and Connolly’s techniques are surprisingly simple to recreate at home. Set the mood along your roofline with the brand’s Permanent Outdoor Lights Prism, add pops of color with the Outdoor Clear Bulb String Lights, and cast a dramatic wash across exterior walls with the Outdoor UpDown Wall Light.

For peak spooky, try placing a white sheet over the inside of a window and shining red light toward it from within, accenting the mood with glowing contrast lights under your roofline. Or pick a main lighting color scheme for the entire house, like jack-o-lantern orange, and use an accent color near the entryway, to make the whole display feel that much more dramatic.

Another pro tip: Don’t forget the shadows! Choose one decoration or part of the house to spotlight, then let the surrounding area stay dark. A single well-lit skeleton can somehow feel scarier than a whole yard of brightly lit ones. Don’t ask why — I don’t make the rules.

Govee’s smart outdoor lights can be adjusted with just a few taps through the Govee Home app, offering a huge library of preset scenes and colors, making it easy to experiment with effects until you find a look that works for your home’s unique style.

And the fun doesn’t have to end when Halloween is over. From festive holiday celebrations and backyard parties, to everyday outdoor ambiance, the same smart lighting setup can be customized for virtually any occasion — making it a stylish addition to your home all year round.

#8137. Why The First Animated 'Hobbit' Is Good For Your Kids

In 1977, the animated version of The Hobbit made a classic book even more powerful than ever.

Back on November 27, 1977, kids watching network TV were introduced to the “greatest adventure” of all time. Although the original Star Wars blew everyone’s minds that summer and forever altered the way we think about blockbuster movies, the Jules Bass and Arthur Rankin Jr. version of The Hobbit quietly pushed the most famous fantasy origin story of all into the mainstream. 45 years later, the impact of the animated Hobbit cannot be overstated.

Clocking at just 77 minutes (and apparently, not an hour and a half as many remember it), the animated version of The Hobbit from Rankin and Bass captures the breezy and jaunty quality of J.R.R. Tolkien’s 1937 children’s novel The Hobbit. Of course, even by 1977, The Hobbit had been retroactively relegated to “prequel” status, making it something of an underdog next to the sprawling, and mega-popular Lord of the Rings trilogy of novels, which had been published, originally from 1954 to 1955. Before this, in 1951, Tolkien had revised The Hobbit, to make it more closely aligned with the spirit of The Lord of the Rings, making the slightly more childish version of the book a historical memory.

Bilbo Baggins (Orson Bean) and Gollum (Theodore Isidore Gottlieb) in 'The Hobbit.'

However, the 1977 animated Hobbit, firmly took the world of Middle-earth and made the adventure for children. With their experiences on other animated kids’ specials like Frosty the Snowman, Rankin and Bass upped their game significantly for The Hobbit, mostly because they had amazing source material to work with. While hardcore Tolkien heads are very aware of the various songs throughout the book versions of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, for the casual viewer in 1977, the staggering amount of music in the animated Hobbit might have seemed weird. However, it was Jules Bass himself who adapted a good chunk of Tolkien’s lyrics directly from the book and then assisted composer Maury Laws, in making it all happen.

The famous Glenn Yarbrough-sung folksy ballad, “The Greatest Adventure,” was, in fact, the only song that was original to the movie, and not derived from the pages of The Hobbit. This single fact is the microcosm that demonstrates the overall brilliance of this version of The Hobbit; it’s both wildly faithful to the source material, but also morphs into a significantly separate adaptation. Just as Bilbo’s stories of his meeting with Gollum later turned out to be unreliable, the 1977 Hobbit succeeded in turning Tolkien’s book into a modern folk tale. Depending on who was retelling the story, the story could change. Before 1977, this hadn’t happened yet with The Hobbit, and other than Tolkien’s revisions, alternate versions of the story simply couldn’t exist.

As scholars and students of folk tales and fairy tales will tell you; what ensures that a story survives isn’t just the preservation of the text, but instead, the retellings of a story is what creates immortality. In the time before the printed word, this was accomplished through the oral tradition, but in the late 20th century, film adaptations began to do something similar.

With its unforgettable animation style, brilliant pacing, hilarious moments, excellent casting, and yes, whimsically endearing music, The Hobbit was the first of its kind: A new take on what had already been an instant classic in 1937. Like the film version of The Wizard of Oz, the 1977 Hobbit sublimated a wonderful kids’ book into a brilliant piece of modern animation. Today, we might think of the 1977 Hobbit as retro. But the reason why it was so important is that, when it comes to amazing fantasy adaptions, the future began right here.

You can rent The Hobbit on Amazon Prime Video right here. It is also included in Fatherly’s 100 Best Kids Movies Ever.

#8136. I Was Treated for Depression for Years. Nobody Asked About ADHD.

I wish I had been more curious to find deeper answers sooner.

I started taking antidepressants in my late teens. One didn’t seem to change much, so I tried another. I kept asking for help, taking the medications I was prescribed, and waiting for the point when everyday life would stop feeling like a group project I was somehow doing alone.

Some of those medications were incredibly difficult to come off of. And after all that effort, I was still exhausted. Still overwhelmed. Still wondering why things that looked ordinary from the outside took so much out of me.

I thought I was depressed. Anxiety seemed possible, too. Those explanations made sense with the information I had, so I kept trying to get better within them. When treatment didn’t change the parts of life I was struggling with, I didn’t think, Maybe there’s another question to ask. I thought, What the hell is wrong with me?

Then other people in my family were diagnosed with ADHD, and I began looking at my own history differently.

I want to be clear: A family diagnosis didn’t diagnose me. It made me curious. For the first time, I wondered whether what I’d understood as depression had been ADHD all along — or whether ADHD explained the difficulties that treatment had never touched.

The picture of ADHD I’d grown up with was a little boy who couldn’t sit still. I didn’t know to look for a woman who could appear to be holding it together while privately using every last bit of energy to do so.

A finished task looks like a finished task. You can’t see how long it took her to start it. An appointment she remembered looks like an appointment she remembered. You can’t see the reminders. A mom who gets everyone through the day looks like a mom who’s managing. You don’t necessarily see her sitting afterward, wondering why it took absolutely everything she had.

That invisible effort can become your normal. You assume everyone is working this hard behind the scenes. Then you blame yourself for needing so much effort in the first place.

I now host Chaos & Caffeine, an ADHD parenting podcast, and I’ve talked with ADHD specialist Dr. Jennifer Dall about ways ADHD can be missed in women. We discussed masking, burnout, emotional overwhelm, and the maddening experience of being unable to begin a task you genuinely want to do.

If you’ve never experienced that last one, I know how it sounds. Just do the thing. Thank you. Incredible idea. Why didn’t I think of that while spending half the day wanting to do the thing?

From the outside, difficulty getting started can look like laziness. Doing everything at the last minute can look like a bad habit. Being worn out after a day of keeping up can look like someone who needs to manage stress better. Over time, those judgments get inside your head. You stop describing what’s happening and start describing yourself as the problem.

Dr. Dall and I also talked about hormones. Puberty can make ADHD symptoms harder to manage or more noticeable. Later hormonal changes — during pregnancy, postpartum, perimenopause, and menopause — can affect how a woman experiences symptoms or how well her old coping strategies work. That conversation made me think about how young I was when I first sought help, and how much of my history I had never known to bring up.

I’m not saying every hard moment in my life was ADHD. Depression and anxiety are real, and they can exist alongside ADHD. Antidepressants help many people. I can’t go back and declare that everyone who treated me got it wrong.

But I can say this: I kept asking for help because something wasn’t getting better. I wish that had prompted more curiosity about what was still happening in my daily life.

If this sounds painfully familiar, please don’t use my story to diagnose yourself or stop taking medication. Some antidepressants need to be tapered with a prescriber’s help; I know firsthand that coming off certain ones can be hard. Instead, tell a qualified clinician what treatment hasn’t changed. Describe the tasks, the time management, the overwhelm, and the effort it takes to look fine. Talk about what you remember from childhood and whether ADHD runs in your family. Ask if a fuller evaluation makes sense.

You don’t have to walk into an appointment knowing the answer. You’re allowed to walk in saying, “Something still isn’t adding up.”

That’s what I wish someone had told me when I was younger. I wasn’t failing at getting better because I still needed help. I was trying to explain a struggle I didn’t yet have all the words for.

It took diagnoses in my family to make me ask a different question about myself. If another woman has spent years following a treatment plan and still quietly wondering why life feels so damn hard, I hope someone listens when she says it isn’t working. And then I hope they ask what else might be going on.

Danielle Kelly is the host of the ADHD parenting podcast Chaos & Caffeine, which reaches thousands of families each month and was recently named one of the Best Kids With ADHD Podcasts of 2026 by PodRanker.

When I redid my home office, I knew I wanted it to give Practical Magic energy. This gorgeous, gothic-glam rug anchors my entire vision for the space. The snake-and-floral design by Martyn Lawrence Bullard for Ruggable feels moody and luxe, and its machine-washable, stain-resistant fabric means it’ll hold up to my very real, not-always-luxe life as a busy working mom. I’m so obsessed with it. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

This adorable notebook lives on my desk year-round because it is exactly the kind of beautiful, nature-forward aesthetic I want surrounding me every single day. The illustrated mushroom cover is rich, detailed, and has that perfect witchy botanical vibe that feels equally at home in October as it does in March. The A5 size is ideal for a nightstand, a coffee table, or a desk without taking over the whole space; the paper quality is thick and lovely, and it is the kind of object that makes people pick it up and comment on it every time they see it. The Halloween decor that is really just gorgeous everyday stationery that happens to have a very good autumn energy! — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social

In fall, I'm obsessed with wearing witchy perfumes — and this year Granado has put out a pair of "gothic, fruity" scents that I am obsessed with. My favorite is their fig scent, which smells so beautifully of the deep, mossy woods and fall harvests of dark fruits. Along with the main fig note, it smells of rose, date, labdanum, and cedarwood. I want to bathe in it. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social

I very much treat books like art in my house, using them year-round to create little vignettes. So I could not resist adding a few “spooky” books to my library. A clothbound edition of Frankenstein featuring an anatomical heart pattern, stacked with Dracula, or a black-edged copy of The Haunting of Hill House? It’s moody, it’s witchy, it’s gorgeous... especially paired with a couple of antique candleholders or dark crystals. It definitely delivers the gothic library look I love. — Julie Sprankles

This particular Nautilus Puzzle has earned its place in my fall decor and activity rotation because it's just too pretty to put away. The Nautilus wooden puzzles are laser-cut with the most intricate, unexpected whimsy pieces hidden throughout that make the whole experience feel like discovering little surprises as you go, and the Japanese Bridge image is absolutely stunning in those deep greens and golds that feel made for autumn. The 237-piece count is the perfect weekend afternoon size where you feel genuinely accomplished when you finish without losing your mind over it, and the wooden pieces have a satisfying weight and quality that makes regular cardboard puzzles feel like a downgrade forever after. Fall cozy activity that doubles as a beautiful display piece while it is in progress! After I finish these, I put Mod Podge all over them and frame. — Katie Garrity

This is the perfect shade for witch nails — and honestly, I will not stop wearing this color even after spooky season is over. Love it on my toes, too! — Sarah Aswell

I mean, does this not look like something a witch would keep on an old wooden shelf next to her jars of dried herbs and tinctures? The amber glass vessel has that old-world apothecary vibe that looks so pretty lit or unlit, and the tobacco and patchouli scent makes my house smell so cozy and maybe just a little mysterious too. When it’s burned out, I’m going to clean out the jar and use it to hold matches on my mantel, which seems just as witchy and whimsical. — Julie Sprankles

I’m buying these for my daughter because Monica + Andy’s Halloween pajamas are exactly the kind of whimsical, quality set that feels special rather than just a cheap seasonal find. The organic cotton is incredibly soft, the prints are genuinely cute without being overwhelming, and the fit is generous enough that she can wear them through the whole season without growing out of them in three washes. The Halloween tradition starts the moment they go on and immediately becomes a non-negotiable part of the season! — Katie Garrity

I love these witchy candles! They come with crystals in the wax and a blend of essential oils, all chosen for a specific purpose. I love the Defense candle, which mixes smoky quartz and cedarwood, among other scents, to create a protective shield around you. So fun, and definitely fun year-round and not just around Halloween. — Sarah Aswell

These claw clips have full witchy fall energy. The Philocaly acrylic clips come in deep jewel tones, smoky neutrals, and rich autumn shades that look like they were designed specifically for the season, and the clear acrylic has a quality and weight that makes them feel like actual accessories rather than just functional hair tools. They hold an entire head of hair all day without snapping, slipping, or breaking, which means your messy bun stays exactly where you put it through every haunted hayride, apple picking adventure, and cozy bookstore visit on the fall agenda. — Katie Garrity

This is the most witch-coded leather jacket I have ever put upon my shoulders, and I am here for it! This is so fun and feminine while being just a little bit quirky, and I do not want to stop wearing it even after spooky season ends. I love wearing it with a belt or pairing it with the (also witchy) black satin skirt that Quince sells, too. — Sarah Aswell

I’m clearly a huge fan of decor that pulls double duty, like this beautiful little incense burner. The glossy black ceramic dish features a celestial star design, with a gold crescent moon right in the center to hold an incense stick. It’s also perfect as a tiny trinket dish for tossing your rings in at the end of the day! And at under $20, it (a) looks much pricier than it is and (b) is such an affordable dose of witchy charm. — Julie Sprankles

For the witchy fall vibes guide, this sweater is doing everything right — the oversized hooded zip-up silhouette is cozy and effortless in a way that reads as intentionally mysterious rather than just comfortable, and the rich fall colorways are exactly the kind of moody, autumnal palette that makes any outfit feel like it has an aesthetic. It is SO soft, has a relaxed fit, and the kind of piece you throw on over literally anything and immediately look like you have your whole fall wardrobe figured out. — Katie Garrity

This Kwendy collab is technically one of Magenta’s Halloween collections, but let me tell you — these mugs are way too pretty to retire on Nov. 1. The rich auburn color and shining gold wrap of celestial illustrations are meant to be enchanting and, well, I’m enchanted! Inspired by creator Wendy’s love of “mystical oddities” and “apothecary treasures,” it’s just the perfect vessel for my morning lattes and teas. I’m deeply unwell with obsession over this entire collection, tbh. The quality and artistry are stunning. — Julie Sprankles

I got a witchy bra set this month, thanks to Knix's new limited-edition A Court of Thorns & Roses collection, and I will not be taking it off year-round. Are you really living until you have a pair of period underwear with constellations on it? I need more reasons to look forward to my period. And YES, I got the matching boxers for my partner. — Sarah Aswell

I truly believe every room in the house deserves a bit of witchiness, and this pillow brings that to my living room. It’s black cotton velvet with gorgeous embroidery and a contrasting fringe border, so it reads as elevated gothic glam. I like that it works so well for Halloween, but then for the rest of the year it serves as a cheeky reminder that being a little bad can feel really good sometimes. — Julie Sprankles

I was looking for something to finish off all of my witchy looks, and then I found these: black pearl earrings that bring my spooky self to a perfect 10. There is something so beautiful and magical about a black pearl, and these earrings are understated but send a strong message of witchiness that is not surpassed. These are also responsibly sourced from Tahiti, so no danger of bad karma or curses. — Sarah Aswell

I currently have this lantern on my entry table, and I feel like it gives my foyer just the most delicious pop of fairy-tale forest energy. It’s etched black metal with intricate forest cutouts and a golden interior, so a lit candle inside casts flickering shadows and such a cozy glow. Oh, and there’s a bonus that brings me immense joy: When I blow out the candle, the smoke drifts up and out the top opening like a chimney in a storybook cottage. — Julie Sprankles

Every witch needs her potions, right? One of my favorite things about being a tea drinker is the ritual of it, and Dona’s tea concentrates genuinely make that ritual feel extra special: You mix the concentrate with milk, then heat it, steam it, or pour it over ice. This lineup (Masala Chai, Cardamom Rose, Turmeric) seems like it would be right at home in an apothecary! I like to sprinkle some spice on top of mine and then enjoy my oh-so-yummy latte out of an oversized mug. — Julie Sprankles

Launched just in time for Halloween, you cannot get more gothic and witchy than this perfume. The notes include cypress, black peppercorn, rose, saffron, Peru balsam, smoldering frankincense, leathered woods, and musk, and I can't wear it without feeling like I'm wearing a black floor-length gown and running through the woods toward an abandoned church. I will not stop wearing this on Nov. 1, no way. — Sarah Aswell

I’ve always thought pointed-toe shoes inherently feel a little witchy, so, naturally, I packed these perfect Rothy’s flats for my recent trip to Salem. The tortoise knit is a fun take on fall’s animal-print moment, and the roomy toe box and cushioned insole kept my feet happy while I wandered the witchiest streets in America. Safe to say I will be wearing these everywhere all year long. — Julie Sprankles

Still not sure how to make the whimsigoth style stick? We asked a practicing Witch, an interior designer, and an event strategist for their best advice on keeping the magic alive.
